en: The charge of tautology regarding the *bhūtādi* sūtra has been stated; however, that is indeed to be reconsidered. For, having established as a proven fact that the mantra "tāvānasya" refers to Brahman, the fact that the *jyotiḥ* passage does not refer to anything other than Brahman follows from the natural force of the pronoun *yat* which refers back to it, and this is the very subject matter of the first sūtra.

Regarding the doubt that such a statement may not have Brahman as its primary purport, there is not even the slightest room for the charge of redundancy, since the fact that the Gāyatrī passage also has Brahman as its purport—by virtue of its being composed of the "beings" (*bhūta*) and so forth—is precisely what is established by the sūtra *bhūtādipāda*. Furthermore, since the intended meaning of the passages in the venerable Bhāṣya is exceedingly clear, it is evident to anyone who has seen the Bhāṣya that to raise the objection of redundancy despite such clarity is based solely on delusion or malice, given the actual difference in the subject matter (*prameya*).

Furthermore, the argument beginning with "What more? Because it consists of four feet," etc., is also untenable. This is because speech and the rest are mentioned for the sake of another purpose and are therefore secondary, just like the elements (*bhūta*) and so forth. To explain: by means of praise—such as being the agent of singing and protection—according to the principle of *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) functioning as a reason, the statement "for all this has its foundation in her" is uttered regarding the Gāyatrī; this is done to establish her nature as the Self of all through a figurative attribution of identity, rather than to assert that she is the primary subject. Thus, such a distinction of statements is made regarding the Gāyatrī, as if they were of different levels of status, but not as a declaration of her primacy.

For this very reason, just as it is said, "That which is Gāyatrī is indeed this earth," it was not stated [in the previous section] that "That which is Gāyatrī is indeed this speech. Otherwise, he would have spoken in that same manner for the sake of consistency with the subsequent sections. However, the fact that the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as being identical to Gāyatrī was not specifically mentioned is of no consequence. As for the followers of Ānandatīrtha, they accept that the four aphorisms constitute a single topical section (*adhikaraṇa*), and cite the passage from the *Agni-sūkta* beginning with: "My ears fly open; my eye is this light placed within the heart."

They present either the statement from the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, "That light which shines beyond this heaven," as the illustrative example; or, having accepted a difference in the subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*), they explain that the statement from the *Agni-sūkta* mentioned previously is the example for the sūtra "Because of the mention of the feet" (*jyotiścaraṇābhidhānāt*), while the aforementioned *Chāndogya* statement is the example for the subsequent triad of sūtras. They state the connection [of these topics] by raising a doubt—based on the previous section—that the quality of being "hidden in the cave" might belong to something else, and by the objection raised against the *Nanda* section.

To explain: since this text establishes the concordance (*samanvaya*) here in Brahman of the term "light" (*jyotis*), which is well-known in the world as something else, there is a connection with the scripture. In the passage, "He who knows it hidden in the cave," it is stated that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is situated within the cave of the heart. That state of being situated in the cave is perceived in reference to a certain light in the verse: "My ears fly apart, my vision flies apart; this [world]... In that sentence, the meaning is: "My ears fly apart from the light; my vision also flies apart."

This light placed within the heart also exists in absolute contradiction to the ears and other [senses]. My mind, moreover, moves in extreme opposition [to this]. Therefore, with an uncomprehending intellect, what indeed shall I say? What shall I contemplate now? And if this [light] were anything other than Viṣṇu, then it would follow that the state of being composed of bliss (ānandamayatva) belongs to that [other entity] alone; thus it must be determined.

In this regard, the following must be considered: first of all, the connection [between the two passages] is untenable. This is because there is no recognition of identity between "being hidden in the cave" and "being placed in the heart," as they lack a uniform nature; moreover, this absence of identity is even more evident in the Chāndogya passage. On the contrary, by teaching the identity of the light within the person with the digestive fire (*jāṭharajyotis*) through the statement, "This light which is within the person," it is precisely the non-existence of such identity that is made known. Furthermore, although the Gāyatrī is heard in the phrase "that which is within the heart," in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since the Gāyatrī and the light are distinct, it is impossible for the former to imply the latter through the medium of the light.

Accepting that the four aphorisms constitute a single topical section (*ekādhikaraṇatva*), it is also incorrect to cite the passage from the aforementioned hymn to Agni as an illustration; for in that case, since there would be an absence of the distinctions consisting of the designation of meters, the mention of the elements, and the instruction on the quarters (*pāda*), the inconsistency with the aphorisms concerning the designation of meters and the elements would not arise.

As for the resolution stated in the *Candrikā*—that in response to the aforementioned objection, the light mentioned in the *Chāndogya* (in the passage "That which is placed within the heart of the light," from the *Āgneyī-sūkta*) is one and the same as the light in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, because it is recognized through the word "light" (*jyotis*) and the attribute of being situated in the heart ("this which is within the heart"), according to the principle of the section on different recensions (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa-nyāya*), and thus the cited Sūtra is not inconsistent—that is incorrect.

Because the light (*jyotis*) heard in the *Chāndogya* passage exists as abiding in a region transcending all things beyond the sky, whereas the light mentioned in the *Agni-sūkta* is situated within the heart; and because it is impossible to conceive of these two lights as one, this case does not fall under the principle of "different recensions" (*śākhāntara-nyāya*). Furthermore, since the *Agni-sūkta* describes [the light] as being far from the ears and other senses, while the *Chāndogya* states, "This is seen and heard," the identity of name for these two distinct lights—just as in the case of the *Māsa-agni-hotra* and the *Naiyamika-agni-hotra*—does not necessitate an identity of substance.

As for the objection raised—that the non-contradiction between those two [texts] is established through a difference in form—the resolution stated in the *Candrikā* is also incorrect. For if the identity of the two lights were already ascertained, one could postulate the possibility of non-contradiction based on a difference in form, and the establishment of that identity would depend upon such a postulation; thus, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

And as for what is stated in the *Candrikā*: "Nor should it be suspected that, because the *Agni-sūkta* in the prima facie view is devoted to Agni by the force of its name (*samākhyā*), while the *Chāndogya* passage is devoted to the *Gāyatrī* metre, there is no possibility of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) due to the lack of identity between their respective objects"—having raised this objection, [the text] replies: since it is heard in scripture that the *Gāyatrī* is of the nature of light in the statement, "Light indeed is Brahman-splendor, the *Gāyatrī*," the words "light" (*tejas*) and "Agni" do not have significantly different meanings; therefore, the word "Gāyatrī" may apply to Agni, or the word "Agni" may apply to the *Gāyatrī*.

The proposed resolution—that because the *Agni-sūkta* can, like the *Chāndogya*, refer to fire (just as the *Chāndogya* can, like the *Agni-sūkta*, refer to Gāyatrī), both passages share a single meaning and thus there is no possibility of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)—is indeed laughable. For even if one employs figurative designation (*gauṇa-vyapadeśa*) regarding Gāyatrī as the cause of the splendor of Brahman—just as one says "clarified butter is life"—the fact that this splendor does not actually possess the nature of fire means that the identity of the two passages cannot be established merely on that basis. Thus, their unity remains unproven.

Otherwise, just as one observes the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the words "fire" and "the word *gāyatrī*," the designation "the sacrificer is the *prastara*" would result in the identity of the sacrificer and the *prastara*, whereby the throwing of the *prastara* would have to be performed by the sacrificer himself using the *sūktavāka*.

Furthermore, it is not tenable to cite the Chāndogya passage as an illustration for the principle of unification based on the four sūtras; for in the Chāndogya passage there is no mention of "investigation" (vicāraṇā). Moreover, the identity between the Jyotis mentioned in the Agni-sūkta and that found in the Chāndogya—according to the manner already stated—is untenable. Finally, there is no reason to determine the meaning by means of a mark (liṅga) occurring in another passage while abandoning the numerous unique scriptural marks (śruti-liṅga) contained within one's own passage.

And as for what is stated in the *Candrikā*: "Although one might object that there are scriptural indications (*śruti-liṅga*) such as 'That which is indeed Brahman' located within its own context to show that the [light] mentioned in the *Chāndogya* is Brahman, nevertheless, by subverting those scriptural indications and hymns—which have scope—through the non-contingent (*niravakāśa*) Viṣṇu-indications situated within their respective hymns, the author of the Sūtras has stated the indication found in the *Agni-sūkta* in order to demonstrate the concordance (*samanvaya*) of all Vedāntas with Viṣṇu; thus, the light situated in the *Chāndogya* is Viṣṇu."

The claim that this is a sublation based on the meaning of the Sūtra—"because the movement of this very light is described in the Agni-sūkta"—is incorrect. This is because the sublation of a Śruti by an unconditioned Liṅga (indicative mark) is established by the logic of the *antarādhikaraṇa* and the *ākāśādhikaraṇa*. Since the two Śrutis bearing the name (*samākhyā*) are set aside by the Liṅga of "dwelling within the feet" and so forth—which is otherwise unaccountable—and since the status of the Agni-sūkta as referring to Brahman is established through its similarity to the logic of the *antarāditya-vidyā*, there is no need for a definitive determination [of the subject] by means of that [Agni-sūkta]; thus, the attempt to designate it [as Brahman] by way of that [sūkta] is futile.

Furthermore, although that light might be the Supreme Self on the strength of an unambiguous indicative mark (*liṅga*), the doubt that this light refers to something else remains unresolved by it, because of the force of the scriptural statement (*śruti*) regarding its identity with the internal fire (*jāṭharāgni*)—a claim supported by an unambiguous [textual] corroboration. Moreover, in this view, the sūtra "Because of the mention of the metre" (*chandobhidhānāt*) does not imply a reason consisting of the description of a specific ritual procedure; for there is no reason to establish the identity between the Agni-hymn that conveys that [meaning] and the Gāyatrī-vidyā.

Furthermore, how could the word *jyotis* (light) [denote Brahman] in that context? For, just as with the word *jyotis*, the word *gāyatrī* also has no other scope [for its primary meaning], and thus it cannot be established as referring to something else in contradiction [to that primary meaning]. Moreover, if the *śruti* (direct scriptural statement) were to override an unqualified *liṅga* (indicative mark), then the word *jyotis* itself would necessarily be overridden by it. This is because both are equal in their inability to tolerate being set aside by another means of proof (*anyathāsiddhi*). For this very reason, there is no implication of the probandum (*sādhyākṣepakatva*) either. Since the word *gāyatrī* is not mentioned in close proximity (*asamabhivyāhāra*) here, even if the *jyotis* in this instance were different from Brahman, it does not follow that the *jyotis* found in the *Agnisūkta* is different from Brahman. As for the impossibility of the identity of the two, that has already been stated; such is the direction of the argument.

The position that they have different substrata (*bhinnādhikaraṇapakṣa*) is, however, even more impossible. This is because the statement "because of the mention of meters" (*chandobhidhānāt*)—just as in the case of [the sūtras] "Not so, on account of the word 'modification' and the word 'this'" (*na vikāraśabdānneti cetaḥ*) and so forth—indicates a single substratum (*aikādhikaraṇya*). Furthermore, the claim that the section beginning with "because of the mention of meters" is intended for the determination of the word *gāyatrī* occurring in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* is also not its natural meaning; for if that were the case, it would simply have to be stated as "The *gāyatrī* is that, on account of its characteristic mark" (*gāyatrī talliṅgāt*). It has been declared that the light situated in the heart is Viṣṇu.

And that [light] is heard in the Chāndogya Śruti: "The light which is beyond this heaven. And that is recited as being the Gāyatrī. Since the word "Gāyatrī" is conventionally established (*ruḍha*) only for a meter, the objection that "the light residing in the heart is not Viṣṇu" is not a natural conclusion, because the arrangement [of the argument] is intended to determine the meaning of the word "Gāyatrī" by refuting such objections. Furthermore, even if the light mentioned in the Chāndogya were not Brahman due to its association with the word "Gāyatrī," there is no implication that the light in the Agni-sūkta is not Brahman.
Because it has already been stated that the identity of the two is impossible; and because the word "gāyatrī," which is not mentioned in the Agni-sūkta, cannot imply that [Agni].

As for what was stated in the *Candrikā*—the assumption that in both views of the same locus (*aikādhikaraṇya*), both sentences serve as examples; and likewise, that just as in the sentence found in the *Agni-sūkta*, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is supported by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) assisted by the context (*prakaraṇa*), so too in the *Chāndogya*, because of the opening "Gāyatrī is all this" and the conclusion "This is that four-footed, sixfold Gāyatrī," the section concerns Gāyatrī, and thus the prima facie view is supported by the scriptural statement regarding light (*jyotiḥ-śruti*) assisted by that context.

Because the reasoning of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is common [to both], and because in the *Agnisūkta* there is a mention of "feet" characterized by unsurpassed majesty—just as in the final conclusion (siddhānta)—and because in the *Chāndogya* as well there is a mention of "feet" in the form of unsurpassed majesty stating that "they do not surpass this," the two are treated as a single topic due to the commonality of the reasoning for the final conclusion.

Just as in the sections concerning the *āghāra* libation and the *agnihotra*, although there is a difference in the examples—namely "he performs the *āghāra*" and "he offers the *agnihotra*"—the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that these are not injunctions for sacrifice because they lack the form of a sacrifice characterized by a material substance (*dravya*) and a deity (*devatā*), and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that there is no such lack of form because the deity and so forth are obtained through the wording of the mantras and other means, are common to both cases; thus, they belong to a single section (*ekādhikaraṇatā*). Likewise, the justification for citing two separate sentences [as distinct examples] is also established. However, even that is not correct.

Since there is no mention of "vicaraṇa" (movement) regarding the *jyotis* mentioned in the *Chāndogya*, the argument presented as a proof for citing both passages—on the grounds that the reasoning for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is common even if the initial topic (*ādikaraṇa*) is one—is unestablished.

As for what was stated in the *Candrikā*: "Just as in the *Agni-sūkta*, [the statement] 'they do not surpass this' indicates unsurpassed majesty; thus, in the *Chāndogya* as well, there is indeed a mention of its 'vicaraṇa'"—that too is not correct.

Because the "wandering" (*vicaraṇa*) described in the *Agni-sūkta*—beginning with "My ears fly apart, my eye [flies apart]"—which consists of the upward movement of the ears and other senses beyond light in the form of a contradictory flight, cannot logically be designated by the same word as the "wandering" described in the *Chāndogya*—stated as "they do not exceed this"—which consists of not exceeding the *Gāyatrī* [meter]; for these two have mutually distinct essential natures. Furthermore, it is not appropriate to assume that the quality of possessing unsurpassed majesty, which is implied by those two passages, constitutes their primary denotation, when it is possible to adopt a more straightforward interpretation rather than resorting to a strained one.

Furthermore, if both statements were intended here as the subject matter, then—just as it was said "because of the mention of the *chandas* (metre)"—one ought to have said "because of the mention of Agni. There would thus be no reason for the omission of that mention. As for the statement in the *Candrikā* that "the word *chandas* is also indicative (*upalakṣaka*) of Agni," that is not correct; for even then, the two distinct modes of instruction (*upadeśabheda*) and the lack of explicit designation (*avyapadeśa*) would remain unaccounted for.

As for the statement in the *Candrikā* that "the argument of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), namely 'because of the difference in instruction,' and the argument of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), namely 'because of the feet beginning with the elements,' are unique to the Chāndogya passage alone," this is indeed unacceptable; for since it could have been stated in exactly the same way under the sūtra *chandobhidhānāt*, it would result in the futility of accepting [the principle of] "indication" (*upalakṣaṇatva*) there.

The analogy cited from the *Āghārāgnihotrādhikaraṇa* is likewise inappropriate. In that particular section, it is argued that sentences such as "He offers the Agnihotra" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*) and "He pours the Āghāra libation" (*āghāram āghārayati*) do not enjoin a ritual action (*karma*). This is because, since neither a material substance (*dravya*) nor a deity (*devatā*) is mentioned therein, there is an absence of the form of a sacrifice (*yajña*), which is characterized by both substance and deity.

However, regarding the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position that the *Agnihotra* statement is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the collection of rites enjoined by statements such as "one offers with milk" and "one offers with curd," and that the *Āghāra* statement is a restatement of the collection of rites enjoined by statements such as "one pours the *āghāra* straight" and "one pours the *āghāra* upwards"—[the reply is: it is not possible for the statement concerning curd and so forth to enjoin merely the quality of curd and so on. This is because, according to your view, since the *Agnihotra* statement does not enjoin an action, no substratum (*guṇin*) for that quality is established.

Nor is it possible for there to be an injunction of an action qualified by attributes such as curd, because that would result in an excessive complexity of injunctions (*vidhigaurava*). Therefore, only the sentence concerning the *agnihotra* and so forth is the injunction of the action; therein, the substance is obtained through the sentences concerning curd and the like, while the deity is established from the wording of the mantra used in the performance of the oblation (*homa*). Furthermore, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it has been stated that just as a common factor grasping both [the action and its accessories] is absent, so too in the present case, a factor common to the arguments of both the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion is unestablished.

As for what is stated in the *Candrikā*—namely, that the argument of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), "due to the difference in instruction," and the argument of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), "in the section on the elements and so forth" (*bhūtādipāda*), are unique to the Chāndogya passage alone; and that, in this regard, according to Bhaṭṭa’s view in the section on explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), one discussion concerns explanatory passages, mantras, and so forth in common, while another concerns explanatory passages exclusively—this illustration of a two-part discussion is also not tenable.

For according to the principle of *arthavāda*, words occurring in an *arthavāda* such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity," as well as words occurring in a mantra such as "Spread yourself wide," denote an existing fact independently of the words occurring in an injunction (*vidhi*), such as "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu," or the words occurring in an injunction such as "He spreads [the cake] on the sacrificial plate."

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument is as follows: "The words such as *vāyavya* occurring in injunctive sentences (*vidhivākya*) enjoin a qualified meaning independently of the words found in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). Thus, from the mantras and arthavādas, some historical narrative is understood—similar to those found in the Mahābhārata, Rāmāyaṇa, and so forth—but nothing that is to be performed [is understood]. Therefore, because there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), the mantras and arthavādas do not possess authority regarding Dharma. [To this, the siddhāntin replies: Even in the absence of syntactic unity at the level of individual words (*padaikavākyatva*), the injunctive sentence, in order to impel a person toward action...

Since *arthavādas* and mantras depend respectively upon the glorification of the matter to be enjoined (*vidheya*) and the manifestation of the deity, and since they—being embraced by the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*), which culminates in the comprehension of a fruitful meaning—depend upon a human purpose, they convey excellence (*prāśastya*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā). Thus, because of the syntactic connection between the two sentences—"Vāyu is his deity for this animal sacrifice, and since Vāyu, by his very nature, is swift-moving and bestows fruit quickly, therefore one should immolate this excellent *vāyavya* animal"—the *arthavādas* form a single syntactical unit with the injunctive sentence.

The authority of the Dharma [is established]. Likewise, the authority of the mantras is also established solely through their syntactic unity with injunctions (*vidhi*); this is one line of inquiry common to both mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). Since Vāyu bestows fruit very quickly, the injunction enjoins a person only by depending upon the reason stated in the explanatory passage, namely, "one should sacrifice an animal to Vāyu. Therefore, because it is dependent [on something else], its authority—which consists in being independent—would be lost; such is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). [In response: For dependence indeed means the communication of a matter already known through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If the intended inference in the *arthavāda* were: "The action under discussion must be performed because it possesses a fruit and has a deity as its agent, like the service of a king," then there would be invalidity characterized by dependence on another injunction (*vidhi*). But this is not the case. Rather, by the presentation of the fact that it possesses a fruit and a deity as its agent, the excellence (*prāśastya*) of the action is indicated. Since the conclusion of all *arthavāda* injunctions lies in the sense that "an excellent action must be performed," syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is thereby obtained; how then [could there be invalidity]?

The requirement of dependence on other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara-sāpekṣatva*) is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), while the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that an injunction is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is a different investigation, one common to all explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). In that regard, since the establishment of the specific mode of validity—namely, independence from other means of knowledge—effected by the second investigation depends upon the general establishment of validity effected by the first investigation, there is a mutual dependence between the two investigations; however, as in that case, there is no such mutual dependence between the two investigations here. As with that [case], here too, between the two investigations...

Furthermore, because there is an absence of both types of reasons—general and specific—and because the disparity [between the two views] is clear to those who know it. As for the structure of the first section (*adhikaraṇa*) according to the followers of Ānandatīrtha: the doubt is whether this light (*jyotis*) is Agni or Viṣṇu. Since this hymn (*sūkta*) is a hymn to Agni, the word "light" occurring therein refers to Agni. Nor should one suspect a sublation by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being situated in the cave, as in the phrase "that which is placed in the heart," for a *śruti* supported by the context cannot be sublated by a weaker *liṅga*. Furthermore, the *liṅga* is not without scope, just as the *śruti* is not.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is argued that because the indicative mark (*liṅga*) [of "hearing" and so forth] finds scope within the digestive fire (*jāṭhara-jātavedas*), the stated light (*jyotis*) is appropriately identified as fire, since the context (*prakaraṇa*) and the direct statement (*śruti*)—which are stronger than an indicative mark that has scope—are applicable here. In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, the context is sublated by the indicative mark of "hearing and so forth" which has no other scope; thus, the light is Viṣṇu alone, as the term "light" is established through both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) in the sense of Viṣṇu, just as in the case of the word "Mahāyogin. This is clearly explained in the *Candrikā* and other works of his school.

In this regard, the following should be considered: since it has been established in the two preceding sections that a Śruti text is sublated by an indicative mark (liṅga) that admits of no other application, a suspicion that the present passage has another purpose cannot arise here. Furthermore, because the context (prakaraṇa) is weaker than an indicative mark, a doubt of the aforementioned kind cannot be raised with its assistance; for it is established by the principle of *kaimutya* (how much more so) that a context is necessarily sublated by a powerful indicative mark due to the latter’s lack of alternative application. By this, the hypothesis stated in the *Candrikā*—that there might be a suspicion of the passage referring to Agni due to the proximity of the word "Agni" in the phrase "tvam agre"—is also refuted.

Since proximity (*sannidhāna*) is weaker than context (*prakaraṇa*), its sublation is established by the maxim of the "hard cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikā*). Furthermore, if the words *jyotis* and *agni* were intended to refer to a deity, their meaning would already be exhausted by the logic of the section on the "Inner Controller" (*antaradhikaraṇa*); if they were intended to refer to the elemental entity, their meaning would be exhausted by the logic of the section on "Ether and so forth" (*ākāśādyadhikaraṇa*), which is unavoidable. Nor is it correct to argue that there is a stronger doubt due to the favoring of the context; for if the Śruti refers to Viṣṇu, the context can also be shown to refer to Viṣṇu, making it impossible for it to refer to anything else.

Nor is it reasonable to imagine that the context has a different purport on the grounds of the conventional designation "Agni-sūkta" (Hymn to Agni) and so forth; for just as the designations "Akṣi-vidyā" (Knowledge of the Eye) and "Āditya-vidyā" (Knowledge of the Sun) are established merely by the presence of the words "eye" and "sun," and just as a verse dedicated to Gārhapatya is designated "Aindrī" (dedicated to Indra) merely by the presence of the word "Indra," so too the designation of a hymn dedicated to Viṣṇu as an "Agni-sūkta" is established merely by the presence of the word "Agni."

As for the argument in the *Candrikā* that supports the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by objecting according to the stated method—that the indicative mark (*liṅga*), which has scope elsewhere, can be set aside by the scriptural statement (*śruti*) regarding the gastric fire because it too has scope there—that too is incorrect. For, since being "placed in the heart" is not established in relation to the gastric fire, the indicative mark is actually without scope (*niravakāśa*). Furthermore, it is impossible to assume that the mark has scope elsewhere when such an assumption contradicts its well-known association with the gastric fire. Moreover, qualities such as being distant from the ears and so forth cannot possibly belong to the gastric fire.

However, that initial objection (pūrvapakṣa), even when covered by that [explanation], is indeed untenable according to our own system, because it is impossible to apply the introductory statement (ādikaraṇa) with the intention of a prima facie argument and a final conclusion (pūrvapakṣa-siddhānta).

As for what was stated in the *Candrikā*: "This is a hymn to Agni (*agnisūkta*), not a hymn to Viṣṇu (*viṣṇusūkta*). Because this [argument] is accompanied by the worldly convention—well-known among teachers—that it is a hymn to Agni and lacks the status of being a hymn to Viṣṇu, it obstructs the *śruti*, even though that [inferential mark] is otherwise without scope. Thus, the strength of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) based solely on its lack of scope is weaker than the strength of the *śruti* based on both its lack of scope and its accompaniment by the aforementioned worldly convention; consequently, the strength derived from the plurality of inferential marks is [also] weaker.

The argument that the Sūkta must refer to Agni because its strength is naturally inherent in its nature as a Śruti (Vedic revelation), and thus it is logically consistent for it to have that meaning, constitutes the presentation of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa). However, even that is not capable of withstanding scrutiny; for, as in the case of the conventional designations "Prāṇavidyā," "Akṣividya," or "Ādityavidyā," and as in the well-known application of the Aindrī mantra, a usage established by such means cannot—according to the aforementioned reasoning—be determinative of a specific meaning when that usage is otherwise accounted for.

For this very reason, although there is no difference in their having Viṣṇu as their sole object, the conventional usage—such as "this is the Puruṣasūkta, this is the Nārāyaṇasūkta; this is not the Puruṣasūkta, this is not the Nārāyaṇasūkta; this is the Viṣṇusūkta, this is not the Viṣṇusūkta"—is justified by the presence or absence of specific words [denoting those names]. Even though the absence of such specific words leads to the conventional designation of a text as not being a particular Sūkta, that absence cannot determine the lack of intent toward that deity; therefore, in the absence of such corroboration, the Vedic text itself lacks the capacity for superior authority.

The strength of the *liṅga* (indicative power), however, being based on its lack of any other scope (*niravakāśatva*), is entirely without exception; thus, when there is a sublater (*bādhaka*), the designation (*samākhyā*) such as the "Agni-sūkta" is not capable of being decisive here. Due to the strength derived from both its lack of scope and its multiplicity, even the strength resulting from the accompaniment of the *sūkta* and the status of being a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is not operative. Furthermore, the strength based on the status of being a *śruti* has already been refuted previously. Moreover, in the Chāndogya passage, no further doubt of the kind mentioned arises.

The objection raised by others—that the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises because the word "light" (*jyotis*) cannot apply to Brahman when it coexists with darkness, on the grounds that being the opposite of darkness is the basis for the application of the term "light"—is also not correct. This is because the status of being the opposite of darkness cannot be the basis for the application of the word "light," as this would contradict numerous usages such as "procreation is light," "the Virāṭ meter is light," and "the Trivṛt, Pañcadaśa, Saptadaśa, and Ekaviṃśa [stomas]—these indeed are the lights. Thus, there is no contradiction with such extensive applications.

Since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for the co-existence of darkness with Brahman—which consists of the splendor of the sun—the suitability of "being illuminative" alone as the ground for the application of the term *jyotis* is established. Or, even if one were to entertain the doubt that being opposed to darkness is somehow the ground for the application of the word *jyotis*, nevertheless, because that [opposition to darkness] is common to the sun and other luminaries, describing it as a support for the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the "mere light" (the sun) is entirely inconsistent; thus, the aforementioned prima facie argument is not tenable.
Since the prima facie argument itself is untenable, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) which refutes it is likewise untenable. Furthermore—
The remoteness of Karṇa and others from Viṣṇu does not indeed exist elsewhere;
however, the Śruti, Sūktas, and so forth concerning Agni find their scope in the Supreme Self.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the scriptural mention of "light" (*jyotis*) refers to Viṣṇu on the basis of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of being distant from the ears and so forth is not tenable; for that inferential mark is common to Śiva as well. Thus, in the *Atharvaśikhā*: "Then Pippalāda, Aṅgiras, and Sanatkumāra said to Atharvan: 'O Blessed One, what meditation (*dhyāna*) is to be employed first, and what is to be meditated upon? What is that meditation, who is the meditator (*dhyātṛ*), and what is the object of meditation (*dhyeya*)? Having thus introduced the inquiry concerning the nature of meditation, the meditator, and the object of meditation, he [the Lord]..."

To these [sages], Atharvan said: "The syllable *om* is employed at the beginning; this syllable 'dhyānam' (meditation) is that which is to be meditated upon. Having stated that the Supreme Brahman is the object of meditation following the *praṇava* (*om*), and having explained the pervasion of the *praṇava* by its three measures through the passage beginning with "Its four feet are the four Vedas," he declared: "Because it is employed at the beginning of meditation, because all the instruments [of action] are withdrawn therein, and because it is to be held (*dhāryam*) through concentration (*dhāraṇāt*), it is the fourth Brahman."

By this [passage], having presented the reason for the suitability as an object of meditation (*dhyeya*) of the Supreme Brahman—known as the *praṇava*, consisting of the fourth *mātrā* situated at the end, which transcends all operations of the senses—the text concludes with "One should meditate upon the Lord who is to be meditated upon. Since this establishes that Śiva alone is the essential nature of the object of meditation, there is no impairment of Śiva’s distance from the ears and other organs, even though He is the knower of all organs. This is the meaning in the aforementioned interrogative sentence—"to the Creator" being the understood remainder.

*Dhyānam*—that which is meditated upon is *dhyāna*, meaning the object of meditation, that which is to be meditated upon (*dhyāyitavyam*)—suitable for instruction to disciples, sons, and so forth; or else, suitable for meditation. This is the intended meaning here: what did the first-born Vighātu meditate upon as being fit for meditation, and what did he say to Bhava and the other sons? The remainder is clear in meaning.

And in the *Mantra-upaniṣad*, having introduced Śiva with the words, "When there was darkness, there was neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being; Śiva alone existed," and having stated by the phrase, "No one has grasped Him from above, nor from across, nor in the middle," that no one has ever grasped Him anywhere, and having declared, "He does not stand within the range of sight—such is His form," it is heard as the reason for that: "No one sees Him with the eye. In this context, "with the eye" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) [for the other senses as well].

No one knows him even by other senses; therefore, his form does not stand within the range of sight—“sight” here meaning right vision (*samyagdarśana*). Thus, the fact that Śiva is beyond the reach of the eyes, ears, and so forth is established by scripture and is indeed beyond dispute.

The statement in the *Candrikā* that "the state of having ears and other apertures" means nothing other than "having a majesty that cannot be delimited by such [measurements]" is indeed incorrect. This is because, by the verse "my ears fly wide open, my vision flies wide open," it is stated that the ears and other organs transcend light; thus, if its unsurpassed majesty were understood through that [verse], then—as was already pointed out during the refutation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—there would be a lack of propriety in the word "designation" (*abhidhāna*) in the phrase "because of the designation as feet" (*caraṇābhidhānāt*).

Furthermore, its commonality with Śiva has been established by demonstrating that even Viṣṇu and others are dependent upon Śiva, in the section concerning the internal organs such as the mind and their attributes. Moreover, the claim that the scriptural mention of "light" (jyotis) is primarily applicable to Viṣṇu alone on the basis of its conventional usage among the learned is not tenable; for just as there is the term "light" in the Nārāyaṇa section, so too in the Mantropaniṣad, the term "Iśāna" is seen to refer to Śiva in the passage, "The imperishable Iśāna is light. Thus, the conventional usage of that term is observed in Śiva as well.

The claim that "this is not a Viṣṇu-hymn" is merely a popular notion among reciters; however, this notion is rooted in ignorance, just as there is a popular notion that when the mantra *dhānyam asi dhinuhi*—which is employed in a sacrifice where meat is the oblation—must be modified to *māṃsam asi*, one should instead modify it to *mṛgo ’si*. As for the statement in the *Candrikā* that this popular notion arises simply because the word "Viṣṇu" and others are absent, that is not correct. It is improper to assume that a popular notion, which is corroborated by the consensus of many people, is based on ignorance. Furthermore, the example cited [in the *Candrikā*] is itself rooted in one's own delusion.

For it is agreed by those learned in logic that since the word *dhānya* denotes grain with its husk and is specified as the material substance for the sacrificial oblation in the form of the *puroḍāśa*, when meat is the oblation, it is proper to substitute the word *mṛga* (deer), which denotes the material substance of that [meat] oblation. Furthermore, as stated in the *Candrikā*: "Fire does not possess an unbounded majesty, because it is heard in scripture as having limited power—as in 'Agni is indeed the lowest among the gods'—as being fearful—as in 'From fear of him, Agni burns'—as being subject to avoidance—as in 'They do not die [from his heat]'—and as being subject to death and so forth—as in 'Lightning, lightning, the thunderbolt, the moon, the sun, and fire are Agni'."

As for the scriptural passages concerning "the foremost" (*agri*) and so forth—such as "By the foremost, the foremost is kindled," "The gods [know] him as the light of lights," "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light," "Viṣṇu alone is the light," "I am the fire, I am the oblation," and "That is the light of even the lights"—it has been stated that these find their scope in Viṣṇu according to such Śrutis and Smṛtis; the same should be understood regarding other hymns (*sūkta*) as well.

For instance: in the hymn to Indra, "No one born, O Indra, nor yet to be born, is thy equal"; likewise, "The ruler of this moving world, the beholder of heaven, the ruler, O Indra, of what stands still"; likewise, in the hymn to Bṛhaspati, "Thou art the progenitor of all sacred prayers (brahmaṇas)"; likewise, in the hymn to Sūrya, "Sūrya is the soul of the moving and the standing world"; and likewise, in the Viśvakarman hymn, "He who has eyes on every side, who is our father and progenitor"—such are the marks of Brahman found therein.

Furthermore, in the verse "O purifier, with that eye wherewith thou beholdest the active world of men, O Varuṇa," there is an invocation of the Sun by means of the words *pāvaka* (purifier) and *varuṇa*.

Likewise, in the hymn to Varuṇa, there is an address to Varuṇa using words such as "Āditya" and so forth, beginning with "Now we [worship] Āditya. Similarly, in the hymn to Agni, after addressing Agni with "Thou art Indra, the bull of the virtuous; thou art Viṣṇu, the wide-striding, worthy of homage," the use of words such as "Indra" and "Viṣṇu" is appropriate only if the aforementioned hymns refer to Brahman—the Reality denoted by the term *srava*—and not otherwise. Thus, it is stated that the purpose of this [section] is to establish the coordination (*samanvaya*) of all names occurring throughout the hymns.

This [interpretation] should be rejected because it is cumbersome to resort to the view that the word "etcetera" (ādi) in the terms *tatpakṣa* and *hetu* functions as an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), given the absence of such a word there. Furthermore, if the determination were made by the very light mentioned in the *Agnisūkta*, then the sūtra *jyotirdarśanāt* would result in a mere redundancy.

As for the argument in the *Candrikā*—that in the section on "Because of the perception of light" (*jyotirdarśanāt*), the objection that the marks such as "dying" suggest the light is the individual soul (*jīva*) is refuted by stating that these marks will be explained as being included within the opening and closing passages concerning Brahman through the use of causative (*ṇic*) forms, and thus there is no redundancy—that too must be rejected. For it is more appropriate to establish right here, by means of the "sandwich" (*saṃdaṃśa*) principle, that those marks such as "dying" are intended for another purpose (the glorification of the preceding subject) even with respect to Brahman.

As for the description of this as a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) based on the three sūtras beginning with "Because of the mention of the *chandas*": it is as follows—here, the application of the name "Gāyatrī," which is well-known elsewhere than in the Vedic context, is being established. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, starting from "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this," it is heard: "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven..."

In this regard, there arises a doubt: is *gāyatrī* a specific type of meter (*chandas*) or Viṣṇu? On account of the well-known usage of the term *gāyatrī* and because of the mention of its nature as speech in the statement, "Speech indeed is this *gāyatrī*," it must be a specific meter. Nor can this be set aside by the scriptural mention of "light" (*jyotis*), for it is impossible for one scriptural passage to sublate another scriptural passage. Furthermore, since the word *tejas* (splendor) is a synonym for "light," and because of the scriptural hearing, "The *gāyatrī* is indeed splendor," that [application of the term] is appropriate for the *gāyatrī* itself. Moreover, the word *gāyatrī* is not conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for Viṣṇu, as there is no evidence for such a usage. Any indicative mark (*liṅga*) would be sublated by conventional meaning.

Furthermore, the principle of "dependence upon that" (tadadhīnatva) does not apply here, because that which is in the form of the Veda is eternal. Thus, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that this light (*jyotis*) is also of that very nature, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is: Gāyatrī is indeed Viṣṇu. For it is thus—the meaning is that there is scriptural evidence (*darśana*). This is because the scripture hears of Gāyatrī as the agent of singing and protecting (*gāna-trāṇa-kartṛtva*), and because that [agency] cannot exist in a mere meter (*chandas*). Therefore, the light is also Viṣṇu alone. And its primacy is due to His dependence [upon Him]. Nor is there any contradiction with its eternity. [For it is said: "Intrinsic nature, the living being, karma, substance, time, scripture, and action..."
By whose grace these things exist, and by whose indifference they do not exist.

Thus, because it is heard that even eternal things depend upon Him, this is also determined by the designation of the quarters beginning with "the elements" (bhūta). Having restated the sixfold nature of the Gāyatrī in the words, "This is that very Gāyatrī, four-footed and sixfold," and having designated its four-footed nature, the mantra from the Puruṣasūkta is cited there for corroboration: "That has been declared by a Ṛg-verse: 'Of such extent is His greatness... Of this Puruṣa, the greatness is of the extent previously described; not only is it of such extent, but the Puruṣa is even greater than that aforementioned greatness.

How so? All beings constitute one foot of this [Brahman], while its three feet consisting of immortal essence abide in heaven. This would be the case if Gāyatrī and Jyotis (Light) were said to refer to one and the same entity. Nor should it be suspected that there is a contradiction between the statement "its three feet are the immortal in heaven" regarding Gāyatrī—since she is said to reside in heaven—and the statement regarding Jyotis that it is "beyond heaven," since it is beyond heaven; for such a difference in teaching is justified by the different perspectives regarding the three worlds or the seven worlds.

For instance—with reference to the three worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar—the realms of Śvetadvīpa, Anantāsana, and Vaikuṇṭha, situated above the intermediate space (antarikṣa) which rises one hundred thousand yojanas, are called "divi" (in heaven) because they possess luminosity; thus, the three forms residing therein are designated as being "in heaven."

Since Indra’s abode (*indrasadana*) is a heaven (*div*) in relation to the seven worlds, Vaikuṇṭha is beyond that heaven; since Meru is also a heaven, Anantāsana is beyond that heaven; since the solar orb (*sūryamaṇḍala*) is also a heaven, Śvetadvīpa is beyond that heaven; and since the triad of forms residing there is also a heaven, it is logical that [the Lord] is beyond that heaven as well. Therefore, even though there are two types of teachings, there is no contradiction, and thus in both cases it is the one and same reality called Viṣṇu that is being described. Consequently, the conclusion is that Gāyatrī is indeed Viṣṇu, and He alone is the light consisting of bliss (*jyotirānandamaya*).

In this regard, the following is considered: if the term *gāyatrī* is what must be connected here, then for what purpose is the citation of the *jyotis* passage in the Commentary? It cannot be for the purpose of raising an objection against the previous section (*adhikaraṇa*), because even if that objection were raised, it would not apply under the view that the *jyotis* passage is the subject matter of both sections; furthermore, under the position that the subject matter of the *Jyotiḥ-sūtra* is precisely the passage from the *Agni-sūkta* mentioned there, such an objection would not arise at all. And if no objection is raised, the inquiry would be futile.

Furthermore, since it was not previously stated that the word *gāyatrī* does not refer to Brahman, and because the doubt "Is it not so, on account of its being a designation of a metre? (*chando'bhidhānāt*) would not even arise [if that were true], this objection is invalid. Moreover, if—out of a desire to avoid this defect—it is intended that the very name "Light" (*jyotis*) found in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad is what should be connected [to the Sūtra], then there is the deficiency of not mentioning the name that ought to be connected. Furthermore, the objection that "the reason 'on account of its being a designation of a metre' (*chando'bhidhānāt*) merely establishes the opponent's own position" is also not appropriate.

As for the statement in the *Candrikā* that "the citation of the *Jyotiḥ* passage in relation to the subject matter of the *Gāyatrī* passage is for the purpose of demonstrating the objection against the *Jyotir-adhikaraṇa* in the *pūrvapakṣa*; and the citation of the *Gāyatrī* passage in relation to the subject matter of the *Jyotiḥ* passage is for the purpose of showing the seed of the *pūrvapakṣa* consisting of the word 'Gāyatrī' itself"—that is incorrect.

Because the discussion begins with the words "The Gāyatrī indeed," even though the light mentioned in the Chāndogya is a meter (*chandas*), there is no implication that the light mentioned in the Agni-sūkta—which has been established as Brahman due to its being far from the ears and so forth—is also a meter; thus, such an inquiry would be futile. If it is argued that this doubt arises precisely because the opponents have already asserted the identity of the two, we reply: no, for since the qualities of being far from the ears and so forth and those of being the seer and being heard are entirely non-contradictory, it has already been stated that there is no sublation of the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

As for what is stated in the *Candrikā*—having raised an objection against the previously mentioned view that the light (*jyotis*) is the *Gāyatrī*, and having argued that since the earth, which is described as non-different from the *Gāyatrī* in the passage "This indeed is she, this which is the earth," is said to be the locus of all beings in the statement "For on this [earth] all these beings are established," attributes such as being the cause of stability would also necessarily belong to that [earth], thereby making possible an objection to the *Janmādi-sūtra*; thus the fruitfulness of the inquiry is described—that is weak.

By stating merely that "all this" has some substrate as apprehended through perception, there is no implication of the eightfold agency (aṣṭakartṛtva) favored by you—consisting of being the cause of the birth, maintenance, and dissolution of the entire universe, both sentient and insentient—as declared in the Sūtra on "Birth and so forth" (Janmādy-asya yataḥ). Furthermore, even with that much, the purpose of the *Jyotiḥ* passage is not achieved.

By this, the claim made in the *Candrikā*—that the section concerning the "Self Consisting of Bliss" (*ānandamaya-adhikaraṇa*) implies the section concerning the "Light" (*jyotiḥ-adhikaraṇa*) even without invoking it, on the grounds that the Chāndogya passage "within the heart" mentions the Light as being situated in the heart which is a property of the Self Consisting of Bliss—is also refuted. This is because, as previously stated, there is no recognition [of identity] due to the difference between "being situated in the cave" (*guhā-nihitatva*) and "being situated in the heart" (*hṛdaya-nihitatva*), and because it has already been explained that the section concerning the "Self Consisting of Bliss" does not imply the other.

Furthermore, even though the Gāyatrī is a Vedic metre, the mere fact that it begins [the passage] does not establish that the light (jyotis) is a metre; for, upon hearing the word "atha" which marks a break in the context—as in "Now this light" (*athaiṣa jyotiḥ*) where the word "this" (*etad*) refers back to what has been previously mentioned—it is impossible for the word "which" (*yat*) in the phrase "The light beyond this heaven" (*yadataḥ paro divo jyotiḥ*) to likewise refer back to something already stated.

In our view, however, there is no fault; for by raising and then refuting the objection regarding a break in the context at the very point where [the Sūtra] says "because of the mention of the meters" (*chandobhidhānāt*), it is established that in the phrase "that which is beyond this" (*yadataḥ paraḥ*), the word *yat* refers precisely to what has been previously introduced, and not—as in the case of "Now this is the Jyotis" (*athaiṣa jyotiḥ*)—to something about to be introduced later. For this very reason, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the Gāyatrī is [Brahman] is also untenable.

Furthermore, since it was stated in the previous section that even by the mere mark (*liṅga*) of being distant from the ear and so forth—which has no other scope—the *śruti* concerning light, which does have other scope, is sublated; and since here, by the mark of having the earth as its feet—which has no other scope—conjoined with the *śruti* "That which is Brahman" (*yad vai tad brahma*), the sublation of the *śruti* concerning Gāyatrī is established by the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutika-nyāya*), the aforementioned prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) cannot arise.

As for what is stated in the *Candrikā*—namely, the description of the rise of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) based on an additional doubt: "Since there are other well-known names of the Lord (*bhagavannāman*) applicable to Viṣṇu, the word 'Gāyatrī' cannot refer to the Lord because the employment of words like 'Gāyatrī', which are well-known elsewhere [for the Vedic verse], would otherwise be purposeless"—that is incorrect. For this doubt is not specifically mentioned in the context of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "ether" (*ākāśa*) and so forth, and thus it cannot be resolved by that [specific mention]. Furthermore, a resolution of that doubt is not established within the Sūtra itself.

Because the arrangement [of the text] would result in the fault of stating "because of the mention of desire (*chanda*) and so forth in the Sūtra," the statement in the *Candrikā*—that this [objection] applies equally to terms such as "ether" (*ākāśa*), and that the citation of a further objection regarding the term "Gāyatrī" was intended to give rise to an additional doubt—is to be disregarded.

As for what was stated in the *Candrikā*: "It is appropriate that the light (*jyotis*) mentioned in the *Agni-sūkta* is Viṣṇu, because there is no difference in its designation. But here, although the light mentioned in the locative sentence 'from heaven' (*divaḥ*) may be Viṣṇu by virtue of the scriptural mention of 'light,' Gāyatrī—being situated in a sentence containing the contradictory locative designation 'in heaven' (*divi*)—is not Viṣṇu; therefore, there is another [reason] which is not common [to both]. This too is incorrect.

It is improper to assert that the absence of Viṣṇu’s supremacy in that context is caused by the fact that while supremacy established through recognition is obstructed by scriptural instruction, supremacy prompted by other causes is not so obstructed. This is because it has already been stated that there is no recognition here, since even in that case, there exists an instruction regarding distance from the ears and so forth—which contradicts the "seeing" and other qualities found in the Chāndogya passage. For this very reason, the argument beginning with "because of the use of the fifth case-ending" is also untenable.

This is because the designation in the fifth case (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*) is a powerful reason for [the passage] being about Viṣṇu; for just as its being about Viṣṇu in the case of *jyotis* is established by another reason—the mention of its feet—so too its being about Viṣṇu in the case of *gāyatrī* is possible through other reasons such as its being the Self of all (*sarvātmatva*). Therefore, the difference in instruction (*upadeśabheda*) does not constitute an obstacle there. For if *gāyatrī* were identical with *jyotis* on account of the introductory reference to *jyotis*, and if it were non-different from that, then its being about Viṣṇu could have been stated [directly]; however, since there is a difference in instruction, the doubt may arise that there is no such non-difference.

In this context, however, since the Gāyatrī is introduced at the outset, if a doubt were raised regarding the luminous being (*jyotis*) being a meter (*chandas*), then the statement concerning its difference in form would indeed be favorable to the conclusion that it is not a meter.

Now, one might object: "Since the Gāyatrī is Viṣṇu, the luminous being here must also be established as Viṣṇu; and that [identity] is supported by the introductory statement. This is not so. For once the primary concordance of the name "Gāyatrī" with Viṣṇu is established, there is no fault even if the name "Luminous Being" (*jyotis*) lacks such concordance. Indeed, it has been stated that if the luminous being here were different [from Viṣṇu], it would not follow that the luminous being mentioned in the preceding section is also different, because the reasons for their identity are distinct.

Furthermore, when there is no mention [of the opponent], it is not logical for a proponent who desires [to refute] to state an objection and its resolution; for this would result in the rejection of the stated meaning and lack of coherence. Since neither [party] would be established as the subject to be taught, it is logical to object to only one part [of the argument]. If that were the case, it would follow that one must explicitly name the person being objected to.

As for what is stated in the *Candrikā*—namely, the demonstration of a further objection that "this light is not Viṣṇu because of the difference in instruction regarding the perceived and heard qualities such as being distant from the ears and so forth, which are contrary [to Viṣṇu's nature] as found in the hymns concerning Agni; and therefore Gāyatrī also is not Viṣṇu"—that too is not valid, precisely by the same reasoning used to refute the previously mentioned objection, since even if the light were something other [than Viṣṇu], it would not contradict Gāyatrī’s being Viṣṇu.

As for what is stated in the *Candrikā*—namely, the presentation of an additional objection that while the contradiction of one *śruti* (the mention of fire) established elsewhere may be permissible, it is not proper to contradict the multiple words such as "Gāyatrī," "Speech" (*vāk*), and "Earth" which are established elsewhere—that too is entirely untenable. This is because in the *Antarā-dhikaraṇa*, we observe a contradiction by means of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) even when there is a multiplicity of *śruti*s; furthermore, in the present case, a multiplicity of *śruti*s is not established due to the absence of multiple *śruti*s concerning a single subject. Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Moreover, since the terms "Speech" and "Gāyatrī" are not synonyms, their sublation by an indicative mark is logical, just as in the case of terms such as "Prāṇa" and "Mātariśvan."

And as for what was stated in the *Candrikā*—namely, that in the *Antarādhikaraṇa*, the sublation of the well-known status of Indra and others established elsewhere is appropriately achieved by way of their lack of renown here—and that there is no such "way" (or means) here—that is not so; because in the present case as well, there exists a "way" consisting in [the Lord's] being the self of all beings and so forth.

As for what was stated in the *Candrikā*: "And this [is] based on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): it is logical that the non-creation of ether and so forth has been stated; for the nature of the produced elemental ether, such as its being a cavity (*vivara*), and the ground for the application of the word 'light' (*jyotis*), are dependent upon Īśvara, because they are produced together with the substratum (*dharmin*). However, since the Veda in the form of the *Gāyatrī* is beginningless, its nature—the ground for the application [of the word 'Veda'] such as being the agent of singing and protecting—is not dependent upon Īśvara. This presentation of a further objection is also not correct.

The eternity of the Veda does not consist in the eternality of its constituent phonemes or words, for that would entail the absurd consequence that even the poetry of poets and the like would be eternal. Rather, it consists in the eternality of the sequence [of sounds]. And since that sequence is brought about by utterance, how could it not be dependent upon the intellect of God? For even if the eternity consisting in beginninglessness were opposed to being produced—which consists in having a beginning—it is not opposed to dependence upon the intellect of God.

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is also not tenable; for in the preceding section, it was established that the *gāyatrī* scriptural passage can be sublated by the *jyotis* (light) scriptural passage because the latter has Brahman as its ultimate purport. Therefore, even Jayatīrtha’s statement in the *Tattvaprakāśikā*—that it is impossible for one scriptural passage to sublate another scriptural passage—is not correct, due to the distinction between what has been definitively determined and what has not. Nor is it sound to assume the intention that the *gāyatrī* scriptural passage possesses greater strength simply because it occurs in the opening context (*upakrama*).
For it is improper for your opponent, who maintains that the initial statement is stronger than the subsequent reasoning based on Brahman, to advance such a prima facie argument.

If it is argued: "But if Gāyatrī is not Viṣṇu, then in the passage 'Now that which is beyond this' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.7), the word 'light' (*jyotis*)—which stands in grammatical apposition with the pronoun 'that' (*yat*) in the correlative reference to what was previously indicated by 'that which is beyond this'—must also refer to Him; thus, light too would not be Viṣṇu. This is not so. For in the passage "Now this is light" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.7), the word 'this' (*etad*) refers back to the subject under discussion. However, because the word 'that' (*yat*) belongs to a different context due to the preceding particle 'now' (*atha*), it cannot refer back to the subject under discussion; rather, it is more appropriate for it to refer to that which is about to be introduced. Thus, the word 'light' does not refer to Viṣṇu there.

Furthermore, because that [word "light"] lacks the capacity for prior reference—unlike words such as "this" (idam) which possess multiple meanings—and because the feminine gender in the phrase "that which is light" (*yā jyotiḥ*) is appropriate only if it refers to the Gāyatrī; and since it was already stated previously that the statement "the Gāyatrī is indeed light" (*tejo vai gāyatrī*) is established otherwise—as in the case of "clarified butter is indeed life-force" (*āyur ghṛtam*) regarding the Gāyatrī which is the cause of spiritual luster and splendor—therefore, in the absence of any evidence to grasp a single subject for both the sentences concerning "light" and the Gāyatrī, the word "light" cannot be established as referring to the Vedic meter even if the word "Gāyatrī" does so.

Furthermore, even if one were to somehow assume a single coherent statement (*ekavākyatā*), since the conclusion has already been determined, the word *jyotis* would have to conform to the word *gāyatrī*; consequently, the word *brahman* itself would result in being the referent, and it would not be reasonable to assume that the words *jyotis* and *gāyatrī* refer to the meter. Thus, the literal meaning of the words in the Sūtra according to the Siddhāntin’s position is untenable. Moreover, if the ablative-ending term *ceto'rpaṇāt* and so forth functions as a provider of the reason (*hetu*), then it is natural and spontaneous for the phrase *tathā hi darśanam* to function as a provider of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

For it is improper to assume that the phrase "tathā hi" and so forth serves to provide a reason (*hetu*), and likewise improper to assume that "cetorpaṇa" and so forth serves to state a purpose (*prayojana*). Furthermore, the word *tathā* is well-known to denote similarity; by that, the contemplation of similarity alone is understood as the natural meaning. Indeed, the indivisible particle *tathā hi* is naturally inclined toward a formal proposition (*pratijñā*) for the justification of what has been stated. However, it lacks such natural fitness when applied to the meaning you have proposed. Moreover, the lack of connection with the two subsequent sūtras has already been stated.

There is not a single word in the Sūtra that supports the impossibility of dependence (*tādadhīnya*) as presented in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). Furthermore, a conclusion established outside the Sūtra (*utsūtra-siddhānta*) is improper. For this very reason, just as [the Sūtra] says "prāṇa" and so forth, indicating the refutation of that [dependence] through an extended application (*atideśa*), it is not proper [to claim such a refutation] here because there is no such extended application.
As for what is stated in the *Candrikā*:
"Just as beginningless qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth are dependent upon their substrates (*guṇin*)," etc.
Likewise, let the dependence upon the Lord exist for the sake of the security of the beginningless scripture.

Just as in the Vaiśeṣika system, even though the dimensions of space and so forth are beginningless and eternal, they are dependent upon their substrata, such as space; just as in the Advaita system, the beginningless relation between the Self and ignorance, as well as the non-distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, are dependent upon the ignorance and other factors of the related entities; or just as in the Prābhākara system, liberation—which is the beginningless prior non-existence of suffering—is dependent upon knowledge; or as in another system, the beginningless prior non-existence of demerit is dependent upon the non-performance of prohibited acts; so too [is this case].

The argument that, although there is no origination of the *gāyatrī* nor of the basis for the application of its name (*pravṛttinimitta*), its dependence on Viṣṇu remains established, is not correct. For, when the doubt arises as to how the quality residing in the *gāyatrī*—namely, its being the agent of singing and protecting (*gāna-trāṇa*)—can be dependent on the Brahman which is not its substrate, this objection is not resolved by merely establishing the dependence of qualities upon their own substrates. Indeed, if the eternal *gāyatrī* and its inherent nature were dependent on another, examples such as the ether (*ākāśa*) or the sky would not be applicable.

The same applies here because of the absence of the relationship between quality and qualified (*guṇa-guṇibhāva*). For eternal substances such as space (*ākāśa*) and the like are perceived as being self-contained and independent; therefore, their commonality [with other examples] does not make dependence the necessary determinant. Even among non-eternal things, neither the state of being a producer nor the state of being supported is the regulator of dependence, since we frequently observe dependence upon those who do not produce or nourish [the dependent]. If that [dependence] is accepted on the authority of scripture (*śruti*), then that alone should be stated [as the reason]; it should not be based on the existence of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

The prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of suffering does not depend upon knowledge; rather, it consists merely in being an obstacle to the production of its counter-positive, which is the destroyer of that prior non-existence. It is by virtue of this alone that there is the mere conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of [knowledge] having that [non-existence] as its purpose. Similarly, even in the Advaita system, the relationship with beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), the non-distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, and so forth, are merely conventionally designated as "dependent on ignorance" because they possess the property of being counter-positives whose destruction is dependent upon the destruction of ignorance.

Even the prior non-existence of evil depends upon the non-performance of prohibited acts, precisely because of the absence of the performance of prohibited acts—which are the causes for the production of evil. However, it is not the case that the Supreme Self possesses instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) with respect to the nature of the Gāyatrī or its status as the agent of singing and protecting; thus, the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is indeed inappropriate. Furthermore, let there be dependence on the Lord even for the beginningless Veda known as the Gāyatrī, or let there not be; what would follow from that? Nor does the fact that the Gāyatrī is dependent on Him imply that Brahman is denoted by the word "Gāyatrī."

However, because the ground for the application of that term (*tatpada*) depends upon that [dependence], it is established even now. For although a servant depends on a king, one does not observe that the specific qualities inherent in the servant likewise depend on him; thus, in reality, dependence itself is not the determinant for the dependence of those specific qualities.

Even though it is observed that the grounds for the application of terms such as "lamp" (to its light) are dependent upon oil and the like, we do not observe that oil and the like are themselves denoted by the word "lamp"; thus, although the grounds for the application of a term may be dependent on something else, that thing does not itself necessitate the use of that term. Therefore, the four sūtras constitute a single topical section (*aikādhikaraṇya*). In this context, the subject matter is precisely the passage from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad; therein, it is to be established that the word "light" (*jyotis*) refers to the Supreme Self.

In this context, the very mention of the feet as being "anointed with the color of the mantra" is the reason [for the identity of Brahman]. Regarding that, there may be a suspicion of non-establishment (*asiddhi*) because of the mention of *chandas* (Vedic meters). In response to that, by indicating the impossibility of the actual feet existing within those *chandas*, and by indicating that the mention of *chandas* is established through another means, the support is provided by the designation of "feet" such as "beings" (*bhūta*) and so forth even in that case. Furthermore, the removal of the suspicion of non-establishment caused by the difference in instruction is precisely the sequence shown by our commentator; this alone is logical. || 27 ||
May this work by Raghunātha, which refutes the views of others, serve as an ornament for the lotus feet of Śrīmacchaṅkara in his discernment of the system of Light (Jyotiḥ).
Thus ends the section concerning the light.
Now begins the first quarter of the second chapter.
Now begins the section concerning Smṛti.

It is indeed reasonable that only the scriptures of Kapila and others—who were adversaries of the non-dualists such as Manu and others—should be sublated; this is for the purpose of refuting the teachers who raise objections against the easily expounded explanations [of our own system].
May this certain composition, skillfully fashioned with effort by the simple-minded student of Rāghavācārya Sūri, serve as a source of celebration for the assembly of the learned.
If it is argued that this leads to the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis, we say no, because that would lead to the fault of leaving no room for other [Smṛtis]. ||9||

In the preceding chapter, it was established in detail that the Vedāntas have as their purport such a Brahman—non-dual and non-distinct from the inner self—which is characterized by being the material cause, the agent, and so forth, of the world; thus, the status of the Vedāntas as having such Brahman as their purport was demonstrated. That [purport] is now challenged here by raising objections based on contradictions with Smṛti and other sources, and is then vindicated in this chapter; therefore, the relationship between these two chapters is one of subject and object (the former being the subject of the latter). For this very reason, this chapter follows immediately after the first, and its possession of a fruit [is established].

Because it is impossible to effect either the non-implication of attachment or its avoidance without a thorough knowledge of the objects [of cognition], the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvavādī) intends here to challenge the consistency [of the Sāṃkhya system] by pointing out sublaters (bādhaka), whether directly or indirectly. Among these, since a sublater that functions indirectly is more delayed in its operation than a direct sublater, the contradiction with Smṛti and Reasoning—which is a direct sublater of the opponent's own position—was refuted first in the first chapter (prathama-pāda).

Furthermore, regarding the Sūtra *itareṣāṃ cānupalabdheḥ* (and because others are not perceived), since there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishing the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*) and so forth, the memory concerning them is shown to be rootless. By demonstrating that, like the memory of effects, the memory of causes lacks authority due to its similarity in nature, the objection that the contingency of leaving no room for Smṛti would be a refutation was countered by treating it as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*). However, since that desired conclusion is untenable—because the rootlessness [of Smṛti] is not established given that it is rooted in faultless means of valid cognition such as the inferences to be stated later—the contingency of leaving no room for Smṛti remains a valid refutation. Thus, the objection of "leaving no room for Smṛti" (*smṛty-anavakāśa*) is raised once again.

The second [section] is refuted by establishing the fallaciousness of such inferences and so forth that contradict one's own position, through the aforementioned sequence. By this, the objection raised by the author of the *Candrikā*—namely, that because the third and fourth [sections], like the first, consist in the removal of obstacles to one's own position, they should follow immediately after it; whereas the second, consisting in the refutation of the opponent’s position, should be final—is thereby rejected.

When there is a doubt regarding the impossibility of the contingency that memory would have no scope—on the grounds that memory is rooted in inference and other such means—one cannot reach a conclusion regarding the non-contradiction of the memory under discussion without establishing the fallacious nature of those very inferences and other means that are claimed to be its source; therefore, it is necessary to establish that [fallaciousness] precisely at this second stage. If it is argued that, in this way, the demonstration of the fallaciousness of the opponent’s accepted foundational authority should have been performed even before the sūtra "na vilakṣaṇatvāt," [the response is as follows].

On this point, those who know the intended meaning [of the scriptures] maintain that when there is a conflict with *smṛti*, the lack of authority of *smṛti* must be accepted by all proponents of Vedic authority according to the maxim "but in case of conflict, it is not to be relied upon" (*virodhe tvanapekṣam*). Therefore, once the Vedāntas' orientation toward the meaning favored by the Vedāntins has been refuted by relying on arguments such as "having different characteristics" (*vilakṣaṇatva*), it is impossible for the Tantra to possess authority. Consequently, it can only be suspected—on the basis of conflict with *smṛti*—that the Vedāntas do not have Brahman as their ultimate subject matter, and not otherwise.

This is because it is more appropriate to first refute the arguments—such as the "distinctness from Brahman" (*vilakṣaṇatva*)—which directly contradict the doctrine of *brahmādvaita* by means of the subverting proofs (*bādhaka*) stated in the first Sūtra. As for the third and fourth [Sūtras], since there is a mutual contradiction among the Śrutis concerning the elements (*bhūta*) and their products (*bhautika*), and since factors such as being one of two mutually contradictory statements or being accepted by great men cannot serve as grounds for authority, and because no other ground for authority can be satisfactorily stated regarding the Veda; [the author proceeds accordingly].

The distinction between the sections (pādas) is as follows: by the method that for those Vedānta passages devoid of the properties that constitute the grounds for validity, the aforementioned "harmonious consistency" (samanvaya)—characterized by having no other referent than Brahman—is not possible, there is a refutation of scriptural contradictions that are indirectly opposed to the doctrine of Brahman.

These distinctions regarding the feet [of the Vedas] and their adjuncts have been briefly shown by the venerable Bhagavatpāda in the *Śrīmad-bhāṣya*. Now, the second chapter is commenced for the purpose of establishing the following points: the removal of contradictions with Smṛti and reasoning (nyāya) in our own position; the fact that the doctrines concerning Pradhāna and so forth are merely bolstered by fallacious reasoning (nyāyābhāsa); and the consistency of the process of creation and other topics in every Vedānta text.

The distinction between the conditions of the third and fourth quarters has also been demonstrated by those very [commentators]: "The contradiction regarding the functioning [of the Self] with respect to objects such as space was resolved by the third [quarter]; now, in the fourth, the contradiction regarding objects such as the vital breaths is being resolved."
