As for what is stated in the *Candrikā*: "Others, however, declare the purport of the quarters [of the second chapter] as follows: in the first quarter, the removal of contradictions with the Smṛtis of the Sāṃkhya and others, as well as the arguments inferred from them, regarding one's own position; in the second, the statement of the defects in the doctrines of the Sāṃkhya and others; in the third, the removal of mutual contradictions among the Śrutis concerning the five great elements in its former part and the Śrutis concerning the individual soul (*jīva*) in its latter part; and in the fourth quarter, the removal of mutual contradictions among the Śrutis concerning the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*)."

Having restated the distinction based on the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the [four] quarters as explained in the *Nirukta*, [the author says]: "In that regard, because there is no single adjunct in the first and third quarters; and even in the first, because the others are not perceived. By this, Yoga is refuted, as well as [the systems] due to the defects in their own positions. Furthermore, since you yourself have accepted the statement in passages such as, "By this, the remaining unaccepted [systems] are also explained," which declares the defects of other doctrines, [your objection is invalid]. If you argue that the statement regarding their defects in the first [quarter] is for the purpose of removing contradictions with your own position through them, we say no; for that same purpose is served by the statement in the second [quarter] as well.

Otherwise, there would be an inconsistency in the second [pāda] regarding the superimposition (adhyāsa) due to its lack of contradiction. Furthermore, just as in the first pāda, in the passage "But it is seen" (*dṛśyate tu*), there is a removal of the contradiction with reasoning (*tarkavirodha*) in our own position, which establishes the meaning that there exists a cause-and-effect relationship even between two dissimilar things, such as Brahman and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), like a scorpion and cow-dung.

Likewise, in the second case as well—referring to the Sūtra "as the large and the long"—just as a triad (tryaṇuka) arises from a dyad (dvyaṇuka) which is both minute and short, yet is neither minute nor short itself, so too the insentient world will be born from the sentient Brahman; since you have stated this, the refutation of the contradiction with reasoning exists there as well.

Even in the first part of the third chapter, regarding the passage "In between [arise] consciousness and mind," since you have already stated that there is no contradiction with such scriptural texts concerning the vital breath (*prāṇa*), mind (*manas*), and so forth—as in "From this [Self] are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs"—it follows that there is no fixed rule that there must be no contradiction with the scriptural texts on the elements (*bhūta*). If it is argued: "But since the scripture says, 'O gentle one, the mind consists of food (*annamaya*), the vital breath consists of water (*āpomaya*), and speech consists of fire (*tejomayī*),' the mind and the rest are indeed the elements themselves; therefore, the investigation into them is simply an investigation into the elements."

In that case, a similar discussion regarding the vital breath (*prāṇa*) would also have occurred in the fourth book; furthermore, since the vital breath is specified as having "seven courses," the investigation of the sense organs—which was conducted in numerous sections such as "And they are minute" (*aṇavaśca*)—would likewise have been placed in the first part of the third book. Moreover, in the fourth book, under the section "The fashioning of names and forms" (*saṃjñāmūrtikalpti*), you yourself have established the conclusion that in the passage "by this living self" (*anena jīvena*), agency does not belong to the individual soul (*jīva*), but rather to Brahman; therefore, there is no fixed rule that the investigation must concern only the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*).

Furthermore, since the third and fourth [chapters], like the first, consist in the refutation of objections against one's own position (*svapakṣa*), they would follow immediately after the [first] chapter on *ādhāna* (the establishment of the system). However, because the second [chapter] consists in the refutation of the positions of others (*parapakṣa*), it was stated that it should come last—this is the objection raised. To this, it is replied: as for what was said—that in the first and third chapters there is no single common limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)—that is incorrect. For the removal of direct subverters of one's own position is indeed the consistent adjunct (*anugata upādhi*) of the first chapter.

In the commentary introducing the first pāda, which states "the removal of contradictions with Smṛti and Nyāya regarding our own position," the mention of Smṛti and Nyāya as two distinct categories is intended to reveal the reason for prioritizing the resolution of contradictions with Smṛti. This is done by indicating that, although both might directly contradict our own position, Smṛti—being equal to the Veda due to its being composed by omniscient authors and accepted by great men—is more authoritative when considering the underlying reasoning. The status of being more authoritative is established because it is mentioned first in the *dvandva* compound.

According to the rule that "that which is more venerable comes first," even though the contradiction between the preceding and succeeding portions of the third pāda regarding the scriptural texts on the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the luminaries (*dīpta*) has been resolved in this manner, the defining characteristic (*upādhi*) of that pāda remains consistent as the resolution of scriptural texts concerning that which is other than the elemental. Furthermore, this is because your own followers, the Jayatīrthas, have also demonstrated that the defining characteristic of the third pāda consists precisely in its having as its subject matter that which is other than the self (*ātman*).

As for the statement, "Because [the existence] of others is not perceived," and so forth—that should be considered, as it refutes a point we do not intend to deny. For in the phrase "because others are not perceived," what is intended is merely the description of the lack of foundation for the memory of causes, just as there is a lack of foundation for the memory of effects; it is not intended to be a description of the fallibility of inference and other means of knowledge which are held to be rooted in memory.

For this very reason, at the end of the first pāda, the venerable teacher, being about to commence the section primarily concerned with the refutation of opposing views (*parapakṣaniṣedha*), concludes the section primarily concerned with the acceptance of his own position (*svapakṣaparigraha*). Likewise, in the *Yogādhikaraṇa* as well, he has removed the contradiction with the Smṛti of Yoga as a sublation of his own position; however, he has not demonstrated the fallacious nature of the inference and other arguments favored by that school.

Regarding the phrase "and because of the defects in one's own position," the intention described in the Bhāṣya is that since the refutations opposing the doctrine of Brahman propounded by others are common to the opponent's own position as well, the opponents themselves must admit that those [refutations] do not constitute valid refutations; it does not, however, mean that the doctrines of the opponents are inherently defective.

By this [explanation], in the case of the sūtra *śiṣṭāparigrahāḥ* as well, only the refutation of the arguments put forward by the Vaiśeṣikas and others—which are in direct contradiction to the doctrine of Brahman—is accomplished; however, the defects of the inferences they claim are based on their own Smṛtis are not described here. Therefore, these sūtras do not find a connection with the second pāda, which is devoted to the removal of indirect (paramparayā) sublation.

Even the argument beginning with "just as the first foot [of a verse]" and so forth is not valid. For when it is argued by one who maintains the doctrine that "the qualities of the cause produce qualities of their own kind in the effects"—given the acceptance that the world is an effect of the conscious Brahman—that the world would consequently possess consciousness, you might respond: "If you accept that all qualities of a cause invariably produce qualities of their own kind in the effect, then there is a contradiction within your own position; for you yourself admit that from two minute (hrasva) and spherical (parimaṇḍala) atoms, large (mahat) and long (dīrgha) compounds are produced, despite the fact that sphericity and the like [do not produce these]."

Because the quality of the cause produces a quality in its effect that belongs to its own genus, the removal of objections against one’s own position is intended precisely by way of refuting the opposing position in the sūtra "mahaddīrghavadvā" (or like the large and the long); thus, since that sūtra possesses the dual character of both removing objections against one's own position and refuting the opposing position, it is appropriate for it to be included in the second chapter, which is devoted to the refutation of opposing positions.

Nor should it be suspected that, since the Sūtra possesses this dual character, there is no reason for abandoning its placement in the first pāda—which serves to remove the objections against one's own position that arise first—by instead placing it in the second pāda. This is because the removal of the objections against one's own position as accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas is accomplished independently in the first pāda, and since the refutation of their doctrine is introduced independently in the second pāda, its placement therein is logically appropriate.

Regarding the commentary which introduces [the discussion] with the words, "Even in your view, the attainment of the status of an enjoyer [would follow]" (*tvadmate’pi bhoktrāpatteḥ*), and then states: "Now, the establishment of a difference between the liberated soul and the Lord is irrelevant to the chapter on results; therefore, that is certainly not the meaning of this Sūtra," and so forth—[this is said] because even though it concerns the result, it is included here under the heading of "contradiction by reasoning" (*yuktivirodha*). Thus, although this Sūtra is relevant to the chapter on results, there is no lack of consistency here [in its inclusion], for it is included under "contradiction by reasoning" according to the manner stated above. This is why one should not assume a different purpose [for the Sūtra].

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that what is included within both [categories] would not be mentioned even in one of them; thus, because the acceptance of such an inclusion in one place renders this criticism a mere beating of one's own head.

The statement beginning with "also in the first part of the third [chapter]" and so forth is merely a deception for those who have not seen the Bhāṣya, and is therefore entirely false. For when it was established in the sūtra "In between, the intellect" (*antarā vijñānamanasī*) that the origination and dissolution of the self and the elements occur through the direct and reverse orders respectively, the *Ātharvaṇa* [text] enumerates the organs in the interval between the elements and the self, starting with "From this, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is born," and so on. Thus, if one were to search for a different order of their origination and dissolution, there would be a contradiction with the stated order; therefore, [the phrase] "in between" (*antarā*).

If it is argued that "consciousness and the mind [arise] in succession because of their respective marks," this objection is anticipated by the Sūtra. For, if the instruments (the senses) are material, then their arising and dissolution occur precisely through the arising and dissolution of the elements; thus, no other sequence need be sought for these two. This is because the commentary on the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "on account of non-distinction" (*aviśeṣāt*) explains it as being of the nature of a resolution to the contradiction with scriptural texts concerning the elements, which is extremely clear.

Furthermore, it is not correct to say "in the fourth [section] as well," because in the third section—which consists of the removal of contradictions regarding scriptural passages concerning elements other than material ones—it is impossible to include such passages as "likewise the vital breaths" (*tathā prāṇāḥ*) and so forth, which are devoted to removing contradictions regarding scriptural passages concerning material vital breaths and the like; this is stated by the author of the Commentary both in the conclusion of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), "Therefore, there is no contradiction of the origination and dissolution of the elements," and in the conclusion of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

The contradiction regarding the scriptural accounts of the origin of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) has been resolved; now, the contradiction regarding their number is being resolved. This is understood even by a child, for it is clear from examining the introductory commentary on the sūtra, "And because the movement is specified as seven," that although the discussion of the sense organs (*indriya*) occurs there [in the first two chapters], the subject matter of the discussion of the sense organs in the [subsequent] two chapters is distinct.

The statement beginning with "even in the fourth [chapter]" is also not tenable. In the passage "By means of this living self (jīva)... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2), according to the words "having entered," it is understood that the individual soul (jīva) alone is the creator of material names and forms. However, in the passage "In the beginning this was indeed undifferentiated; it was differentiated by name and form" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7), it is the Supreme Lord who is the agent. Since the contradiction regarding the scriptural texts concerning material names and forms has already been refuted, the fact that the restrictive rule of the fourth section (pāda) is not abandoned is perfectly clear.

Since the third and fourth [chapters] also consist of the removal of contradictions within one's own position—just like the first—they would follow immediately after the first. As for the second, since it consists of the refutation of the positions of others, it would logically come last; however, this objection has already been refuted previously. This is the general direction [of the argument]. The followers of Ānandatīrtha, however, say: "In the first [chapter], there is no contradiction with reasoning; in the second, no contradiction with established tradition (samaya); in the third, no contradiction with the Śruti alone; and in the fourth, no contradiction with the Śruti accompanied by reasoning. That is incorrect.

Since the nature of *samaya*—defined as a collection of statements accepted by many people whose scope concerns supramundane objects—is common to the *Smṛti* cited by the author of the *Candrikā*, and since Jayatīrtha states in his *Tattvaprakāśikā* that "conflict regarding *samaya* is the seed of doubt" in the *Smṛti-adhikaraṇa* precisely with the intention that *Smṛtis* are of the nature of *samaya*, it is impossible for *Smṛtis* to fall outside the category of *samaya*. Therefore, the non-contradiction of *Smṛti* is appropriately connected to the term *samaya* itself.

Since Jayatīrtha states that "the Smṛtis consist of reasoning (*yukti*) and so forth," and since there is no difference between Smṛtis and *samayas* (traditional doctrines) in their nature as reasoning, it is appropriate that the contradiction of *samayas* should also be refuted by the first quarter-verse, just like the contradiction of Smṛtis. Furthermore, because *samayas* are themselves specific forms of Smṛti, the refutation of the contradiction of *samayas* is already accomplished by the refutation of the contradiction of Smṛtis; thus, the second quarter-verse is unnecessary for that purpose, as it has already been addressed in the phrase "and others" (*itareṣāṃ ca*).

Nor is Jayatīrtha’s statement—that what was refuted there [in the first pāda] in general is here refuted in detail—particularly sound; for it is equally appropriate to say that the detailed refutation occurs in the second pāda itself, as it does in the case of the Smṛtis, just as it does in the case of the Samayas.

As for what is stated in the *Candrikā*: having raised the objection that it is inappropriate to include the section concerning non-contradiction with Smṛti within the "Section on Reasoning" (*yuktipāda*), [the author] replies that because the Smṛtis such as those of the Pāśupatas are of the nature of formal commitments (*samaya*), they serve as corroboration for the author's own position; and because they consist of both scriptural citations and reasoning, they possess the character of the "Fourfold Nature" (*caturātmakatā*). Therefore, although the non-contradiction [of these Smṛtis] is not included in any specific section that addresses contradictions with individual [Smṛtis], since it must be included somewhere within the chapter on non-contradiction (*avirodhādhyāya*), and there is no reason to bypass it at the outset, it is placed first by virtue of its being fourfold.

It has been settled that [the contradiction] must be addressed at the very beginning of the chapter because it is powerful and must be refuted first. That is incorrect; for Jayatīrtha has stated that since Vedic Smṛtis are not invalid, there is no contradiction with the causality of the world as declared by Śruti; furthermore, since the prima facie arguments (pūrvapakṣas) based on Smṛtis such as those of the Vaiśeṣikas, Buddhists, and Jains have already been demonstrated in the *Candrikā* within the very section on Smṛti (*Smṛtyadhikaraṇa*), and because your intended aim is merely to resolve contradictions with Vedic Smṛtis alone.

Since it is impossible to maintain the insistence that only the four types of systems beginning with Sāṃkhya and Pāśupata are excluded from the very beginning [of the inquiry], [the objection is untenable].

Regarding the conflict between the scriptural texts on unity—such as "At the end, all become one in the Imperishable"—and the scriptural texts on difference, and regarding the possibility of resolving the mutual contradiction between the scriptural text indicating the individual soul's agency (as in *Itaravyapadeśāt*) and the scriptural texts such as "Nārāyaṇa alone indeed existed," [the opponent] assumes the subordinate status of the stronger scripture [of unity]. [He argues: "The clay does not speak because it is insentient; the cause must be non-existent at the time of dissolution because it is a real entity like its effects; that which is under dispute is without a cause, having an insentient cause."

Furthermore, the claim that [the first quarter] is included within the first section by postulating a resolution to contradictions with such reasonings as "the soul is not the cause of the world because it is an effect, like the falling of a riverbank or curd," or "Viṣṇu is not the creator of the world because he is non-different from the soul," is indeed inappropriate.

Thus, in the third pāda, which is devoted to resolving contradictions with the *Śruti* alone—specifically in the section on ether (*viyad-adhikaraṇa*) which aims to resolve the contradiction between the two *Śruti* passages, "From the Self, space was produced" (*ātmana ākāśaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ*) and "Space is indeed beginningless" (*anādirvā ayamākāśaḥ*)—[the author] states that if one were to accept the production of space, it would contradict experience, reasoning, and many scriptural statements, and so forth. This refers to the reasoning shown by Jayatīrtha, namely "Ether is not produced because it is all-pervading," which establishes the beginninglessness of ether based on the *Śruti*. Furthermore, this is addressed in the second section (*adhikaraṇa*) by the sūtra: "By this, air is explained."

In the section beginning with "But there is no possibility [of the origin of Being], because that which exists cannot arise" (*asaṃbhavastu sato’nupapatteḥ*), which resolves the contradiction between the two scriptural passages—"Vāyu is their calf"—and "That deity who blows here is indeed without beginning"—it was demonstrated that the quality of being the object of worship for all deities, as well as the reasoning regarding its superior sentience, which establishes that [Brahman] is without beginning, would be impossible if it were subject to origination. This is shown through the refutation of the contradiction between those scriptures and the statement, "O gentle one, in the beginning this was Being alone. Thus, [the text] refers to Brahman.

By the passage beginning with "of the sky and wind, which are impossible to produce and are similar to [the sky and wind] that are not produced," and ending with "because of the strength of the scriptural testimony on birth (*janma-śruti*) together with its reasoning"—this refers to the reasoning you stated; and by the reasoning you stated in the section on "Water" (*āpaḥ*), which aims to resolve the contradiction with the scriptural texts "from fire, water" and "he created those waters," namely: "The subject of dispute, water, is born from fire, because it is water, like sweat, etc."—[it follows] solely from his meditating upon that.

Furthermore, regarding your argument based on the logic of the creator—that because Viṣṇu is the creator of the universe, he cannot be the destroyer, as in the world one observes that the slayer is someone other than the father—this is countered by the *talliṅgāt saḥ* (Brahma Sūtra 1.3.42) section, which resolves the contradiction between the two scriptural passages, "That into which they enter when departing" and "May Rudra, the Destroyer, not enter me," thereby establishing Viṣṇu’s role as the agent of dissolution. Moreover, in the section beginning with *antarā vijñānamanasī* (Brahma Sūtra 2.3.15), the scriptural statement "Higher than the Imperishable [is the Supreme]" and the injunction "The wise man should restrain speech and mind; he should restrain that in knowledge" establish the same.

Regarding the phrase "in the self" (*ātmani*), since the principle of mind (*manastattva*) that was previously situated has already dissolved [into the self], this passage is intended to resolve the apparent contradiction concerning the dissolution of the subtle body (*liṅga*)—both in its order of emergence and its reverse order. It is not the case that everything dissolves only by way of reverse order; rather, for some it is in direct order and for others in reverse order. For instance, it is heard in scripture that the principle of discernment (*vijñānatattva*) arises from the principle of mind, as in the Vedic text: "And from the mind, discernment."

Furthermore, regarding that [perception], there is the observation of logical signs supporting the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): namely, that the dissolution of the subsequently arisen reality of consciousness occurs only later, while the dissolution of the previously existing reality of the mind occurs only earlier.

By these and other arguments, the contradiction between the two scriptural passages cited in the section beginning with "The knower is therefore [eternal]"—namely, "He is eternal among the eternal" and "All these emerge from the conscious Self"—is resolved. This establishes that the individual soul (*jīva*) is not subject to origination, as stated in the following: "The soul does not possess origination because it is beginningless like the Lord. Nor is the reason (*hetu*) identical to the probandum (*sādhya*), for what is intended by "beginninglessness" is the state of being devoid of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Furthermore, there is no dispute regarding this point, as it would otherwise entail the absurdity of the soul having no origination at all. Alternatively, we define "beginninglessness" as the absence of a cause.

And there is no dispute even regarding that [the soul's pervasiveness], because of the absence of any perceived cause for [contradiction]—namely, the argument you stated regarding the soul's lack of causes—and because of the *Kāṣāyaṇa-śruti*: "The selves are indeed pervasive, conscious, devoid of qualities, all-encompassing, of all forms, and infinite," as well as the *Gaupavana-śruti*: "This self is indeed atomic; it goes toward both merit and demerit. Thus, in order to resolve the contradiction concerning the soul's pervasiveness and atomicity, and to establish the pervasiveness of the individual soul (jīva), [the scripture states]: "So atomic is this self..."

Regarding the argument you stated—that there is a perception of pleasure and so forth pervading the body because of tactile cognition occurring throughout the entire body—the *Gaupavana Śruti* demonstrates the distinction [of the soul from the body] in the section beginning with "He is eternal, partless... and continues: "Endowed with merit and joined with demerit, he returns to this world and the next; he is liberated; he becomes one-fold, seven-fold, not hundred-fold; he becomes five-fold, seven-fold, and ten-fold."

Furthermore, based on the *Pārāśarya-Āyaṇa-Śruti*—"He goes [to the worlds] a hundredfold and a thousandfold; he is liberated"—which aims to resolve the contradiction regarding the unity and plurality of the individual soul (*jīva*) by establishing its uniform nature, and based on the reasoning you yourself have stated—namely, "It is indeed possible for one who has realized the Self through the power of yoga to possess a multiplicity of bodies," etc., which concerns the capacity to assume multiple bodies—and because this state persists as long as the Self exists, there is no fault, as seen in the *Sūtra*: "There is no defect, for that is observed" (Br.Sū. 3.2.7), and because he attains dissolution [in Brahman], leading to infinity.

It is postulated that, in order to resolve the contradiction with scripture regarding both impermanence and permanence, the argument you have stated—that the nature of the reflection consists in its being reflected by an adventitious limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that possesses an origin—is untenable because a reflection necessarily originates when its limiting adjunct originates. Furthermore, in the section concerning the manifestation of what already exists—as in the case of masculinity and so forth—there is the scriptural testimony: "The self of consciousness, together with all the gods, is bliss, is strength, is vigor"; thus, "when he is liberated from suffering, he becomes blissful."

Furthermore, regarding the contradiction between the *Pauṅgi-śruti*—which states that "one who was ignorant becomes a knower through liberation"—and the argument you have stated (that the soul is not blissful because it would otherwise entail its constant experience thereof), as well as the contradiction between the scriptural passage from the section "The agent [is the soul], because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless" which teaches that agency belongs to the Lord alone, and the scriptural passage "Whatever action one performs, one attains that," which indicates the soul's agency through the attainment of results—in order to resolve these contradictions concerning the soul:

The agency of the Lord alone, through His unique connection [with the world], has been established by the argument of parsimony (*lāghava*) which proves the absence of agency [in others] in passages such as "because of the designation of another" (*itaravyapadeśāt*). For this very reason, the agency of both [the individual soul and the Lord] together has also been refuted.

Regarding your statement that "there would be parsimony of hypothesis (kalpanālāghava) if the agency were accepted as belonging to the Lord alone," this is countered by the following: since there exists the reasoning you have stated—which establishes the absence of being a reflection of the one Lord by showing that reflections lack a single common nature—this reasoning serves to resolve the contradiction between the scripture cited in the *Ābhāsa eva ca* section (*rūpaṃ rūpam*) and the scripture inferred from the context which teaches the absence of reflectionhood. Therefore, it is appropriate to place these sections precisely in the first pāda, where contradictions with reasoning are resolved.

And here, since there is a rule that a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) necessarily possesses the property of being non-authoritative (*apramāṇatva*)—which pervades its status as an instrument for producing a cognition whose object contradicts its own [contrary] object—it follows without impediment that the capacity for such valid cognition residing in the Vedānta texts entails the lack of authority of the Sāṃkhya Smṛti, which teaches a contradictory object regarding that same subject matter. This is because the aforementioned capacity for valid cognition established in the Vedānta would otherwise be inexplicable without the non-authority of that Smṛti.

Furthermore, since the resulting contingency of establishing such validity would contradict the knowledge that Brahman lacks the capacity for invalidity, there is the following *tarka* (reductio): "If the Vedāntas were directed toward the aforementioned Brahman, then they would possess invalidity, which pervades the state of being a means of producing a cognition whose object contradicts [the Vedāntas] themselves. Because this *tarka* directly opposes the opponent's position and serves to refute it, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is consistent with the chapter (*adhyāya*) and the section (*pāda*).

In this regard, there arises the doubt: "Is it improper or proper that the Vedāntas have as their primary purport the Brahman described [by the Sāṃkhya]? For that purpose, [the further doubt]: "Does there exist a proof for the authority of the Sāṃkhya Smṛti, or not? And for that purpose, [the final doubt]: "Is the Sāṃkhya Smṛti rooted in a cognition produced by unimpaired instruments (*akṣata-karaṇa*), or not? [The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*): The Vedāntas do not have as their purport the aforementioned Brahman. If that were the case, it would follow that the Sāṃkhya Smṛti lacks authority; and this is not an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

For its authority is beyond reproach, just like that of the Vedas, because it was composed by an omniscient being and is accepted by the great multitude. Indeed, reliability (*āpti*) is the seed of authority; and that is equal in the *Tantra* as it is in the Veda, for the author of the *Tantra* is just like the author of the Veda. This is because he possesses the omniscience established by the Śruti: "He who, at the beginning, sustains with his knowledges Kapila, born of the sages, and beholds him as he is being born."

It should not be argued that because the knowledge of Īśvara is eternal and thus its causes cannot be suspected of possessing defects, the validity of the Vedas rooted in it can be ascertained, whereas for the knowledge of Kapila and others—which is produced and thus its causes may be suspected of possessing defects—the ascertainment of validity is impossible. For, in the case of Kapila and others whose supreme knowledge has manifested through the grace of the Blessed One, it is improper to suspect their knowledge of being rooted in defects; indeed, there is no basis whatsoever for attributing defects such as deceitfulness to them.

Furthermore, there is no room here for the principle that "in the case of a contradiction, one should be independent [of the other], for when there is no [contradiction], there is inference," because that principle applies only when there is a contradiction with a scripture whose purport has been definitively established. Nor can it be suspected that the purport is determined there by means of the introductory passages (*upakrama*) and so forth, since the Sāṃkhya teachers, relying on the support of the *Balarāma-tarka-avastambha*, have described its purport as being precisely their own intended meaning.

If this were so, one might object that it would follow that the *smṛtis* of Manu and others would also lack authority; for since the "acceptance by great men" (*mahājanaparigraha*), which is the seed of authority, is equally present there as well, it would be improper to accept such a consequence. To this it must be said: no, because those [Manu’s *smṛtis*] have scope regarding matters to be performed (*anuṣṭheya-artha*), and thus one cannot assume they intend to convey meanings that contradict the *Sāṃkhya-smṛti*. However, the *Sāṃkhya-smṛtis*, being directed solely toward the science of the self (*adhyātma-darśana*), are without scope [in the realm of ritual action].

For this very reason, the following [opinion] is refuted: that when the Veda and the Tantra possess equal authority, a definitive conclusion must be stated based on the Veda alone, rather than a conclusion being reached in accordance with the Tantra. This is because the Veda also possesses its own scope regarding dharma and other matters. Nor is it the case that the Upaniṣads lack their own scope; for even they can be shown to have their own scope according to the method of the Sāṃkhya and others. To explain: first of all, the causal statements do not have as their purport the fact that Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, nor do they have as their purport the fact that He is its agent (*kartṛ*), because this would contradict the arguments to be presented later.

Nor can sentences that teach the Supreme Self as non-different from the inner self (pratyagātman) be taken in their literal sense; for that would lead to the undesirable consequence of there being no distinction between the performance of beneficial acts and liberation from bondage. In this very manner, the defects in the position of absolute non-duality (advaita) and so forth should be inferred. Thus, according to the method stated in the *Sāṃkhyapravacana*, those sentences in the creation-texts that indicate the state of being the material cause (prakṛti) are merely figurative, insofar as they refer to the ownership of Pradhāna—which is the material cause of the universe—by the Lord.

One must follow this unavoidable conclusion: that certain sentences teaching agency refer to a subordinate Lord (avāntareśvara), while others are merely figurative; and that sentences such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) teach the inclusion [of the individual self] within the sphere of pure consciousness (cinmaṇḍala). Accordingly, the Sāṃkhya Sūtras state: "The status of being a supervisor arises from proximity, like a magnet; [the attribution of agency to the Self] is a praise of the liberated Self, or it refers to the perfected one who is meditated upon; thus there is no contradiction with the Śruti on non-duality, because [the texts concerning agency] refer to the universal class (jāti)," and so forth.

Regarding this, the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) states: "But even so, the fact that He is heard of in scripture as the presiding controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) of the entire aggregate beginning with primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is not tenable; for in the world, the designation 'presiding controller' applies only to one who undergoes transformation through volition and the like. To this, he replies: "That" (*tat*). If presiding control and the status of creator were said to consist in volition, then this fault would indeed arise. However, we maintain that the Puruṣa’s presiding control, in the form of creation and so forth, results from mere proximity (*saṃnidhāna*), like a magnet.

Just as the magnet possesses the power of extracting a thorn by its mere proximity and not through volition or other such means, even so, the primordial Puruṣa causes Prakṛti to transform into the form of the Great Principle (mahat-tattva) and the rest through mere conjunction alone. This is precisely what is meant by "creation with an adjunct" (sopadhika-sraṣṭṛtva).

If this is so, what is the status of those scriptural passages (*śruti*) that establish the existence of an *Īśvara*? To this he says: "Mukta... and so on. According to the appropriate application, some scriptural passage is for the purpose of enjoining the knowability of the liberated self (*muktātman*), which is the mere generality of the Self (*kevalātmasāmānya*); it takes the form of praise by virtue of the mere proximity of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and is intended to inspire interest (*prarocanārtha*). Furthermore, some scriptural passage—such as those establishing the power of creation preceded by volition (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth—is devoted to the meditation upon eternity and other attributes of the established [deities] such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, even though they are non-eternal *Īśvaras* possessed of egoism (*abhimāna*) and the like, because they possess a figurative (*gauṇa*) form of eternity and so forth. [Objection: But if there is thus a plurality of *Puruṣas*...
The self of beings is indeed one alone, residing in every single being;
it appears as both one and many, like the moon reflected in water.
The Self is eternal, omnipresent, immutable, and free from defects;
it is one, yet it appears divided through its power of māyā, not by its own nature.

Thus, [the opponent argues that] such scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti*) which establish the identity of the Self (*ātmaikya*) would be untenable. To this, he replies: "There is no contradiction with the non-dualistic scriptures" (*nādvaitaśruti*). There is indeed no contradiction regarding the scriptures on the identity of the Self; for those [scriptures] have as their purport the genus (*jāti*), that is, the universal (*sāmānya*) or the state of having a single form. This is because the non-dualistic scriptures intend precisely that [genus]. [The opponent objects: "But [if it is the genus], then there is no impetus toward liberation (*akhaṇḍatve tatra prayojanābhāvāt*). This is the meaning.

Is it not the case that this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is untenable? For the aforementioned defects have already been raised here and there within the very chapter on *Samanvaya*. To explain: in the *Īkṣatyadhikaraṇa*, the commentary on the prima facie view states that "the status of being a cause is possible for the Pradhāna because it is manifold and its transformation is feasible—just like clay and so forth—but not for Brahman, which is unitary and uncomposite. Thus, since the status of being the material cause (*upādānatva*) has been rejected in respect to Brahman, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) cannot arise without establishing that [status]; consequently, even the fallacious reasoning (*nyāyābhāsa*) known as "the contingency of the whole [Brahman] undergoing modification" (*kṛtsnaprasakti*) follows.

In that context, [the opponent's position] is intended to be refuted. Thus, the claim that in some instances the act of "seeing" (īkṣaṇa) is merely figurative has also been refuted in that very same place. Likewise, in the section concerning invisibility (adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa):
"But a similarity with the conscious Self is not possible for insentient things;
therefore, let it be understood that the Pradhāna alone, being insentient, is the source of the world."
Thus, because the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is raised in the *Nibandha*:
"This world is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of Brahman, who is changeless;
it arises from beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and does not require similarity [with its cause]."

Thus, by the formulation of this established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the very meaning of the section beginning with "Because of having different characteristics" (*vilakṣaṇatvāt*) has been stated. Furthermore, in the *Jijñāsā-sūtra* itself, having raised the doubt that the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman are non-different despite the superimposition of contradictory attributes—such as omniscience and being the agent of all versus the absence thereof—the subject matter for proving the falsity of that [difference] was established; thus, the meaning of the section beginning with "Because of its non-difference from that" (*tadananyatvāt*) has also been clarified.

If it is argued that even here, in the section beginning with "And [the world] is of the nature of [Prakṛti]," the very meaning of the sūtras such as "Because of the difference in nature" (BraSū 2.1.4) has been shown by the statement, "This world is seen to have parts, to be insentient, and to be impure," and therefore the final conclusion must necessarily be in accordance with that; [Response: This is not so. For in that context, the purpose was merely to show that the world cannot be the effect of Brahman because of its difference in nature from Him, and not to establish that the world is actually the effect of Prakṛti. Otherwise, the subsequent sūtras, such as "But [it is] from [Brahman], on account of [the world] being designated as such" (BraSū 2.1.14), would be rendered meaningless. Furthermore, the refutation of the Sāṅkhya doctrine occurs later, in the third chapter, under the sūtra "Not from both, on account of the impossibility" (BraSū 2.2.59). Therefore, the view that the world is the effect of Prakṛti is not the intended meaning of those sūtras. Consequently, the final conclusion remains that the world is indeed the effect of Brahman alone.

On this point, they argue as follows: In the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*, having demonstrated the lack of natural consistency in the reason for the established conclusion—namely, that it is impossible for the Supreme Self, whose nature is eternal consciousness, to possess primary omniscience, and that if one were to admit produced knowledge (*janyajñāna*) to account for it, the consequence would be that the Self possesses a body—it was shown that the impossibility of [the Self] being the material cause due to its partlessness (*niravayavatva*) and other attributes serves to strengthen the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). Nevertheless, the very logic used to refute that [impossibility] is precisely what is relied upon in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of this present section (*pāda*).

As it has been stated there in the *Siddhāntabhāṣya*: "But how, even by means of reasoning (*tarka*), the causality of Brahman alone can be established and not that of the *pradhāna* and so forth, will be explained at length in the section beginning with 'Not because of dissimilarity' (*na vilakṣaṇatvāt*) and so on. By this, the aforementioned commentary on the *Prakṛtyadhikaraṇa* is also explained as being consistent [with this view]. The same should be understood elsewhere as well.

As for what is stated in the *Candrikā*: "Since the Vedāntas have many aspects, persons of dependent intellect cannot determine their meaning by themselves; therefore, when the meaning must be ascertained through Smṛti, the Smṛtis of Manu and others—being concerned with matters to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*)—possess scope (*sāvakāśatva*). However, the Smṛti of Kapila, which is established in already accomplished facts (*siddhārtha*), deals with right vision (*samyagdarśana*) as the means to liberation; since it cannot be directed toward anything else, it would entail the defect of having no scope (*niravakāśatva*). Therefore, the Vedāntas [should be interpreted] in accordance with that."

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the Vedānta texts should be explained as having an insentient cause as their primary purport; however, since there are many statements in the *Smṛtis* of Manu and others, as well as in the Purāṇas and so forth, which assert that Brahman is the cause, it would follow that those [other] texts would be rendered purposeless—a fault that must be avoided. Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the Vedānta texts should be explained in accordance with them as having a sentient cause as their primary purport. Having thus restated the prima facie view and the established conclusion according to our own tradition, [the author replies]: "That is not so, because of the uniformity of interpretation regarding the single, primary purport of the Vedānta texts toward a sentient cause," as stated here.

Furthermore, the objection raised against the prima facie position—that because the *Samanvaya-adhyāya* has already established [the point], no further doubts can arise from many quarters—is refuted by that very same reasoning. For although it was previously stated that the well-known Vedānta texts do not contradict other [scriptures] regarding their specific nature as referring to the Cause, there remains no logical inconsistency in the doubt that, according to the method of the Sāṃkhya teachers, none of the Vedānta texts might have any purpose other than [establishing] Brahman.

As for what was stated in the *Candrikā*—namely, that since the lack of authority of Smṛtis such as those concerning "covering everything" has already been declared in the *Pūrvatantra* due to their conflict with Śruti regarding touch, no suspicion of the Śruti’s lack of natural consistency can arise here due to conflict with Smṛti, and thus this constitutes a second refutation of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that too is not correct. For it has been established in the *pūrvapakṣa* itself that the principle of the *Pūrvatantra* applies only when there is a conflict with a Śruti whose intended meaning has been determined, according to the rule: "But in case of conflict, [the Smṛti] would be independent [of Śruti]."

Furthermore, in the *Candrikā*, a third objection was stated against the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the word "Smṛti" in the Sūtra: since it is possible for that term to refer exclusively to non-Vedic Smṛtis (as opposed to Vedic ones), it would be improper to restrict it by stating that it refers only to the Smṛti of Kapila. The rebuttal to this is as follows: although there exist many Smṛtis concerning the inner self (*adhyātma*), an effort has been made specifically to refute only the Smṛtis of Sāṃkhya and Yoga.

Indeed, Sāṃkhya and Yoga are renowned in the world as the means for accomplishing the supreme goal of man (puruṣārtha), they are accepted by the learned (śiṣṭas), and they are reinforced by Vedic evidence (liṅga). This is evident to those who have studied the Śrīmad Bhāṣya, which states: "Having known that cause attained through Sāṃkhya and Yoga, one is released from all fetters. This passage aims merely to explain the seed of the insistence on refuting the Smṛti of Sāṃkhya.

As for what was stated in the *Candrikā*—that the doctrine of Kaṇāda and others is refuted in passages such as "or like the large and the long," and likewise that the Sāṃkhya doctrine is refuted in the sūtra "And because of the impossibility of construction, [the world] is not [produced by] inference"—this fourth objection is also untenable.

Because there is no fault, given that the Smṛti concerning the causes [of the world]—which shares the same characteristics as the Smṛti concerning effects such as Mahat—is not baseless; for while the Smṛti concerning effects is contradicted by flawless Śruti and is therefore baseless, the suspicion that the Smṛti concerning causes might likewise lack a basis is removed by the fact that it is rooted in flawless means of knowledge such as inference, which will be explained as the subject matter (*prameya*) of this very section. Furthermore, there is no fault because the invalidity of the inference intended to prove that [baselessness] is itself the subject matter of the section beginning with "the impossibility of design" (*racanānupapatteś ca*).

This is the essential conclusion here: when there is a conflict between two [authorities] of equal strength, it must be stated that the one with scope (sāvakāśa) is restricted by the one without scope (niravakāśa). However, such a case does not exist in the present instance. This is because the Smṛtis that conform to the Vedas have their basis established and their authority is certain. On the other hand, as long as the basis for the Sāṅkhya Smṛtis—which contradict the Vedas—is being inferred, their lack of authority is already determined due to their contradiction with directly perceived Śruti; since their basis is established as being rooted in error, deception, and so forth, there is no room for the postulation of a foundational Śruti.

And thus, since it has been stated that the ascertainment of validity is not possible for [the Smṛti] that is non-existent, our position is not contradicted because the suspicion of an undesired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) against the aforementioned reasoning has been refuted. This very point was indicated by the Author of the Sūtras himself when he sought to establish the invalidity of other Smṛtis; for it would be impossible to establish the invalidity of other Smṛtis if one did not first accept their validity. This is because the Sāṃkhya Smṛti possesses the ground for invalidity, namely, that its subject matter contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Now, if it is argued that Śruti and Smṛti possess equal force, that is poorly stated.

This is because scripture (*śruti*) possesses authority only when it is independent of attainment through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), whereas tradition (*smṛti*) is dependent upon them. Kapila and others, having perceived an object through another means of knowledge, composed traditions with the desire to communicate that [knowledge]. Otherwise, how could traditions have their root in reliability (*āpti*)? Or, in the absence of that, how could they possess authority? Furthermore, being rooted in a self-evident reliability does not entail a loss of independence.

Because, as soon as a cognition arises, there is the possibility that it is produced by defects, and thus the suspicion of its invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) spreads. If it is objected: "In that case, would it not follow that you must accept the Veda to be of human origin (*pauruṣeya*), just like the logicians (*tārkika*)? We reply: No. For the logicians maintain that the validity of the Veda is due to its being composed by a reliable person (*āpta*), and not intrinsic (*svataḥ*). Thus says their aphorism: "The authority of the Veda [is established] from its being taught by him."

Furthermore, this [argument] is vitiated by the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): the establishment of the omniscient Lord depends on the establishment of the authority of the Veda because it was spoken by Him; and the establishment of the omniscient Lord, who is known through the authoritative Veda, depends on that [authority of the Veda] being established. However, for the followers of the Upaniṣads, this is not the case, due to the distinction that they accept the intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) of knowledge at its very origin. Nor can error be suspected even in the case of eternal cognition, because cognitions are generally valid unless there is a subverting factor (*bādhaka*).

If it is argued: "But surely this contradicts our own tenet; for since the general class of the perceptible is illusory, it follows that even the knowledge of God possesses the nature of an error, characterized by having an illusory object"—we reply: No, for being an error does not consist merely in having an illusory object. For if it did, then even the cognition "this silver is indeterminable" or "non-existent" would result in being invalid (*aprāmāṇya*). Rather, [error] consists in not apprehending that [object] as it truly is. And this is not possible for the cognition of a cow, which takes as its object the cow (or the silver) as it is, namely, as something that is indeterminable or as possessing the property of indeterminability.

Furthermore, there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for the eternality of the knowledge of Kapila and others. Therefore, since the suspicion of any defect has been entirely removed, the Smṛti of the Sāṅkhya (Kapila) cannot possess equal authority with the Śruti or the Smṛti rooted in it; thus, it is not logical to establish a distinction between them based on the criteria of "having scope" (*sāvakāśatva*) and "lacking scope" (*niravakāśatva*). Moreover, it is well known that Kapila, the proponent of the Sāṅkhya which contradicts the Veda, is not one who is to be propounded by the Śruti.

Regarding the term "Kapila," although there is a general scriptural mention, it refers to another Kapila—namely, Vāsudeva, who was born from the seed of Viṣṇu and who consumed the sons of Sagara. Nor should it be argued that even this much does not resolve the doubt concerning the meaning of the word "Kapila. For the statement "the exalted seer" (ṛṣiṃ prabhūtam) occurs in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad; and it has been determined in the *Camasādhikaraṇa* that this passage is naturally intended to establish the non-dual Brahman. Consequently, it can be ascertained that the very Kapila who follows the doctrine of non-duality and is a partial incarnation of Vāsudeva is the one being propounded here.

Furthermore, the reading currently used by contemporary Vaidikas is indeed "kiṃcana" (whatever). Since the Śruti passage—"Manu said that [is] the medicine"—which indicates the authority of Manu's statement alone, is active, it is inconsistent to claim that his statement lacks scope; otherwise, the word "kiṃcana" would be rendered redundant. Manu, however, stated:
"Seeing the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self, as equal, the one who sacrifices to the Self attains self-sovereignty."
Thus, by praising the doctrine of universal selfhood (*sārvātmya*), the Sāṃkhya system is understood to be censured;

for Kapila does not accept universal selfhood, as he does not admit the non-difference of the Self (*ātman*). Furthermore, the Smṛtis that follow the Śruti state: having introduced the Supreme Brahman with the words "That which is subtle and unknowable," and saying "He is indeed the inner Self of beings, called the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*"), they further declare, "O best of the twice-born, from Him was produced the Unmanifest, consisting of the three qualities. Likewise, elsewhere it is said: "The Unmanifest is dissolved into the inactive Puruṣa-Brahman."
Therefore, listen to this summary: Nārāyaṇa, the ancient one, is all this;
at the time of creation he brings forth creation, and at the time of dissolution he consumes it once again.
Thus it is said in the Purāṇas. And in the Bhagavadgītā:
"I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire world.

Furthermore, Āpastamba recites with reference to the Supreme Self alone: "From Him all bodies originate; He is the root, eternal and permanent. These are the passages declaring God to be the cause. In the Mahābhārata:
"O King, are there many Puruṣas, or is it indeed only one? Having thus deliberated:
"O King, there are many Puruṣas for those who have not investigated Sāṃkhya and Yoga."
Having thus presented the opposing view, he refutes it by beginning as follows:
"Just as a single source is said for many persons, so shall I describe that universal Person who is pre-eminent in qualities. Then, continuing:
My inner self, yours, and those of others residing within their bodies—all these have that [Self] as their witness; it is never to be grasped by anyone, anywhere.
"Having a universal head, universal arms, and universal feet, eyes, and nose, he moves alone among beings, wandering at will according to his pleasure.
Thus [is described] the state of being the self of all, as stated in the Commentary. (1)
And because it lacks a source, he declares the lack of authority for the Sāṃkhya Smṛti with the sūtra:
"And because the others are not perceived" (2.1.2).

This means that the other principles—those other than Pradhāna, namely Mahat and the rest—are not perceived in either worldly experience or the Veda. Thus, the Kāpila Smṛti, which teaches an independent Pradhāna, is non-authoritative due to its lack of a foundation, just like the Kāpila Smṛti that teaches Mahat-tattva and the other categories. It has already been demonstrated in the commentary and sub-commentary on the sūtra "Not because of the inclusion of the number" (1.4.11) how Mahat-tattva and the others are not established by Śruti and other means of valid knowledge.

In this context, the lack of authority of the Sāṃkhya Smṛti was stated in the first sūtra due to its contradiction with the flawless Śruti upon which it is based. In the second [sūtra], its lack of authority is established because of its being rootless (*nirmūlatva*). Regarding "rootlessness," the absence of a "root"—defined as being grounded in a cognition produced by unimpaired instruments of knowledge concerning the same subject matter—is the reason for its lack of authority. To avoid the fallacy of over-extension (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the Veda, it should be understood that the qualification "being a Smṛti" is either explicitly mentioned or implied as a further specification of the reason.

As for that which was stated in the *Candrikā*—namely, having restated the meaning of the sūtra "na saṃkhyopasaṃgrahāt" (not so, because of the inclusion of the number), where the opponents argued that the Sāṃkhya doctrine is untenable because the others, such as the *mahat* and so forth, are not perceived—the refutation offered there, namely that this is incorrect because the perception of the *mahat* and so forth in the Śruti and other texts has already been demonstrated, is also not valid.

Because the meaning of this sūtra—which concerns the invalidity of the memory of the cause on the grounds that it shares the same character as the memory of effects such as the mahat-tattva and others which are [in fact] rootless—does not touch upon the refutation [of the opponent's position]. Furthermore, since the venerable Bhāṣya, intending to show that the invalidity of the memory of the cause follows from the invalidity of the memory of the effect, has demonstrated the aforementioned meaning of the sūtra with extreme clarity, no doubt can arise regarding any other meaning. || 2 ||
By this, Yoga is refuted. (Sūtra 3)

In this context, the connection with the chapter and the section [of the *Brahmasūtra*] arises from the contradiction of the *Yoga-smṛti*, which is in direct opposition to the teaching concerning Brahman. He states the doubt and the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Is there a restriction [of the Vedas] by the *Yoga-smṛti* or not, given the harmony (*samanvaya*)?
Regarding Dharma, the Veda has scope; but there must be a restriction by that which has no scope."

Thus, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the doubt and so forth is to be understood according to the direction previously stated. As for that which was stated in the *Candrikā*: "In response to the further objection that since Yoga is accepted by such scriptural passages as 'This knowledge and the entire rule of Yoga,' it is not equal to Sāṃkhya, [the author replies] 'by this' (etena)," that is not correct. For in such scriptural passages as "Having known that cause, which is to be attained through Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and having known God, one is released from all bonds," Sāṃkhya is also accepted; therefore, there is no ground for such an objection.

In this regard, the objection has been stated that if Vedic knowledge alone is the meaning of the word *sāṃkhya*, then here too, let the meaning of the word *yoga* be simply the means to knowledge. This is based on an examination of the heart of the venerable *Bhāṣya*. For instance, having cited Vedic indications concerning *yoga* in passages such as "This is the yoga," "This is the science of yoga," and "The method of yoga," [it is shown that] even in the *Yoga-śāstra*, yoga is accepted as being for the sake of perfect vision (*samyag-darśana*) itself, in the statement: "Now, yoga is the means to the vision of reality."

Therefore, because it shares a portion of its subject matter with what is already established, the *Yoga-smṛti*—like the *Aṣṭaka*-smṛti and others—will likewise not be subject to refutation. This further objection is set aside by means of an extended application (*atideśa*). Having thus established the basis for this further objection, [the Sūtra states]: "Now, Yoga is the means for the vision of reality."

Since this is demonstrated in the commentary on the aphorism of the *Yogaśāstra* composed by Hiraṇyagarbha, it is understood that this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is based upon the *Hairaṇyagarbha-smṛti*. And in that regard, a further objection is indeed possible; it is as follows: the Vedic scripture beginning with "He who [in the beginning] produced the seer Kapila" does not refer to Kapila as an incarnation of Vāsudeva, because it is impossible for that primordial being, established as unborn, to be one who bestows grace upon others. Furthermore, it would be inappropriate to assume he acts out of mere sport (*līlā*) when another explanation is available.

Nor can it refer to Kapila, the author of the *Sāṃkhya-tantra*, because of the incongruity with the preceding words; for he is well known as the son of Hiraṇyagarbha. Rather, in accordance with the recognition of signs such as being the "first-born," established by many Vedic texts—such as "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning" and "He who ordains Brahmā in the beginning, beholding Hiraṇyagarbha being born"—one [instance of the] word *Kapila* must set aside even the very famous author of the *tantra*.

One should not abandon the well-established meaning and interpret [the text] as referring solely to Hiraṇyagarbha, who is of a single tawny color. Nor is there a lack of authority for the aforementioned Smṛti due to its contradiction with the independent Veda; for, in accordance with the Śruti statement, "Whatever Manu said is medicine," which declares the authority of Hiraṇyagarbha’s words alone, the Vedāntas themselves must be explained in conformity with that. Otherwise, the word "kiñcana" (whatever) would result in being rendered meaningless.

It should not be suspected that the cited scripture (*śruti*) teaches the authority of only those statements not [explicitly] mentioned, and not of the statements of Hiraṇyagarbha; for in that passage, the word "Manu" refers to Hiraṇyagarbha as the presiding deity of the collective mind (*samaṣṭimanobhimānin*). To explain: this is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the injunction found in the Taittirīya branch, "One should make the two Mānavī verses the *dhāyyās*," which states, "Whatever Manu said... [is authoritative].

From the very hearing of the words "the sacrificer who desires to sacrifice" in the two ṛks prescribed by that injunction—namely, *devānāṃ ya inmano yajamāna iyakṣati*—it is understood that they reveal Hiraṇyagarbha as the presiding deity of the mind (*manas*). Likewise, because the word *mānavī* occurring in the injunction has the sense of "revealing Manu," since it would be impossible [otherwise] if the word *manu* referred merely to the Manu who is the author of the Smṛtis.

Since the mantra contained within the injunction refers to Hiraṇyagarbha, for the sake of its consistency with that [injunction], the specific Ṛgvedic verse included in the injunctive sentence must be interpreted in accordance with it; likewise, it is appropriate that the word "manu" occurring in the explanatory passage (arthavāda) concerning that [verse] should also refer to Hiraṇyagarbha.

Furthermore, because this Yoga-śāstra of Hiraṇyagarbha propounds Īśvara, even though it follows the Vedānta position, its refutation by the logic of "and because others are not perceived" is clearly [inapplicable]; for the Śruti itself, which expresses that the authority [of Hiraṇyagarbha] consists merely in his statement "whatever [is here]," establishes the validity of the Smṛtis concerning the effects [of karma] and so forth along with their very roots.

Otherwise, as it has been stated that the word "kiṃcana" would be redundant, the additional doubt raised by the statement "ṭha" is also resolved in the Bhāṣya: "Even when there is agreement regarding one part of the meaning, there is no disagreement regarding another part of the meaning. He states the established conclusion (siddhānta): "Even though [the capacity] is obtained, it is not valid cognition because the Yoga [scripture] lacks [that specific] purport; nevertheless, there is no restriction [on its authority] regarding non-Vedic primary principles and the like."

The point is this: let it be granted that those two [sūktas] reveal Hiraṇyagarbha; nevertheless, the taddhita suffix occurring in the injunction does not have as its primary meaning a relationship with a revealer of that [Hiraṇyagarbha]. Rather, in accordance with the supplementary passage (vākyaśeṣa), "Whatever [there is]," one must accept the meaning: "seen by Manu" (*mānavī*)—that they were seen by Manu.

Thus, since even those two which reveal Hiraṇyagarbha can possibly be considered "seen by Manu" by virtue of being included within the *manusūkta*, it is not appropriate to resort to the forced interpretation that the word *manu* refers to Hiraṇyagarbha by abandoning its well-known conventional meaning.

And thus, since it is impossible to preserve the authority of the portions of the Yoga-śāstra taught in the Bhāṣya—such as its being grounded in renunciation (*nivṛtti-niṣṭha*) through instructions on wandering mendicancy (*pravrajyā*) and so forth, which concern the unattached, qualityless *puruṣa*—by postulating an intended meaning (*tātparya*) for those portions that contradicts perception regarding the *pradhāna* and other [categories], one must conclude that there is no intended meaning at all for those portions according to their literal sense.

Even though there is no primary intention [to discuss that], its presentation is for the purpose of first explaining a yoga whose object is gross; this is because the Supreme Self is so extremely subtle that it is impossible to join the mind to It by means of [gross] light. Regarding that: "In the first [case], there is no emergence of the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*); in the second, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*);
and in the third, an additional doubt is untenable."

Thus, all that has been stated by the author of the *Candrikā* is refuted; this is the general direction [of the argument]. As for Ānandatīrtha, however—he maintains that the three sūtras beginning with "smṛtyanavakāśaḥ" (ŚBh 2.1.1) constitute a single topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) intended to refute contradictions with Smṛti. In that regard, since the Vedas—whose syllables are like those of a whirling wheel—are not rooted in human authority, whereas the Pāśupata and other Smṛtis composed by omniscient beings are rooted in the direct perception of Rudra and others, they possess greater authority than Śruti. Consequently, the meaning of the Veda must be described in accordance with them; thus, it is not logical that Viṣṇu is the cause of the world.

Since the *Pāśupata* and other such *smṛtis* state that Rudra and others alone are the cause of the universe, this being the prima facie view—it is concluded: because the *smṛtis* such as the *Pāñcarātra*, which are rooted in the direct perception of Viṣṇu and others, possess equal authority [to the Vedas], yet due to the observation of corroboration in the *śrutis* for what is stated by Viṣṇu and others—being thus more authoritative than those concerning Rudra and others on account of having been composed by those respective Viṣṇus and others—they constitute a sublation. Furthermore, there is an even greater sublation by the *śruti* when supported by such *smṛtis*. Therefore, the *Pāśupata* and other such *smṛtis* lack authority.

Therefore, there is no inconsistency in the systematic coherence (*samanvaya*) of Viṣṇu as the cause of the world on the basis of the authority of the *Nokta* Veda. In this regard, many prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣas*) have been stated in the *Candrikā* and other works, specifically by relying upon each of the non-Vedic Smṛtis individually. For instance, in the *Candrikā*: "In this context, regarding those such as the Pāśupatas and Sāṅkhyas whose view is that the Veda is not of human origin and is authoritative, the Śruti must be interpreted according to their Smṛti; thus, the prima facie argument is based on the authority of the Śruti [as understood through them]."

However, for those such as Kaṇāda and others who hold that the Veda possesses authority because it was composed by a person, the fact that their own Smṛtis have clear meaning and are supported by reasoning serves as the basis for their position; thus, they too are opponents (*pūrvapakṣins*). In the view of the Buddhists and others, however, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is simply that the Veda, being composed by a person, is not authoritative due to its contradiction with the Buddhist and other scriptures composed by reliable authorities (*āpta*). For this very reason, in the *Sudhā*, the term "Buddhist and others" (*boddhādi*) is used in the phrase "the Pāśupatas, Sāṃkhyas, Buddhists, Ārhats, and so forth."

They say that since there is no evidence for restriction [of the Veda], such restriction—though not Vedic—is acceptable because it is established by logic (*nyāya*). That is incorrect; for, since many Āgamas composed by Rudra are observed to be mutually contradictory, and since many other Āgamas composed by him are likewise observed to be mutually contradictory, it is impossible to suspect a violation of the natural sense of the non-human (apauruṣeya) Śruti by resorting to the view that the Pāśupata Smṛti—which contradicts those other Āgamas composed by him—is rooted in a trustworthy source (*āptimūlaka*).

Nor is it appropriate for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) to rely on the scriptures of Kaṇāda and others, for even they are remembered as having received such weapons only through the instruction of Rudra. As for Kapila and Kamalāsana (Viṣṇu), their status as authoritative sources has already been demonstrated by scripture. If it is objected: "In that case, since Sāṃkhya and Yoga are mutually contradictory, the consequence would be that neither is authoritative; how then can the prima facie position be established even in your own system?"—this is due to a failure to understand our intention.

For instance: in the first section (*adhikaraṇa*), by the logic of the "established conclusion based on a related subject" (*yogādhikaraṇasiddhāntanyāya*), the *Yoga-smṛti* has its purport (*tātparya*) on the portion concerning the Lord (*Īśvara*); however, regarding the other portion, there is no contradiction. This is because, as a means of propounding yoga, it possesses scope (*sāvakāśatā*) like the *smṛtis* of Manu and others. Alternatively, in the second [section] as well, since the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises without obstruction—either by relying on the logic of the "established conclusion based on a related subject" with respect to the first [portion], or by relying on the lack of authority (*anāptatva*) in the author even with respect to the second [portion].

Furthermore, because the Smṛtis composed by Paśupati are mutually contradictory, there is no basis for determining the authority of any one among them. It has thus been stated that a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) relying upon their authority is not tenable. By this same reasoning, a prima facie argument that relies on the Smṛtis of the Buddhists and others—which contradict the Smṛtis of the Pāñcarātra and so forth—is also refuted; for it is difficult to ascertain that the Smṛtis of the Śākyas and others, composed by him [the Buddha], are rooted in authoritative sources when they contradict the Smṛtis of the Pāñcarātra and others composed by the Blessed Lord.

Furthermore, since it was previously established that the claims regarding Rudra and others—such as their being the cause of the world—as stated in the Pāśupata and other texts, correspond with the Śrutis exactly as they are, the greater authority of the Pāñcarātra and other systems over the Pāśupata Smṛti is not proven in respect to the aspect of being the cause of the world.

As for the phrase "and because others are not perceived," this means that since those things other than the supersensible (atīndriya) mentioned in the Pāśupata Smṛtis—namely, the results [of practice], the performance [of rites], and the non-abandonment of the duties prescribed therein—are not perceived through direct perception even when performed, the authority of the Pāśupata and other Smṛtis is restricted to those parts alone. This is not so; for the non-perception of results can also be explained by way of deficiency (vaiguṇya).

Furthermore, in the case of the argument "not because of dissimilarity" (*na vilakṣaṇatvāt*), you yourself have already established that there is likewise a non-perception of the result in instances such as the *kārīrī* sacrifice. If you argue that, since the authority of the Veda is certain, you postulate a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) therein to account for that [non-perception], we reply: in this case as well, since the lack of authority is not certain, it is more appropriate to postulate such a thing in order to preserve the authority that is established by default (*utsarga*). If you claim that the lack of authority here is determined by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then the aphorism (*sūtra*) would be rendered useless.

Even when a matter has already been determined, the statement of another reason is appropriate only if that new reason is capable of establishing its own probandum independently, without depending upon the previous reason; however, this is not possible here. By this, the argument regarding *yoga* is refuted. Specifically, the interpretation of the phrase "thereby *yoga* is answered" as follows—namely, that one might suspect the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the *Yoga-smṛti* because it does not contradict perceived facts, only for that authority to be denied on the grounds that the stated sequence (such as "first one's own body, then the breaking of the limbs") is not observed—is also not tenable.

In the phrase "of the others," since there is the possibility that a sequence is intended—just as there is for the appropriate results—the third sūtra would also be redundant according to your own view.
May this work of Raghunātha, the disciple of the venerable teacher Rāghavācārya— the lion among the Mīmāṃsā logicians— be for the delight of the virtuous.
Thus ends the section concerning Smṛti.
Now begins the section concerning "Non-dissimilarity":
"Not so, because of its dissimilarity; and its being such [is known] from the Word. (2.1.4)

Here, the connection with the beginning of the chapter arises from the refutation of an argument that directly contradicts Brahman’s being the material cause of the world. As for the claim that it is acceptable to admit the lack of authority of the Sāṃkhya-smṛti because it would otherwise entail the lack of authority of those Smṛtis that conform to Śruti—that is incorrect; for it is the Sāṃkhya-smṛti itself that conforms to Śruti. Indeed, the lack of authority of the Sāṃkhya-smṛti cannot be established merely on the grounds of its contradiction with Śruti passages asserting that Brahman is the material cause of ether and the rest.

Because it is impossible for the Śrutis to teach that Brahman is the material cause (*prakṛti*) of ether and the rest due to its contradiction with reasoning such as "having different characteristics" (*vilakṣaṇatva*), and because, according to the method stated by Saṃkhyācārya—which supports the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the *Smṛtyadhikaraṇa*—the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of those Śrutis teaching that Brahman is the material cause of ether and the rest must be established; thus, the objection [raised here] follows immediately after [that discussion].

It should be understood that even if the Smṛtis rooted in those [Vedas] are consistent with the *samanvaya* (harmonization), the contradiction of the *samanvaya* by means of logical arguments (*nyāya*)—which possess unimpeded pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property of being a subject (*pakṣadharmatā*)—is beyond dispute. Here, a doubt arises as to whether the aforementioned harmonization is tenable or not; for that purpose, there is the question: in proving that Brahman is not the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, are the reasons such as "being of a different nature" (*vilakṣaṇatva*) defective or non-defective? [In response to this: "Pradhāna alone, because it consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion (*sukha-duḥkha-moha*), is the material cause of such a world, and not Brahman."

Because they are not of that nature; for the relationship of material cause and effect, consisting of the state of being the original source and its modification, is observed only between two things of the same class (*sajātīya*). In this context, the specific pervasion (*viśeṣavyāpti*) has ignorance (*avidyā*) as its illustrative example. As for the general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*), namely "whatever is different in character is not of that as its material cause," the illustrative example is: "just as a jar, which is different in character from gold, is not of gold as its material cause. This is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), which is stated as: "because of being different in character" (*vilakṣaṇatvāt*).

Because this world differs from Brahman in being insentient and so forth, there is an absence of similarity; therefore, Brahman is not its material cause. Alternatively, this world does not possess the nature of Brahman, nor is it the material source of Brahman, because of their difference in character (*vilakṣaṇatvāt*). The meaning of the Sūtra is that both "being such" (*tathātva*)—meaning identity—and "difference in character" (*vailakṣaṇya*) are established by the word of the Śruti. And the Śruti cited in the Commentary, "It became both consciousness and unconsciousness," makes known the difference between Brahman and the world through the distinction between the sentient and the insentient.

As for what is stated in the *Candrikā*: "According to our own method, since the invalidity of the opponent's means of knowledge was already established previously by way of contradiction with one's own means of knowledge, it is proper here to refute only the invalidity of one's own means of knowledge, rather than avoiding the contradiction with logic regarding one's own position"—thus a refutation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is offered according to that manner; that is incorrect.

Since it was previously suspected that the principles stated in the Sāṃkhya system—which aim to determine the meaning of the Śruti—are more powerful, if one were not to establish their weakness, the refutation of the contradiction with the Sāṃkhya Smṛti would remain incomplete; therefore, in order to resolve that matter, it is necessary to state the weakness of such principles, which makes the aforementioned prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) indispensable.
