Otherwise, without completing the investigation into the absence of contradiction with the Smṛti under discussion, the consideration of challenging the *samanvaya* (the concordance of the Vedas) based solely on logical contradictions would result in a lack of coherence.

Furthermore, avoiding the issue of the validity or invalidity of one's own means of knowledge is not appropriate here. This is because those who maintain the authority of the Veda—such as Kapila, Brahmā (Kamalāsana), and others—cannot even entertain the doubt that it is invalid. Moreover, if Buddhists, Jains, and others are the opponents (*pūrvapakṣin*), it is impossible to prove the authority of the Veda by means of its eternity and so forth, which they do not accept and which would fail to establish their own validity. Finally, if the letters [of the Veda] were eternal, it would follow that the scriptures of the Buddhists and others would also possess authority.

Furthermore, the constancy of the sequential order [of the Veda] cannot be established without the authority of the Veda itself; for mere reasoning is common to Buddhists and others as well. If one attempts to establish that [constancy] by means of the self-validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) of cognition, then pursuing its distinction from other forms of eternity and asserting its establishment through scripture (*śruti*) would be redundant. This is because the authority of the *Kārīrī* and other such scriptural injunctions is already established by that very self-validity which must necessarily be accepted for the sake of the Veda's own authority. Moreover, there is no sublation of the object (*viṣaya-bādha*) even in those cases.

For this reason, one might suspect that there is a denial [of the Veda's authorship] therein; however, since there is no contradiction between the causal nature taught by the Śruti—which is characterized by intrinsic fitness—and the non-production of an effect in certain instances, on the contrary, it is the eternality of the sentence itself that contradicts perception. Furthermore, the postulation of an alternative explanation for that [perceived contradiction] is not easily established without the authority of the Veda.

As for the objection raised in the *Candrikā*—that this [section] is redundant because the doubt regarding the impossibility of Brahman being the material cause due to its distinctness (*vailakṣaṇya*) has already been refuted in the very section on "being an object of perception" (*dṛśyatva*) according to your own school—that too is incorrect. For although the logic of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) from that [earlier] section is presented in works such as the *Nibandha* in order to reinforce the present *pūrvapakṣa* and *siddhānta*, the subject matter (*prameya*) of that [earlier] section does not apply here.

As for the objection raised in the *Candrikā*—namely, that even if there is a rule that an effect must resemble its sole material cause (*upādāna*), in your view it is possible for Brahman to be the material cause while simultaneously being the efficient cause (as desired by the Siddhāntin), despite its lack of similarity to the world (just as a spider is not similar to its web)—this is refuted as follows: that [objection] is also incorrect. Even in the case of the spider, it is only the non-conscious saliva and so forth belonging to it that constitute the material cause, and the agency belongs solely to the intellect (*buddhi*).

For the Sāṃkhya opponent who asserts that the empirical usage of the Self as an agent arises merely through non-association [with the intellect], there is no agreement regarding the possibility of a conscious entity having an unconscious material cause; furthermore, my own position does not, according to the Sāṃkhya method, serve as a reason for the opponent's objection not to arise.

Furthermore, the objection raised in the *Candrikā*—namely, that according to your view, since ignorance (*avidyā*) or that which is qualified by it is the material cause, and because that cause shares the same characteristics as the world while the pure Brahman is of a different nature, yet the Self remains the substrate for the world's attributes and the delusion of the non-self in the Self is accepted even by the Sāṃkhyas and others, how can the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) even arise?—is also refuted by this very [argument].

Even when there is a difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), that which is qualified by those adjuncts is not distinct from the pure [Brahman]; therefore, it is easily understood even by a child—according to the Sāṃkhya method—that it is not logical for that [qualified entity] to be the material cause (*upādāna*). However, the status of being a material cause, in the form of being a cause non-different from its effect, belongs to the Pure [Brahman] as well. Yet, in order to indicate that this is of the nature of being the material cause through illusory manifestation (*vivarta-upādānatā*), it is stated that the Pure [Brahman] is the substratum of error (*bhrama-adhiṣṭhāna*). And such a status of being a material cause is not accepted by the Sāṃkhyas.

This is because they have refuted both the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) and the theory of the indescribable appearance (*anirvacanīyakhyāti*). Accordingly, the Sāṃkhya Sūtras state: "The plurality of spirits (*puruṣa*) follows from the fixed order of birth and so forth; the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is what differs, but not that which possesses it (*tadvān*); [bondage] does not arise even from ignorance (*avidyā*), for bondage by means of a non-entity is impossible; if it were an entity, there would be a loss of the established tenet; and if it possessed both contradictory forms, such a thing is never perceived."

Regarding this, the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) says: "Now, even if there is oneness of consciousness (*caitanya*), one might argue that the systematic order [of experience] can be established by admitting the distinctness of each [consciousness] as qualified by its respective limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). To this, he replies: "The limiting adjunct alone. It is only the limiting adjunct that is manifold; however, that which possesses it—the self as qualified by the adjunct—should not be admitted as manifold. The meaning is that if the qualified entity were distinct [from the pure consciousness], it would follow that even in other systems of philosophy the manifoldness of existence itself must be admitted. "Both contradictory [characters]" means being different from the real (*sat*) and different from the unreal (*asat*).

Furthermore, even in the view that the world is an indescribable manifestation (*anirvacanīya-khyāti*), since silver-superimposition is never observed in cases such as a clay pot or glass, it is necessary that the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the object superimposed (*āropya*) share similar characteristics; thus, the opponent’s doubt—that the status of Brahman as the material cause of the illusory transformation (*vivarta-upādānatā*) is impossible—is indeed very easy to maintain.

Furthermore, as for what was stated in the *Candrikā*: "Moreover, in my view, it is the similarity with non-Vedic Smṛti, denoted by the word 'tathātva' (being so), that is to be negated; but in your view, it is the state of having Brahman as the sole cause—which is not so denoted—that is negated. Thus, because of this difference, [the Sūtra] 'Smṛty-anavakāśa' (No room for Smṛti) refers to the opponent's argument under discussion as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), whereas in your view, the refutation is stated regarding Brahman, which is not the subject under discussion. This too is weak.

In my view as well, in the two preceding sections (*adhikaraṇas*), the Vedānta texts were established as being devoted to Brahman as the cause of the world; therefore, it is precisely the status of being the material cause of the world—which was present as a constituent of the probandum (*sādhya*)—and which was presented by the word *tathātva* (being such), that must be negated. Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the second sūtra introduced with "Or else" (*yadvā*), there is the fact that the world, which is under discussion as the locus of the agency and material causality constituting the probandum, possesses a dissimilarity (*vailakṣaṇya*) that serves as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Nor is it the case that this second interpretation is not approved by the author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakāra*).

As for the claim that the assertion "the conscious Brahman is the cause and material source (prakṛti) of the world" is untenable because this effect is of a different nature (vilakṣaṇatva), it must be said that this is not so, because such an interpretation is observed there. Therefore, in accordance with the conclusion of this section (adhikaraṇa) in the Bhāṣya—which states that "conscious Brahman is the cause and material source of the world" based on scripture (āgama) and reasoning consistent with scripture—it is precisely such an interpretation that is approved by the Bhāṣya.

There is no harm even in adopting an interpretation that follows the introductory commentary presented first—namely, that the world does not have Brahman as its material cause (*prakṛti*). For, just as in the sūtra "From which the birth, etc., of this [world proceed]" (*janmādyasya yataḥ*), it is possible here too for the word "this" (*idam*) to refer to the world established through perception and other means of knowledge. Furthermore, it is possible for Brahman, which is the primary subject under discussion, to be the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the difference [from the world]. And finally, it is possible for the word "being such" (*tathātva*) to refer to the property of being the determiner of the status of being a material cause residing in Brahman, which was presented as part of the probandum (*sādhya*) in the two preceding topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*).

In your view, when the word "Smṛti"—which presents itself in the feminine gender—refers by means of a pronoun to the Smṛtis such as the Pāñcarātra with the intention of making known the Śruti, it is not natural that the Śruti, which is being indicated by that very same feminine term in the sūtra *nātmāśruter nityatvācca tābhyaḥ*, should be referred to by the word *idam* (this), which does not possess that feminine gender.

As for the objection raised in the *Candrikā*—that because the difference between the world and Brahman is established by perception, the mention of "from that [word]" (*tatra śabdāt*) in the Sūtra is improper—and its refutation, that is based solely on a failure to see the *Bhāṣya*, since the refutation is extremely clear to those who have seen the *Bhāṣya*. For it is said there: "This distinction between the sentient and the insentient is well-known in the world."

Therefore, because it is dissimilar to Brahman, this world cannot have Brahman as its material cause. Having thus explained the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "because of dissimilarity" (*vilakṣaṇatvāt*), one might further argue: "Having heard that the world has a conscious being as its material cause, I shall understand the entire world to be conscious by that very authority; for we observe the persistence of the nature of the material cause within its modification. As for the non-apprehension of consciousness, that will be due to a particular transformation."

Just as the consciousness of selves, though possessing manifest consciousness, is not perceived during states such as deep sleep or fainting, so too the consciousness of wood, clods of earth, and the like will not be perceived. This [portion of the Sūtra] is intended to dispel such a doubt; for it has been explained that "this entire world is indeed unconscious in its nature, yet based solely on the authority of the Word (Śabda), one might speculate—relying only on the scriptural hearing that the world has consciousness as its material cause—that it possesses consciousness.
And that [speculation] is contradicted by the Word itself. Thus it has been commented upon.

Furthermore, as stated in the *Candrikā*: "Moreover, if the scriptural text 'both consciousness and non-consciousness' (*vijñānaṃ cāvijñānaṃ ca*) is the authority for their distinction, how then is it not an authority for [Brahman's] being the material cause? For the preceding sentence, 'It became both the existent and the non-existent' (*sat ca tyac cābhavat*), establishes its status as the material cause. Furthermore, the words 'consciousness' and 'non-consciousness' do not refer to effect and cause; rather, according to your own position, they refer exclusively to effects, just like the words 'existent' (*sat*) and 'true' (*tyat*). This is because, through the two occurrences of the word 'and' (*ca*), one perceives that 'becoming' (*bhavana*) is connected to each term individually. Such is the objection raised.

That too is not correct. When consciousness (*vijñāna*) is designated as sentient, and then non-consciousness (*avijñāna*) is designated separately from it, a non-sentient entity—distinct from the referent of "sentient"—is established, provided there is no subverting evidence to the contrary. Furthermore, since there exists subverting evidence in the form of scriptural texts stating that [Brahman] is changeless (*nirvikāra*), the scriptural mention of [Brahman] being the material cause (*upādānatva*) must be figurative; thus, the possibility of such a specific objection arises. For this very reason, the argument beginning with "and also because... and so forth is also refuted.

Merely by establishing a substance distinct from volition (*cetanā*), the position of the opponent under discussion is not connected [to the present argument], because even the eight [proponents of the Sāṃkhya system] do not rely on the view that the words "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) and "non-consciousness" (*avijñāna*) refer to cause and effect. Furthermore, the sentience of the cause is indeed accepted by the proponents of Brahman, as established by such scriptural passages as "Truth, Knowledge... and "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving."

Furthermore, as stated in the *Candrikā*: "Moreover, if the cause [of the world's difference from Brahman] were merely some kind of difference despite the absence of being its material cause (*anupādānatva*), then even if [passages such as] 'the clay spoke' do not intend to refer to the presiding deities (*abhimānin*), since a difference by way of purity, impurity, and so forth is established through perception and other means, the second sūtra would be redundant for the purpose of establishing that."

The objection was stated that if the difference [between cause and effect] is based solely on the presence or absence of consciousness (*cetana*), then since non-conscious things like cow dung serve as the material cause (*upādāna*) for non-conscious things like scorpions—and because a conscious being is never observed to have a non-conscious thing as its material cause—the third Sūtra would be untenable. To this, it is replied: For the opponent who asserts that the causal relationship is impossible due to such difference, what is intended here as the subverting factor (*bādhaka*) is merely the *possibility* of such a difference.

And that [nature] consists of the forms of consciousness and unconsciousness, as well as purity and impurity; and purity and impurity are ultimately defined by the presence or absence of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion, as has been demonstrated in the Bhāṣya itself.

Thus, although the opponent (the *ekadeśin*) might somehow resolve the difference based on consciousness and unconsciousness—given that the authority of scripture establishes purity in Brahman according to experience, while he himself accepts the impurity of the world—he cannot resolve the difference based on purity and impurity. Therefore, by the statement "Because of this [world's] being of a different character, it is not so [as Brahman]," the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been strengthened.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, the difference between being conscious and being unconscious is indeed difficult to avoid; thus, by abandoning mere dogmatic assertion (*abhyupagamavāda*), this is the primary resolution. Furthermore, that this is so is supported by a portion of the current sūtra, "And [the soul's existence] from scripture" (*tathātvaṃ ca śabdāt*), as well as by the second sūtra; therefore, this is not even a tangential discussion. 4.

Now, it might be argued that it is not correct to postulate the sentience of the world through the presumption based on the meaning of scripture (*śrutārthāpatti*), because such a presumption cannot arise due to its contradiction with the direct scriptural statement, "Both the conscious and the unconscious. This is indeed what is intended by the portion of the Sūtra beginning with *tathātvaṃ ca śabdāt*. However, that is incorrect.

Since clay and other elements, as well as the sense organs, are considered to be insentient, one might object: "How can it be understood that they possess sentience from such indicative marks as 'the clay spoke,' 'those waters reflected,' 'that fire reflected,' 'these vital breaths, disputing among themselves as to who was superior, went to Brahmā,' and 'they said to Speech, "Chant for us"'"? Furthermore, it should not be argued that the capacity of clay and the like to speak is impossible to conceive because it contradicts direct perception.

There is no room for the suspicion of contradiction regarding the scriptural statement that the clay at the time of the beginning of creation possesses the quality of being a speaker; nor should it be said that, even so, the sentience of contemporary clay remains unestablished, for its sentience is established by the fact that it is derived from a sentient source. And as for the non-perception of effects of a sentient being [in clay], the reason has already been stated. Thus, the scriptural passage, "consciousness and unconsciousness," is to be interpreted on the basis of the manifestation and non-manifestation of sentience.

Having raised the objection that the statement in the *Candrikā*—"By this [the second sūtra] is rendered inappropriate as a refutation, because even if clay and so forth were established as speakers and observers in passages such as 'The clay spoke,' their being such would not avoid the distinction between consciousness and non-consciousness mentioned in the previous sūtra (*śabdāt*), and thus the suspicion that clay and so forth are speakers is untenable"—is refuted, he offers the following resolution: "But the designation of [clay etc. as possessing breath and so forth is due to the persistence of the specific [characteristic]. (Sūtra 5) This means: the designation of clay and the like as having breath, speech, and so on is merely figurative, based on the persistence of their specific nature as material causes. Just as a king, though not actually a charioteer, is called a "charioteer" when he is seated in the chariot, so too clay and the like are metaphorically designated as "speakers" because they are the primary causes of the effects which possess speech and other qualities. Thus, the objection is answered.

The word "tu" (but) dispels the expectation raised by the opponent regarding the subject at hand, and thereby strengthens the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*); it does not, however, refute that position like the word "tu" occurring in the subsequent sūtra. One should not suspect the consciousness of the elements and the sense organs based on such scriptural passages as "the clay spoke," for this kind of expression—"the clay spoke"—is a designation of conscious deities presiding over the clay and speech, who are capable of engaging in activities such as speaking and conversing, which are appropriate for sentient beings. Why? Because of specific distinctions and because of the persistence [of consciousness].

Furthermore, the distinction between the enjoyers (the selves) and the elements and senses—characterized by the division between the conscious and the unconscious—has been stated previously. This distinction would not be tenable if everything were conscious. For this very reason, in the dialogue of the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), the Kauṣītakins read: "These deities, indeed, were disputing as to who was superior," and "All these deities, having recognized the highest good in the vital breath," in order to eliminate the suspicion that they are mere instruments and to establish them as presiding deities.

Furthermore, the Śruti passage beginning with "Fire, having become speech, entered the mouth" shows that the deities follow as benefactors within the sense organs. The detailed meaning of the Sūtra should be consulted in the Bhāṣya and other commentaries.

As for what is stated in the *Candrikā*: "Even though there are *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtras in the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā* and other systems, they exist only in the first quarter (*pāda*) of each respective chapter; whereas in your own system, such [pūrvapakṣa] sūtras are absent even in the first chapter. Furthermore, since the author of the sūtras does not employ the names of Jaimini and others—which would indicate a *pūrvapakṣa* position—anywhere else, it is certain that his style is one of non-composition [of such arguments], as seen in works like the *Vyākaraṇa* and the *Kalpasūtras*. Therefore, the entire scripture consists of some parts that present the opponent's view and some parts that do not reveal the ultimate truth, while some are devoted to meditation (*upāsanā*). Why, then, should this be rejected? [This is the argument from the *Candrikā* which the original text is responding to.]

Otherwise, one quarter or one chapter would constitute the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), while another quarter or another chapter would constitute the established conclusion (*siddhānta*); thus, the objection was stated regarding the two sūtras' function of establishing the prima facie view.

In this regard, the following must be said: since you—preeminent among those who propound meanings contrary to tradition—imagine that the fifth-case portion of the *sūtra* "itaravyapadeśāt hitākaraṇādidoṣaprasakteḥ" constitutes the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), despite its being entirely unobserved in other *sūtras* and even in other systems (*tantra*) as lacking the characteristic marks of a prima facie argument such as the word "if" (*cet*) and so forth; your statement rejecting the composition of a prima facie argument that does not contradict the style established in other systems is nothing but a source of ridicule.

If it is argued that the individual soul (jīva) is an independent agent because its agency is established by scriptural designations and other means, then it would follow that it could not perform what is beneficial nor commit what is harmful; such is the meaning of the sūtra *itaravyapadeśāt* as explained by Jayatīrtha and others.

In your own view as well, it would be improper to introduce a *pūrvapakṣa* sūtra at the beginning of the second chapter, even if such a sūtra has not been seen in the first two pādas of the preceding chapter—just as in the case of the third pāda where [the topic] "even beyond that, Bādarāyaṇa [says there is a possibility]" (*taduparyapi bādarāyaṇaḥ saṃbhavāt*) introduces a discussion that was not seen previously. For the fact that something is not seen in another pāda is no different from its not being seen in another chapter; thus, it is irrelevant. Therefore, the introduction of a *pūrvapakṣa* sūtra at the start of the second chapter is unjustified.

And Jayatīrtha has stated: "In the sūtra *taduparyapi bādarāyaṇaḥ saṃbhavāt* (Brahmasūtra 1.3.26), because it establishes that the gods possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman, there is a connection with the scripture (*śāstra*) and so forth; since this is incidental, a connection with the chapter (*adhyāya*) and so forth need not be sought."

Furthermore, it is observed that in the first chapter of the *Nyāyapañcādhyāyī*, there is the formulation of prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) sūtras such as: "Doubt does not arise from the ascertainment of common or multiple properties, nor from the ascertainment of one property [of two]"; and "Likewise, there would be perpetual doubt due to the ascertainment of contradiction and lack of fixity, because of the constant presence of those properties. Since these are formulated in the second chapter, this [objection] amounts to nothing. 5.
But it is indeed seen. || 6 ||

As for the argument that this world cannot have Brahman as its material cause because it is of a different nature—that which is of a different nature does not have that as its material cause, based on such pervasion (vyāpti)—that is incorrect. For in the world, we observe the production of conscious beings such as scorpions from cow-dung and the like, which are themselves insentient; and we observe the production of insentient things such as hair and nails from sentient beings such as men, who are well-known to be conscious. Thus, the reason [of difference in nature] is inconclusive (vyabhicāra).

[Objection: But surely the bodies of scorpions and the like, which are themselves insentient, are the effects of insentient things such as cow dung; likewise, the bodies of humans and the like, which are themselves insentient, are the causes of insentient things such as hair and nails. [Reply: What follows from that? For by that much, the difference [between cause and effect] is not avoided. Indeed, difference (*vailakṣaṇya*) consists in possessing a distinction that is non-conditional (*anaupādhika*). And this non-conditionality may mean either (1) having a relatum (*anuyogitā*) delimited by a property that does not reside in the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); or (2) possessing properties that reside in each other; or (3) possessing some kind of distinction whatsoever.

Because all three types [of qualities] exist in cow-dung figures and the like, as well as in the bodies, hair, nails, and body-hair of scorpions and the like. To explain: although they are insentient, the bodies of scorpions and humans serve as substrata for experience (*bhogāyatana*), whereas cow-dung, hair, nails, and so forth do not. Furthermore, the color, taste, and other attributes of cow-dung figures and the like are entirely different from those of scorpion bodies, hair, nails, body-hair, and so forth; thus, the distinction in their transformative nature (*pāriṇāmika-svabhāva*) is undeniable.

Furthermore, there is an absolute lack of similarity because the relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) is untenable, and because there exists a subverting argument against the contrary position. Alternatively, the "distinctness" (*vilakṣaṇatva*) employed as the reason consists in possessing difference that is non-contingent (*anaupādhika*), or rather, in possessing mutually exclusive properties that constitute the basis for that difference. And this [distinctness] is observed even in the case of material cause and modification according to the opponent's own doctrine; such is the meaning.

Such is the view of others. Having thus established the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) in the great principle (*mahat*) and the rest, he now states a specific qualification not mentioned in their inference of primordial nature (*prakṛti*): "The inference of the instrument from the effect must be performed through its association with the effect. That inference of the cause—which was stated as being based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) by means of the mark (*liṅga*) of the great principle and so forth—is intended to avoid neutrality; it must be done precisely through association with the effect. This is in accordance with such scriptural passages as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," and "In the beginning, this was darkness alone."

The meaning is as follows: the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest have as their material cause a substance consisting of the three qualities (guṇas) inherent within themselves, because they are effects—just like a statue existing within a stone block or a sprout [within a seed]. The supporting argument for this has already been shown previously. (134) To distinguish that primordial nature (prakṛti) from its effects, he states: "The unmanifest is [known] from the mark of the three qualities. From the effect consisting of the Great Principle and so forth—which is characterized by the mark of the three qualities—the root cause, the Unmanifest, is subtle.

For the qualities such as pleasure (*sukha*) and the rest are directly perceived in the *mahat-tattva*, whereas the quality of *prakṛti* itself is not directly perceived. Thus, the meaning is that *pradhāna* (the primary cause) is the supreme unmanifest (*paramāvyakta*), while the *mahat-tattva* is manifest (*vyakta*) in comparison to it. Now, one might object: "If it is supremely subtle, then its denial would be appropriate. In response to this expectation, he recalls what was stated previously: "Because it is established through its effects, there is no denial [of it]. This is easy to understand.

Thus, upon a critical examination of the Sāṃkhya-sūtra-bhāṣya in this manner, the aforementioned possession of an intrinsic difference between cause and effect is indeed unavoidable. For in this system, it is stated that each respective effect is produced by an *kṛti* (volitional effort) conditioned by its corresponding effect. If the effect were merely primordial matter (*prakṛti*) itself having entered into another state, then prior to the effect, since the state of the effect would not yet have been manifested and thus the effect would not be conditioned by itself, the aforementioned inference would be sublated.

Nor should it be argued that "being assisted by itself," as exemplified by the state of an effect (*kāryāvasthā*), is a constituent part of the probandum (*sādhya*). Even so, since such self-assistance is absent in *prakṛti* when it exists in an unmanifested state of effect, the aforementioned fault remains unavoidable. Furthermore, it is quite clear that if the assistance by itself is not intended, the exclusion of neutrality (*tāṭasthya*) does not occur. Otherwise, there would be an inconsistency with the Sūtra and Bhāṣya: "The inference of the cause from the effect is due to their concomitance."

[Objection: "But surely, even if the inference supported by the general pervasion (sāmānyavyāpti)—'whatever is different in character from something cannot have that as its material cause'—is vitiated by defects such as inconclusiveness (vyabhicāra), the following inferences remain entirely unassailable: 'The ether and so forth do not have Brahman as their material cause, because they lack the persistence of all of Brahman’s essential natures, or because they lack the commonality of Brahman’s essential natures, or because they lack identity with it, just like ignorance (avidyā)'? [Reply: No.

Even according to the opponent’s own view, as stated above, since all the inherent natures (svabhāva) do not persist in the transformations such as the Mahat and so forth, there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the total cessation of the relationship between material cause and effect everywhere; for it is impossible to prove that [the effect] does not have that [cause] as its material cause by means of the non-persistence of all its inherent natures, because the proponent (siddhāntin) accepts that the nature of "Being" (sat) persists in every instance of the subject (pakṣa). Furthermore, in the second inference, the reason (hetu) is unestablished (asiddha); in the third inference, there is an absence of an illustrative example (dṛṣṭāntābhāva), because it is accepted that everything is identical with Brahman as Being-Consciousness (saccidbrahma), and because "being an entity without beginning" (anādibhāvatva) serves as a limiting condition (upādhi). Further details should be understood from the Bhāṣya and other works.

As for the objection raised in the *Candrikā*—"The third [position] is also untenable; because, like cow-dung and the like, there is no transformation of Brahman into the world through the loss of its prior form, the cited example is inappropriate"—that is incorrect. For the point at issue is established merely by demonstrating the difference between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*); thus, the absence of absolute similarity between Brahman and the examples of cow-dung and so forth is irrelevant to the argument. || 6 ||
If it be said that [the world] is non-existent, we say no, because [that statement] is a mere negation. 7.

For if cause and effect were identical, then since the cause exists prior to production, the effect—which is non-different from it—would necessarily also exist; thus one could say that "the existent effect alone is produced. Furthermore, by asserting that the relationship of material cause (*upādāna*) and effect (*upādeya*) is possible even when there is dissimilarity (*vailakṣaṇya*), you have admitted that the conscious world is distinct from the conscious Brahman. Since dissimilarity is the antithesis of non-difference, the identity of the world and Brahman is impossible, and therefore [your position regarding] production is untenable.

Since it is impossible to establish the existence of the effect even when its prior cause exists, it would follow that the effect is non-existent prior to its production. If you argue that this is acceptable because it results in the abandonment of the doctrine of *satkāryavāda* (the pre-existence of the effect), we reply: no, because it is a mere negation. Since the statement you have made is devoid of meaning, it is merely a negating sentence and has nothing at all to negate. Indeed, this negation cannot negate the existence of the effect prior to its production.

To explain: the doctrine known as *satkāryavāda* (the theory that the effect pre-exists) is the position that the production of an effect—which is ultimately real—is its manifestation in the form of the cause prior [to its appearance]. Or, it is the doctrine that the effect is produced only while being manifested in a subtle form beforehand. Of these, the first alternative is already refuted; for, just as now, there would be no loss of the existence of the effect in the form of the cause prior to its production. Indeed, there is no existence of the effect apart from the nature of the cause at present, according to such scriptural passages as: "All this is abandoned by him who knows all this as other than the Self" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 2.4.6).

[Objection: Is it not the case that the phrase "of that which exists as the ultimate reality by way of its prior causal nature" means precisely "of that causal nature which exists as the ultimate reality at the time prior to the production [of the effect]"? Otherwise, the status of being the material cause (*upādānatva*), which consists in the cause being non-different from the effect, would be untenable. And if so, how can there be non-difference between two things of different characteristics? [Reply: This is due to a failure to understand our intention. For we do not assert an identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*) between Brahman and the insentient matter, which stand respectively as the material cause and the product.

Rather, since the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-rūpa*) of the manifold world (*prapañca*), which is imagined within Brahman as its substrate (*upādāna*), is Brahman itself, it lacks existence apart from Brahman—just as the silver imagined in mother-of-pearl lacks existence apart from the mother-of-pearl. Thus, because Brahman exists even prior to the emergence of the manifold world as its ultimate essential nature, this is what is meant by the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).

The second alternative, however, will be established in detail by the venerable Śrīmad-Bhāgavatpāda in the [Brahma-sūtra] passage beginning with "Its non-difference [from Brahman], on account of words such as 'originating' (ārambhaṇa)," etc.; thus, there is nothing at all untenable.

As for what is stated in the *Candrikā*: "If it be argued that [the cause] is an unreal effect (*asatkārya*), we say no; because its [the cause's] nature is a mere negation (*pratiṣedhamātratvāt*). Without requiring the insertion of words (*adhyāhāra*), this connects the reason and the probandum through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and directly implies that Brahman is the cause. "If it be argued that, according to you, the consequence would be an unreal effect," [the reply is]: "No; because the negation of the real effect (*satkāryapratiṣedha*) is a mere negation. Here, by inserting words and through non-coreferential construction (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), the connection is made, and it is pointed out that this does not directly imply that [Brahman is the cause]. Such is the critique stated.

Since it will be stated later that the natural consistency (svārasya) lies precisely in my own commentary by way of refuting the interpretations of those respective [other] commentaries on the Sūtras, it is clear to the learned that this is not a defect at all. || 7 ||
In the case of dissolution as well, it would be equally untenable, just as [in the case of creation]. || 8 ||

Is it not the case that in the Sāṃkhya-sūtra, "destruction is the dissolution into the cause," it is established that for effects, dissolution is simply non-distinction from the cause? And this view is acceptable to you as well, since in the sūtra "because of merging into its own [cause]" (svāpyayāt), you yourself have accepted that the meaning of the word "api" (also) is precisely non-distinction.

Moreover, if upon dissolution at the time of reabsorption Brahman were to attain non-distinction from its effects, it would follow that Brahman possesses the qualities of the effect—namely, grossness, having parts, insentience, finitude, impurity, and so forth; thus, the Upanishadic doctrine that omniscient Brahman is the cause of the world would be untenable. Other interpretations may be seen in the Commentary (Bhāṣya). Nor should it be doubted that because the effect and its qualities dissolve together, the consequence of contact with the qualities of the effect cannot be attributed to Brahman.

For it is impossible to avoid the consequence that the causes [of the world] would possess those attributes of their effects as well. Nor should it be argued: "At that time (the state of dissolution), since the attributes of the effect do not exist, how can there be the possibility of attributing them [to the cause]? Because these attributes are not absolutely non-existent like the horns of a hare; rather, they have simply reached a past state. And thus, the attribution of those attributes existing in a past state is unavoidable. Likewise, the attribution of the past state—which exists in the present as an attribute of the effect—to Brahman is likewise unavoidable.

As for the objection raised in the *Candrikā*: "If, at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), the cause for the destruction of the effect is its having attained the attributes (*dharma*) of Brahman, then since those attributes would be even more destroyed upon the destruction of the effect, it is improper to posit Brahman as the material cause (*upādāna*) at that time"—that is incorrect. For, in the *Sāṃkhyapravacanasūtra* it is stated that "destruction is the dissolution into the cause," and in its commentary (*bhāṣya*) it is further explained that "dissolution is simply the non-differentiation (*avibhāga*) of effects from their cause. Since this is so, the aforementioned doubt is consistent with that [system].

As for the objection raised in the *Candrikā*—namely, that since [the effect] attains non-difference from the cause even during its continued existence (*sthiti*), the term "in dissolution" (*apītau*) in the Sūtra is redundant—that too is incorrect. For one who maintains that "dissolution" (*laya*) is non-distinction (*avibhāga*) with the cause must state that the meaning of the word "dissolution" is precisely the non-distinction of the effect from its past state, occurring at the time of [continued] existence, in order to preclude the usage of the term "dissolution" during that period. Since such [non-distinction] is impossible during the time of continued existence, the inclusion of the word "even" (*api*) is purposeful. || 8 ||
He provides the resolution:
"But it is not so because of the existence of an illustrative example. (Sūtra 9)

There is no inconsistency whatsoever in our view. As for the objection that the Upaniṣadic doctrine is untenable because it follows that, at the time of dissolution, Brahman—having attained non-distinction from its effects—would incur the defects of the effects, such as grossness and unreality, that is not a valid criticism. This is because there exist illustrative examples of causes that, having attained non-distinction from their effects, do not become contaminated by the attributes of those effects.

Just as modifications such as bowls and the like, which have clay as their material cause, exist in a state of differentiation as high, low, or middling varieties, yet upon returning to their material cause, they attain non-differentiation from that cause and do not corrupt the cause with their own specific attributes; however, in your position, there is no such illustrative example. Indeed, merging itself would be impossible if the effect were to persist in the cause with its own attributes. The detailed exposition should be sought in the Bhāṣya and other works.

As for the objection raised in the *Candrikā*—namely, that this [section] is redundant because of the sūtra "But it is seen" (*dṛśyate tu*), which provides an example for the relation of cause and effect even between two dissimilar things, since that very sūtra already stated the example despite the fact that the properties of the effect, such as the scorpion's sting, do not occur in its cause, the cow dung—that is incorrect.

In that regard, since during the period when scorpions and other such creatures exist, they persist as being already distinct from their causes, there is no demonstration of the absence of confusion between their respective properties even when an illustration is given; for that reason, the effort of composing this sūtra is meaningful only to demonstrate that state of non-distinction [which exists prior to manifestation]. || 9 ||
And because of the defect in one's own position. || 10 ||

If it is asked how these faults are common to the opponent’s own position as well: first, regarding what was stated—that this world cannot have Brahman as its material cause because of its dissimilarity—that is equally applicable to the theory that Pradhāna is the material cause. This is because, according to the opponent's own view, the world possesses sound and other qualities while Pradhāna is devoid of sound and so forth; thus, the world possesses a non-conditional difference from Pradhāna (in the form of having Pradhāna as its counter-correlative), since such dissimilarity exists in the world even in that system.

And being "without limiting adjunct" (anaupādhikatva) means having a substratum-ness (anuyogitā) delimited by a property that does not reside in the counter-positive (pratiyogin). This has been clarified in the application of the Sūtra: "Not because of dissimilarity" (na vilakṣaṇatvāt).

In the view of the opponent (the Sāṃkhya), since the effect—possessing the three states of past, future, and present—is eternal, there can be no connection with existence in those [states] for the purpose of the conventional usage of "origination. If it is argued that the application or non-application of such conventions is based on manifestation (*abhivyakti*), then, because manifestation must be established precisely according to the method stated in the Sāṃkhya aphorism, and because manifestation itself is difficult to define, the doctrine of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*) is lost; this is a fault belonging solely to the Sāṃkhya. To explain: is manifestation already existent prior [to the operation of causes) or not? In the first case, the activity of the cause would be useless.

Furthermore, in the second case, since you admit the production of a manifestation (*abhivyakti*) that is distinct from the existing effect and is itself non-existent, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is destroyed right there. Nor can it be argued that because all effects are admitted to be both existent and non-existent prior to the operation of the cause, there is no room for the aforementioned dilemma; for, like a jar or other objects, the manifestation also lacks existence prior to its present state, and thus the operation of the cause is required precisely to remove that non-existence.

It should be stated that the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) remains unimpaired because of its future state, and because there is no contradiction in the existence of a single entity as both existent and non-existent through the distinction of its manifested forms. Even so, this must be rejected, because it leads to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), since one would have to posit a manifestation for the manifestation itself. Furthermore, you yourself have accepted the prior non-existence of manifestation precisely out of fear of such an infinite regress. Thus it has been said in the *Sāṃkhyapravacana*: "Or else, the fault is the same as that regarding origination."

On this point, the commentary states: Just as the production of the production of a jar is accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas and others who maintain the theory of the production of the non-existent (*asad-utpatti*) as being merely its own nature for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), so too we state that the manifestation of manifestation is merely its own nature for the sake of parsimony. The meaning is that there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*) even in the case of manifestation, just as there is none in the case of the production of the non-existent. If it is argued: "Even so, if one does not admit the manifestation of manifestation, then since its existence prior to the operation of the instruments would be untenable, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) would be undermined," we reply: No.

The intention is that the doctrine of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*) is established by the principle that there is merely the manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of what already exists. Furthermore, since manifestation itself lacks manifestation, even though it is non-existent prior [to its own manifestation], this does not result in the fallacy of the doctrine of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*). Nor should it be argued: "In my view, the doctrine of the non-existent effect applies only to that [manifestation], whereas in your view, it would apply to all effects"; for [in our view] the doctrine of the non-existent effect applies only to that [specific instance], while in your view, it would apply to all effects.

Furthermore, since the doctrine of *asatkāryavāda* (the theory that the effect is non-existent in the cause), which is attached to one position, would unavoidably apply elsewhere as well in the absence of a subverting argument; and because in my own position there is no such fault due to the doctrine of *anirvacanīya* (the indeterminable nature of the effect). Consequently, since the opponent also accepts the non-distinction of the cause from the effect at the time of dissolution (*apīti*), the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the properties of the effect—such as its pastness and so forth—applying to the Pradhāna is exactly the same [for both of us]. This is explained more fully and clearly in the Bhāṣya.

As for the objection raised in the *Candrikā*: "Just as clay alone—which is incapable of fetching water—is the material cause of a jar capable of such tasks, so too, although it is possible for the non-intelligent *pradhāna* (which lacks sound and other qualities) to be the material cause of the world (which possesses sound and other qualities), an intelligent being cannot be the material cause of a non-intelligent one; for this is never observed anywhere, and because [the intelligent] is changeless. This criticism—that the fault alleged by the opponent against you applies equally to his own position, and thus it is improper to charge him with a common defect—is also incorrect.

According to the reasoning stated, if the reason consisting in "possessing an unconditioned difference" were opposed to the relationship of material cause and effect, then that same consequence would apply to your own position as well. For, once Brahman’s status as the material cause of the world is refuted by the inference "Brahman is not the material cause of the world because it is conscious," then—due to the contradiction with the inference "Pradhāna is not the material cause of ether and so forth because it is not mentioned in scripture"—it would follow that Pradhāna also cannot be the cause of ether and the rest.

Since the observation of deviation is equal in both cases, it is impossible to avoid the charge that the fault is identical by the same logic; for nowhere in the world is an insentient thing seen to be the material cause of a sentient one. Just as, according to the opponent’s view, the Puruṣa does not undergo modification characterized by transformation merely through conjunction with Prakṛti, so too in my view, there is no contradiction with its being changeless even while being the material cause—given the admission that it is not modified by identity with an effect of unequal reality, and by the admission of its being an illusory material cause (vivartopādānatva). || 10 ||
If it is argued that the object of inference is established otherwise because reasoning lacks a firm foundation, even so, there follows the consequence of the impossibility of liberation. || 11 ||

Furthermore, it is not proper to deny the scriptural nature of Brahman as the cause of the world through mere reasoning alone; for reasonings are based solely on human imagination, and because human intellects vary, they lack a firm foundation. As it has been said: "An object that has been inferred with great effort by skilled logicians may be established in an entirely different way by others who are even more proficient."

Furthermore, even those such as Kapila and Kaṇāda, who are considered to be omniscient, are seen to disagree with one another; therefore, their systems lack stability. If it is argued that [the truth] must be inferred by means of a single reasoning (*tarka*) that is itself non-provisionally established (*apratiṣṭhāna-śūnya*), it cannot be said that there is no reasoning at all that is provisionally established. For if even the reasoning that establishes non-establishment were likewise [non-provisionally established], the desired conclusion would not be proven, and there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total destruction of all worldly and Vedic practices rooted in reasoning. Manu also says:
"One who desires purity in dharma should thoroughly understand the triad of perception, inference, and scripture consisting of various traditions."
He who examines the traditional teaching of Dharma with reasoning that does not contradict the Vedas and the Shastras knows Dharma; no one else does.

By saying this, he thinks as follows: [the opponent might argue] that by abandoning faulty reasoning (*sāvadyatarka*), faultless reasoning (*niravadyastarka*) must be accepted. Even so, although reasoning may be established in some respects, because reasoning is not established regarding the nature of the object of knowledge for the sake of liberation—which is inconceivable and profoundly deep—there would be no liberation at all. This is because of the traditional teaching (*smṛti*): "One should not apply reasoning to those entities which are indeed inconceivable. Alternatively, the meaning is that even so, there would be the undesirable consequence of non-liberation (*anirmokṣaprasaṅga*), that is to say, the consequence of the absence of liberation.

It is agreed by all proponents of liberation that liberation results from right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), and that right knowledge is of one and the same form, because it depends upon the reality of the object; and since there can be no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding a real entity, when this is the case, it is illogical for there to be conflicting views among persons regarding right knowledge. However, a conflict between the knowledges derived from the reasoning (*tarka*) taught by Kapila, Kaṇabhuj, and others is well known due to their mutual contradictions. Consequently, if liberation were otherwise—namely, based on the position of inference—there would be the unavoidable consequence of the absence of liberation, owing to the absence of right knowledge produced by such reasoning.

Alternatively, it is by way of the opposite of what was stated previously. For it was previously asserted that general reasoning (*tarka-sāmānya*) is unstable when devoid of the support of scripture (*śruti*) and so forth; however, this is not tenable. If the very reasoning that establishes the instability of general reasoning were itself unstable—due to its lack of the assistance of scripture and so forth—then the instability of general reasoning would remain unproven.

The meaning of the portion of the objection is as follows: Even if the principles used to determine the meaning of the Vedas were themselves rooted in the Veda, there would result an infinite regress; and even if they were not rooted in the Veda—such as the Śruti and so forth—it is nonetheless necessary that they be firmly established. Thus, it cannot be inferred that the arguments concerning "having different characteristics" (*vilakṣaṇatva*) and the like are unestablished by the aforementioned reasoning. [Reply: Only reasoning that conforms to Śruti and perception, whether directly or through a traditional lineage, is firmly established. Even the reasoning characterized by the "unestablished nature of reasoning" is itself nothing but reasoning that conforms to Śruti.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the Veda losing its authority due to the arguments stated by outsiders. Thus, even though reasoning (*tarka*) that determines the purport of the Veda is sometimes supported by perception, sometimes supported by scripture, and sometimes consistent with principles not opposed to them—and therefore is not irrelevant—the fact remains that even when such reasonings are well-established, the objection is unavoidable: namely, that there would still be the consequence of non-liberation (*anirmokṣa*). This is the essential meaning of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Alternatively, the phrase "because reasoning is unstable" (tarkāpratiṣṭhānāt) means that the general inference—"whatever is different from X is not produced from X"—cannot establish the probandum because it is impossible to make it applicable as a common feature of both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), since it is composed of specific categories. For in the case of the example, the pot, one must state that its difference from gold is the reason for its not being produced from gold; however, that same reason cannot be employed to prove the non-Brahman-originated nature of ether (*ākāśa*) and other elements.

Rather, [the intended meaning] is non-difference from Brahman. And thus, there is no attainment of identity between the delimitors of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) and the delimitors of the reason (*hetutāvacchedaka*) in the case of the example and the subject (*dṛṣṭānta-dārṣṭāntika*). Since the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is impossible when the reason resides in the subject (*pakṣavṛtti-hetu*) without such identity, inference itself becomes impossible. In the *Śāstrayonitva* Sūtra, for the purpose of providing mere probability regarding omniscience established by scripture, it is stated: "Whatever scripture of extensive meaning originates from a particular person, he possesses knowledge even more abundant than that."

Even when a general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*) is presented, there is no inconsistency, because it is not presented as an independent probans for any specific object. Now, one might object: since the delimiters of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) and the delimiters of the reason (*hetutāvacchedaka*) differ between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject (*dārṣṭāntika*), there is no grasp of pervasion for the reason residing in the subject; nevertheless, through the grasp of pervasion—defined by a probandum similar to the one at hand—with respect to a reason similar to the reason at hand, and through the grasp of the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), an inference of the probandum at hand is accepted.

Or rather, let it be intended that there is a specific pervasion (*viśeṣavyāpti*) by means of the example of ignorance (*avidyā*). And in that case, the aforementioned fault does not apply; thus he raises an objection: "Otherwise, it would be inferable" (*anyathānumeyam*). The meaning is: it would be inferable through a pervasion defined by a probandum similar to the probandum in question, or through a specific pervasion, based on a reason similar to the reason in question. Even so—that is, even under the stated position—[the fault remains].

The meaning is as follows: because of the consequence of non-liberation (*anirmokṣaprasaṅga*), if one were to resort to a general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*) based on reasoning—such as "if it has that as its material cause, or if it has Brahman as its material cause, then it would not possess a nature different from that [cause], or else it would not be different from Brahman"—for the sake of avoiding the charge of being irrelevant (*aprayojakatva*), then the aforementioned lack of foundation (*apratiṣṭhitatva*) would recur. Alternatively, the construction is this: the reason "having a different nature" (*vilakṣaṇatva*) is not irrelevant, because it is supported by scriptural texts teaching the changelessness [of Brahman]; thus, since this inference lacks a foundation due to defects such as the unestablished nature of its own form (*svarūpāsiddhi*), there is no liberation.

As for the argument that—because of the presence of the word "ca" (and), it is not logical for this to be a separate reason; and furthermore, it must be inferred otherwise—it is possible that the statement "tarkāpratiṣṭhānāt" (due to the instability of reasoning), which you yourself have accepted as part of a single sūtra, is to be inferred in a manner contrary to my own interpretation of the sūtras beginning with "svapakṣadoṣācca" (and because of defects in one's own position). Thus, being heard as a single syntactical unit with the probandum [of the previous sūtra] and functioning as a specific doubt, there is no loss of the causal relationship even between two dissimilar things.

The *Candrikā* states the following criticism: "Because reasoning is unfounded"—by thus splitting the sentence through its connection with the supplied probandum (*sādhya*), it is improper to state that [the reason] is supplementary to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Furthermore, there would be the consequence of an unwanted syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*) with the opposite of liberation (*anirmokṣa*), and the word 'prasaṅga' would be redundant. That is incorrect; for even in the absence of the word 'ca', since the word 'api' exists with the same meaning, it is appropriate to regard it as another reason (*hetvantara*).

Although, if it were intended to present a different reason (*hetvantara*), it would have been appropriate for the portion establishing that to constitute a separate *sūtra*, nevertheless, the adherence to a single *sūtra* is followed here in order to indicate that the portion "because reasoning is unstable" (*tarkāpratiṣṭhānāt*) also forms a single syntactic unit with the subsequent sentence, as it provides the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) to "non-liberation. [The Sūtras: "On account of seeing [it], [the Self] is not that which is non-scriptural; if it be argued that [the term 'Self'] is secondary, we say no, because of the word 'Self'. "The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman] because of repetition; if it be argued that it is not so because of the word denoting a modification, we say no, because of abundance (*prācurya*)."

If it is argued that [Brahman] does not speak because its "knowability" (jñeyatva) was not mentioned, we say no; for in passages such as "for [He] is wise, according to the context," the status of being a separate sūtra is respected because qualities like "seeing" (īkṣaṇa), "practice" (abhyāsa), and "knowability" do not enter into the meaning of the subsequent sentence. Otherwise, since the non-establishment of reasoning—which is immediately contiguous with the counter-correlate of the "otherness" expressed by the word "anya"—can be construed [with the previous], it would be inferior to accept a remote connection as the counter-correlate by supplying the word "iti" from the preceding sūtra.

Furthermore, the "unfoundedness" (*apratiṣṭhitatva*) of reasoning in general consists in its being fallacious due to the absence of corroborating reasoning (*anukūlatarka*); it does not consist in its being incapable of establishing a probandum through inference. For reasoning itself, as being included within the category of reasoning in general, would likewise be fallacious. Otherwise, since the reasoning favored by the proponent would fail to be established as fallacious, inference in any other way would be impossible. Thus, your interpretation—which aims to show that inference is contradictory on the grounds of the "unfoundedness of reasoning"—is itself inappropriate.

However, there is no fault in taking the word "tarka" to refer to reasoning alone when it is devoid of the assistance of either scripture or perception; for it is improper to assume that [the term] refers to a remainder of a doubt to be refuted, when it is possible for it to mean another reason that establishes the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

It is clear to the learned that, rather than adopting an interpretation based on the reason being subject to the aforementioned contradiction (*vyāhati*), it is more appropriate to construe the Sūtra by accepting the connection with a different probandum (*sādhya*), the resulting split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), and the ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) of the term "non-release" (*anirmokṣa*). In my own view, when the Sūtra is construed according to the first "or else" (*yadvā*) method and the second "or else" method, there is no possibility whatsoever of the suspicion of contradiction arising. Furthermore, if the phrase "due to the consequence of non-release" (*anirmokṣaprasaṅgāt*) is taken to mean "due to the consequence of the absence of liberation," the meaningfulness of the word "consequence" (*prasaṅga*) is exceedingly clear.

As for what is stated in the *Candrikā*: "Is the instability of reasoning (*tarka*) meant to apply to all reasoning whatsoever, or only to that which is not supported by scripture and the like? It cannot be the first, because the very reasoning that establishes the instability of reasoning would itself be unstable, thereby failing to prove that instability; furthermore, one must consider the consequence that the Mīmāṃsā inquiry would never begin, and there would be a contradiction with such scriptural and traditional texts as 'He is to be sought after, he whom one investigates through reasoning,' and so forth. Therefore, it cannot be the second."

The objection was stated that the argument based on dissimilarity (*vailakṣaṇya*), which seeks to prove that Brahman is not the material cause (*anupādānatva*), is supported by the scripture stating that He is "changeless" (*nirvikāra*). That [objection] is extremely weak; for, according to the aforementioned method, it is precisely such an argument—being unsupported by scripture and the like—that the *Bhāṣya* declares to be "unfounded" (*apratiṣṭhita*) through the phrase "by mere reasoning alone" (*kevalena tarkeṇa*), since the alternative [position] is merely imagined by one's own intellect.

As for what was stated—that because reasoning based on dissimilarity (*vailakṣaṇya*) is supported by the scripture stating "the changeless" (*nirvikāram*), it does not possess "isolation" (*kevalatva*) in the sense of being unsupported by scripture and the like—that too is extremely weak. This is because the quality of being changeless is contradicted by the weight of scriptural passages teaching that [Brahman] is the material cause (*upādānatā*). Furthermore, since there is no possibility of modification in the opposite case (if it were not the material cause), its conformity with the scripture "the changeless" is not established. Otherwise, the attempt to prove the causality of the existent (*sat*) and to refute that of the non-existent (*asat*) by the force of reasoning would be improper.

That which is established by the power of reasoning (*tarka*) can be established otherwise by a counter-reasoning (*pratitarka*), and thus reasoning lacks authoritative validity (*aprāmāṇya*). For there is no restrictive rule that a counter-reasoning will proceed only against a reasoning of this specific kind and not against one of such a kind. Furthermore, the argument you have stated is not "dry" (i.e., baseless), because it is consistent with such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent. Moreover, the fact that [your position] does not accord with reality in accordance with scripture applies equally to [the arguments regarding] "being of a different nature" (*vilakṣaṇatva*) and so forth; this is the general direction [of the critique].

Regarding the view of Ānandatīrtha: it has been stated that Viṣṇu’s status as the cause of the world is established on the basis of the authority of the Vedas and other sources. However, if the authority of the Vedas and other sources is contradicted by reasoning (*yukti*), then Brahman’s status as the cause of the world cannot be established; therefore, that [contradiction] must indeed be resolved. The subject matter is the Vedas and so forth themselves. The doubt is whether they are a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not. For instance, the lack of authority in such Vedic texts as "One desiring rain should sacrifice with the Kārīrī" would be unavoidable.

Even when the *Kārīrī* sacrifice has been performed, the non-perception of its fruit constitutes a deviation from the concomitance (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*), which subverts its status as a cause; thus, since [the texts] convey causality regarding things like the *Kārīrī* that are actually devoid of causality—just like the *Pāśupata* and other Smṛtis which teach matters lacking corroboration by visible results—the Veda and similar sources are not authoritative. Furthermore, if one part of the Veda lacks authority, there will be no confidence in the authority of its other parts; therefore, the Śruti and other texts are not valid means of knowledge, and the conclusion that Viṣṇu is the creator of the world is not established. To this, we reply: the aforementioned Śruti and other texts do not possess such a character [of unreliability].

The lack of authority [of such texts] is to be inferred through reasons such as the non-apprehension of what has been stated, as in the case of the *Smṛtis* of the Pāśupatas and others; for the aforementioned deviation from positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*) establishes their status as non-causes. This is because deviation from positive concomitance is observed even in the case of clay, staffs, and so forth, which possess an ascertained causal capacity regarding jars and the like—since the non-production of the effect is not established despite the presence of all other causes except for one’s own specific operation (due to contradiction). Furthermore, it is possible that other necessary causes, such as a qualified agent (*adhikārin*), are absent.

Nor should it be argued that, because of such discrepancies in results, the declaration of the Pāśupatas and others as non-authoritative would be inconsistent; for since their authority has not been established, there is no basis for postulating that their discrepancies are due to the absence of other [causal] factors. Furthermore, the same cannot be said of the Vedas, because they differ from those in their quality of being eternal (*nityatva*). And this eternity is established by the Vedic scripture: "By the word, which is manifold and eternal" (*vācā virūpanityayā*). Moreover, it is impossible to claim that what is eternal lacks authority.

Because the validity of a statement depends upon the defects of the speaker, there is no fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). For the validity of the knowledge produced by such scriptural texts as "By the word, which is eternal and multiform" is established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) and cannot be discarded without a sublation (*apavāda*). Furthermore, no cause for sublation—such as contradiction with other means of valid cognition—is perceived here. Thus, once validity is established, it is logical to conclude that any discrepancy regarding the result (*phala-visaṃvāda*) required to maintain that validity is dependent upon a deficiency in the causal factors. Moreover, the validity of the *Pāśupata* and other such Smṛtis remains unascertained.

"There is no room for such a construction there. Furthermore, since the *Smṛtis* such as the *Pāñcarātra* follow the Veda, they do not lack authority. Therefore, the conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the establishment of Viṣṇu as the cause of the world through the Veda and other sources is unimpeded"—this is how they explain the application of the Sūtra. Regarding this, the following criticism should be considered: since a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) can arise according to our own method even without challenging the authority of the Veda established in the *Pūrvatantra* and elsewhere, it is inappropriate to proceed with the prima facie argument by challenging that authority.

Furthermore, since Kapila, Kaṇabhuj, Pāśupata, and others accept the authority of the Vedas, this doubt does not arise by relying on their doctrines. For in the *Kapila-tantra*, one observes the interpretation of the Śruti through such sūtras as "There is no contradiction with the foundation of non-duality, because [the term 'Self'] refers to the genus," and so forth. Moreover, in the Vaiśeṣika-tantra, the authority of the Veda is stated explicitly in the five chapters of Nyāya by the words, "The authority of the Āmnāya arises from its being His word.
Thus requested by them, O best of the twice-born, I formerly composed this compendium (*saṃhitā*) which is joined with the performance of Vedic rites.

For it is stated in the *Pāśupatāgama*: "That itself is initiation (*dīkṣā*) in the Pāśupata, and that is the Pāśupata yoga. Furthermore, in the *Kāraṇāgama*, having etymologically defined a heretic (*pāṣaṇḍa*) as one who "protects" (*pāti*) the Veda (*veda*) and then "destroys" (*khaṇḍayati*) it—thereby asserting his own system's non-heretical status due to its lack of contradiction with the Veda, while stating that others possess such [heretical] status. Now, if it is argued that there is no prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) here based on the systems of the Jains, Buddhists, and so forth, then in that case, it would be impossible to establish the validity of the Vedas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) through their eternality and intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), which are not accepted by those [systems].

As for the argument that the authority of the Veda is established because there is no contradiction with the meaning of such scriptural passages as "with speech, which is eternal and multiform," that is not so; for even in that case, the contradiction with perception—namely, that "the letter *ga* has arisen" and "the letter *ga* has perished"—is equal. Furthermore, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is common to the Buddhist scriptures as well. The same applies to the non-eternality of the sequential order (*ānupūrvī*).

By this refutation of the discrepancy regarding results, the argument that the authority of passages such as "one should sacrifice with the Kārīrī" is established by their eternality—just like the *Smṛtis* of the Pāśupatas and others—is rejected. This is because, just as there is a discrepancy regarding results in cases such as the Kārīrī, there is an equal discrepancy with perception regarding certain parts [of the Veda], such as "with speech that is eternal by nature"; therefore, it is impossible to establish authority through the aforementioned eternality.

Furthermore, the interpretation of the meaning of the sūtra *dṛśyate tu*—which is recited immediately after the first sūtra, *na vilakṣaṇatvāt*, etc., and which describes the fruit for those qualified [for practice] as being "the fruit is seen," and defines "qualification" (*adhikāra*) as "fitness for the fruit," "freedom from obstructions caused by defects in ritual action," or "the complete assembly of all causes"—is also weak. This is because such an interpretation is useless, as even Buddhists and others do not refute the possibility that the occasional observation of results is merely accidental (*kākatālīya*).

As for the objection that the stated harmony [of the Vedas with reason] cannot be established because the Vedic statement "the clay spoke" (*mṛdabravīt*) and so forth possesses a meaning contradicted by reasoning—such as "clay does not speak because it is insentient"—and thus its authority is lost, which would lead to a lack of confidence in the entire Veda as a class of similar texts: this would indeed be the case if it were merely clay and the like that were being spoken of. But this is not so. It is the deities presiding over clay and the like who are designated there by the words "clay" and so forth. [Objection: Do they pervade the objects of their identification, or do they reside only in a part of them? If the former, are they possessed of a physical body (*vigraha*) or not? Not the first [alternative].

The first [alternative] is not tenable because it would entail their being perceived. Nor the second, because speech and so forth would be impossible. Nor the last; for if one objects that they would be useless since their presence in another location—just as in a place devoid of them—is logically established, we reply: indeed, they possess both omnipresence (*sarvatrānugati*) and corporeality (*vigraha*). And there is no entailment of their being seen, because even though they are omnipresent and corporeal, their non-perception is possible due to a specific capacity (*viśeṣasāmarthya*) distinct from other things. Such is the intended meaning of the Sūtra.

"Is it not better to accept the lack of authority of the Veda than to postulate deities for whom there is no proof and to postulate their specific powers? For this is simpler. Furthermore, that [existence of deities] is not established by the Veda, since there is dispute regarding its authority. To dispel this doubt, he says: "And it is seen. The meaning of the second sūtra is that the presiding deities and their powers are seen by great men. This too is incorrect.

In this case as well, since it is equally impossible to present arguments establishing such a conclusion for those who deny the authority of the Vedas—given that the objection regarding the impossibility of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by relying on the doctrines of Kapila, Kaṇabhuj, and others, and the argument for the conclusion (siddhānta) consisting of the vision of a Great Creator and a presiding deity, are not accepted by them—and furthermore, because the existence of presiding deities as objects of perception for a Great Person cannot be established apart from non-worldly means of knowledge such as Śruti and Smṛti; whereas in my own view, there is no inconsistency whatsoever, as the activity of the Sūtras concerning the presiding deities proceeds precisely without abandoning the authority of the Veda.

Furthermore, there is an objection that this contradicts the statement of non-existence (*asat*) being the cause, such as in the passage: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent; from non-existence, existence was born. To this, he says: "If it be said 'non-existent,' no, because it is a mere negation. The subject under discussion is the causality of the world. The doubt is whether this causality belongs to Viṣṇu or not. The seed of the doubt is the conflict between scriptural passages. In that regard, it is argued that Viṣṇu’s causality of the world is not tenable, because there is a lack of evidence for it. Nor can the scriptural text beginning with "From whence, verily... (*yato vai*) serve as evidence.

Because the Śruti passage beginning with "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1) declares that even the non-existent (asat) can be a cause; and because, although both types of statements are equally Śruti, the Śruti teaching that the non-existent is the cause is more powerful due to its being supported by reasoning in the form of inferences stated in works such as the *Tattvaprakāśikā* and *Candrikā*: (1) "The cause must be non-existent at the time of dissolution, because it is a real entity (vastu), like the effect"; (2) "The disputed entities must be non-existent at the time of dissolution, because they are real entities, like the effect"; and (3) "The disputed entities are non-existent at the time of dissolution, because they possess the nature of being existent (bhāvatva), like the [presently] agreed-upon [entities]. Thus, the non-existent alone [is the cause].

Regarding the objection that [the world] has no cause, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows: It is indeed logical that Viṣṇu is the cause of the world, but not that which is non-existent (asat). For the non-existent, being by its very nature devoid of the quality of existence, is an object of the cognition of negation solely in terms of its own essence. Here, it is refuted that a Vedic statement asserting the causality of the non-existent is contrary to reason. Even though all words are in harmony with Brahman, because [the world] is dependent upon Him, it is meaningful; since, through such arguments as "because it is subordinate to Him," it is accepted that even the secondary (amukhya) [meaning] is denotable, the possibility of the non-existent [being the cause] is precluded.

In the same way, the view that [the non-existent] is established by scripture is refuted. Because the refutation occurs subsequent to the formal agreement (samaya), it follows that the opponent's position, which contradicts reason, is rejected; thus is the application of the sūtra by the followers of Ānandatīrtha: "If it be said that it is 'non-existent,' no, because it is a mere negation.
