Regarding this, the following must be considered: since causality is necessarily bound to a connection with time, it is improper to even entertain the doubt that the non-existent could be a cause.

In this context, the term "non-existent" (*asat*) refers to antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). This is evident from the commentary found in Vyāsatīrtha’s *Candrikā*. As stated in the *Candrikā*: "Here, the word 'non-existent'—whether by taking the suffix *śatṛ* in its Vedic sense as an abstract noun meaning 'the state of not becoming,' or by emphasizing the abstract quality as 'the state of being non-existent'—refers to non-existence. Furthermore, it is his accepted view that antecedent non-existence alone possesses agency (*kartṛtva*), as established in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

For it is stated in the *Candrikā*: "In this context, the inquiry is whether Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of the world is contradicted by reasoning or not. For that purpose, [the inquiry is] whether the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the universe is the creator of the universe or not. For that purpose, [the inquiry is] whether the reasoning about to be stated—which establishes the agency of prior non-existence—is in harmony with scripture or not. For that purpose, [the inquiry concerns] the scriptural text: 'In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent (asat); that non-existence itself made the mind existent' (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.7). Is this scripture teaching the volition of prior non-existence, or of something else?"

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: first of all, the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the universe is the cause of the universe. This is because, like the prior non-existence of a jar with respect to that jar, it possesses an invariable antecedence that is not otherwise established (*ananyathāsiddha-niyatapūrvavṛttitva*). Otherwise, a jar that has already arisen would arise again; however, if prior non-existence is the cause, then due to its absence [after arising], there is no further production of what has already arisen. Furthermore, if prior non-existence were not a cause, there would be no distinction between the color, taste, and other qualities produced by baking (*pākaja*), since the difference among effects depends upon the difference among causes, and there would be no difference in any cause other than prior non-existence in those cases.

And it is heard [in scripture]: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent (asat). This establishes the causality of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). For here, the word "non-existent" does not refer to a void (*śūnya*); for that which is non-existent cannot function as a cause characterized by the necessity of subsequent existence, and because such an interpretation would contradict the statement of existence in the word "it was" (*āsīt*).

And thus, once the causality of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is established, even though it has not been observed in other cases of prior non-existence, the agency of the universal prior non-existence will be proven by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*). This is because the non-existence of all entities at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*) is established by the inference: "The disputed entities are non-existent at the time of dissolution, because they are entities, like an effect"; and because an effect is necessarily possessed of an agent.

Furthermore, it is simpler to postulate the agency of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the created world than to postulate a Lord, His agency, and so forth. Moreover, we observe the use of the instrumental case and others even for an insentient agent, as in "the axe [cuts]" (*svadhitinā chinatti*). Thus, let the universal prior non-existence possess agency, even though it is bodiless and a material cause (*upādāna*), just like the Lord. This is supported by the scriptural passage, "That was non-existent; it made itself the mind" (*asad evedam agre āsīt, tad ātmānam svayam akuruta tan mano 'kuruta*), where the referent of the word "non-existent" (*asat*) is the universal prior non-existence, and where either the word "mind" (*manas*) or the verbal suffix denoting the agent indicates its possession of knowledge, will, and other such qualities.
If it is argued that since an object must be accepted exactly as it is conveyed by its word, agency belongs to prior non-existence alone;

No; for, since it is unnecessary to abandon the natural sense of the words as they appear in the Śruti, the term *tat* must—by the principle that "the [meaning] depends on that" (*tadadhīnatvāt*) and "it is meaningful because it depends on that" (*arthavad iti pravṛttinimittatādadhīnyanyāyena*)—be taken as referring exclusively to Brahman. This is done in order to maintain syntactic unity with numerous Śruti passages such as "from which indeed these beings are born," thereby avoiding the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of accepting whatever meaning might somehow be suggested, which would contradict the intent of the final section (*adhikaraṇa*) of the first chapter, which states: "By this, all [other cases] are explained. Thus, according to the Śruti, it is appropriate that the word refers only to Brahman.

Because the agency of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is not established [in scripture]. In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the doctrine of non-being as the cause would contradict many scriptural passages declaring Brahman to be the cause; thus, the meaning of the scripture would be forced. Now, one might ask: how can there be a prima facie view that disregards the natural force of the word "non-being" (*asat*) found in the scripture?

Since the word *asat* is not used in the sense of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) by way of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), and since even the Vaiśeṣikas and others who maintain the doctrine of prior non-existence do not employ that term for it, the Sūtra-author—in passages such as "because the non-existent is not perceived" (*nāsato ’dṛṣṭatvāt*)—must be understood, according to your own view, as referring to the Void (*śūnya*) alone by that term. Consequently, although there is a possibility that the word *asat* here denotes prior non-existence through the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "that which is other than existent" (*sad-bhinna*)—which is further specified as being "other than a positive entity" (*bhāva-bhinna*)—the word *asat* in this context [refers to the Void].

Regarding the suffix *śatṛ*, whether it is taken as establishing a Vedic state (*chāndasabhāva*)—in which case "non-existence" (*asat*) means "the state of being non-existent" (*asattvam*)—or as emphasizing the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*), such that it refers to "non-being" (*abhāva*), your opponent (the pūrvapakṣin), who through such effort describes the suffix as having the meaning of prior negation (*prāgabhāva*) because prior negation alone possesses the status of the agent, falls into the error of rendering that effort futile. Consequently, since he does not intend for the suffix to denote prior negation in that manner, and since prior negation—as an object of denotation—is distinct from existence by virtue of possessing the nature of an existential attribute (*bhāvadharma*).

The claim that "being a mere negation" culminates in "the state of being real" (*satyabhāvatva*) is unestablished; for, if one analyzes the nature of the reason according to your own method, it is impossible for prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) to be distinct from existence (*sat*). Even if it were somehow possible, by that very same logic, its status as a mere negation would also be possible, thereby resulting in no lack of essential establishment (*svarūpāsiddhi*). Furthermore, since the effort to define the nature of the reason—beginning with the phrase "without having the nature of an absence-property" (*abhāvadharmātmatām antareṇa*)—to refute that [claim] would be futile, [the reason applies] to the word "non-existent" (*asat*).

Understand that there is an inherent lack of propriety in taking [the word "not"] to mean antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Furthermore, since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of antecedent non-existence, its status as the agent cannot be established by scripture. Nor should it be suspected that the very cognition—"After the production of the jar, the antecedent non-existence of the jar existed here"—is itself the proof for its existence.

Immediately after its production, because prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is non-existent, the pot itself is also non-existent prior to its production; thus, since no relation can be established between the pot and its prior non-existence while either is non-existent, the fact that prior non-existence belongs to the pot remains unproven. Nor can it be argued that the relation is simply the state of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and the substratum (*anuyogin*), for that is a specific type of essential relation (*svarūpasaṃbandha*). Since it consists of the individual essences themselves, it is not accepted as a "relation" in the same way that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and other such relations are, because mere cognition does not establish the reality of an object.

This is because the relationship between the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and the substratum (*anuyogin*) can only be a relation if it is itself connected by some other relation; otherwise, it would be subject to the dilemma of being either unrelated or [improperly] related. Furthermore, such a cognition is accounted for by its having the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of the jar as its object. Nor is it the case that prior to its production, there is only the antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the jar in the clay and so forth, and not its absolute non-existence; otherwise, according to the doctrine of the pre-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*), even a rabbit’s horn would result in production through the operation of causal factors.

It cannot be asserted that such a cognition has only prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) as its object and not absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), because the specific distinction mentioned remains unestablished given the lack of difference in non-existence prior to production. Furthermore, according to that [opponent’s] view, the production of a rabbit's horn would have to be admitted; moreover, even a jar already produced would be produced again, and there would be no distinction between qualities such as color and taste produced by baking, if prior non-existence were not a cause.

Regarding the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "because there is no other cause [for the non-existence of the jar] there, since it is non-different [from the jar]," what is stated in the *Candrikā* is not correct. This is because it is impossible to entail the production of a jar already produced by postulating the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of the jar as its cause—given that the jar itself is established as an obstacle (*pratibandhaka*) to itself. Indeed, the existence of the absolute non-existence prior to the production of the jar has already been demonstrated; for it is the very nature of things that a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*) produces only a single effect.

Because there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in postulating a property (*dharma*) rather than a substratum (*dharmin*), and because you yourself have stated that the parsimony consisting in the causality of a previously established antecedent absence (*prāgabhāva*) is superior to the postulation of God and His agency; therefore, that [undesirable] consequence does not follow. Furthermore, due to the absence of causes such as the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of that moment, the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is absent, and thus that consequence does not follow.

Nor does it follow that there would be no distinction between the color, taste, and other qualities produced by baking (*pākaja*), because the cause—other than prior non-existence—is non-different; for the distinction between those qualities is established precisely by conforming to the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), namely, that a specific type of baking, consisting of contact with fire, is the cause of [qualities] delimited by a specific type of heterogeneous color, existence, and so forth. This is because it is impossible to establish their identity against both that causal relation and the contradiction of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, how could it be maintained that a jar already produced would be produced again? Since the production of what has already been produced is being asserted, such an assertion is impossible because it is unestablished (*apasiddha*). This is because the postulation of its causes—the factors that would bring about such a production—is itself untenable; otherwise, one would face the absurd consequence (*āpatti*) of even a rabbit’s horn being produced. Moreover, how is it possible to assert that color (*rūpa*), taste (*rasa*), and so forth—which are perceived as distinct by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—could become each other (e.g., "color becomes taste")? Since taste is simply absent in color, such a transformation is logically impossible. Enough of this.

Granted that the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is established in order to prevent the re-arising of a jar that has already been produced, nevertheless, it is established only as having those specific individual jars as its counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*). This is because there is no proof for a separate prior non-existence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by "universality" (*viśvatva*), and because logicians (*tārkika*) who do not accept that destruction and prior non-existence have counter-correlativity delimited by a general property (*sāmānyadharma*) do not admit such a thing.

Even for those who maintain that [the absence] is a general absence (*sāmānyābhāva*), it is impossible for there to exist at any time—whether it be a moment possessing the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of one particular instance or the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of another particular instance—a destruction or prior non-existence whose counter-positive is delimited by the generality (*sāmānyāvacchinnapratiyogitā*). Following the direction stated by the author of the *Dīdhiti*, since such a destruction can only occur during the Great Dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), it is necessary to accept that, just like the final destruction, only the initial prior non-existence possesses that status; thus, it is the initial prior non-existence alone that must be so designated.

And this being so, the following doubt is indeed appropriate: since it is impossible for that [Brahman], having perished after producing its first effect, to be the agent of subsequent effects such as the second one, how can it possess the status of being the creator of the universe? If you argue that this fault does not apply because one may postulate various powers conducive to each respective effect within the very prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the first effect, we reply: your opponent in the previous argument could not possibly maintain that there are powers distinct from prior non-existence, given his own attempt to establish the non-existence of all things at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*) by using "being an entity" (*bhāvatva*) as the logical reason.

Furthermore, if power (*śakti*) were of the nature of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of an effect, it would necessarily perish upon the destruction of that non-existence, and thus the aforementioned fault would remain unremoved. Moreover, since the Vaiśeṣikas and others who maintain the doctrine of prior non-existence do not accept "power" as a distinct category (*padārtha*), if they were to accept it, a jar that has already been produced would be produced yet again.

Furthermore, if antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) were the cause of origination, there would be no distinction between the color, taste, and other qualities produced by baking (*pākaja*), because their cause—namely, antecedent non-existence—is identical in each case. This is because the argument previously stated in support of the prima facie position—that antecedent non-existence cannot be established as the cause of the effect—would result in its own impossibility. Moreover, if one accepts the category of "potency" (*śakti*), it is impossible to entail the re-origination of a jar that has already been produced, since the potency conducive to its production is destroyed by that very production.

Furthermore, the distinction between color, taste, and other qualities produced by baking is logically accounted for by the distinction between the potencies that serve as their causes. Thus, the category of "potency" must be accepted.

This is because the very establishment of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is difficult to maintain. Nor is it easy to accept the claim made by some that the opponent’s intention is as follows: "There is only one antecedent non-existence which has all effects as its counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*); the specific relation to each respective counter-correlate residing within that [non-existence] perishes through the production of each respective effect. For this contradicts the conclusion stated in the Siddhānta (the established doctrine), which asserts that the antecedent non-existence of each specific effect is itself the cause of that effect.

Furthermore, this contradicts the statement in the *Candrikā* regarding the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that—having accepted that a single antecedent absence possesses the property of having each respective effect as its counter-positive and taking that absence to be the cause—one could, due to a lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*), likewise accept all antecedent absences to be causes; and thus, rather than postulating a Lord and His agency (which is more cumbersome), it would be simpler to postulate antecedent absences as the causes. Moreover, such an antecedent absence as you intend is not established by any prior cognition.

Furthermore, since your opponent (the pūrvapakṣin), while attempting to establish the non-existence of all entities at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), cannot maintain that the relation of being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*) of this or that entity is something positive (*bhāvarūpa*) distinct from antecedent negation (*prāgabhāva*), it follows that this must be a specific essential relation (*svarūpasaṃbandha*) consisting of antecedent negation. Consequently, because an antecedent negation that persists for the sake of producing one effect after another has been produced cannot possibly perish while remaining, the unavoidable consequence is that what has already arisen would have to arise again.

Nor should it be argued that the intended meaning is merely that each specific prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is the agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to its respective effect, and that this alone constitutes the designation of being the "creator of the universe" (*viśvakartṛtva*); for if that were so, Vyāsatīrtha’s presentation of a doubt regarding the meaning of the scriptural passage—"In the beginning this was non-existent; that Non-existent [made] itself the mind"—would be inconsistent. For he asks whether this scripture teaches the volition (*saṃkalpa*) of prior non-existence, or if it has another purpose. Indeed, volition is an effect of prior non-existence.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for that very same destroyed prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) to produce another effect, and because it is established both by experience and by reasoning that every effect possesses a material cause (*upādāna*) just as it possesses an agent (*kartṛ*), the opponent who seeks to prove the non-existence of all entities at the time of dissolution must assert that, with respect to the first effect, the prior non-existence itself is its material cause.

This being the case, since it must necessarily be stated that the material cause persists in the effect that arises subsequent to its volition, to describe that cause—which exists beyond the limits of prior non-existence—as having the nature of "prior non-existence" (prāgabhāva) is utterly incoherent. Furthermore, the property of occupying the same locus as its counter-positive (pratiyogin), which is established in other systems [of philosophy], is impossible in the case of the prior non-existence of the universe as conceived by your opponent, who maintains the existence of a Creator of the universe prior to creation; for [according to him], only positive entities exist at the time of dissolution (pralaya).

Thus, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*)—which transgresses the established boundaries of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)—is utterly untenable. Furthermore, it is heard [in scripture] and observed that the instrumental case and others are prescribed even when an insentient entity functions as an agent; therefore, by accepting a figurative agency for antecedent non-existence based on the meaning of the scriptural text, the prima facie argument does not contradict the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding Viṣṇu’s primary agency.

According to the Advaita method, in the section beginning with "Because of the difference in nature" (*na vilakṣaṇatvāt*), the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that Brahman cannot be the material cause because it is of a different nature from the world; for even if there is a rule that a pure material cause must resemble its effect, in your own view, just as a spider (*ūrṇanābhi*) is the material cause of its web despite being different in nature from it, it is possible for Brahman to be both the efficient cause—as intended by the Siddhāntin—and the material cause, despite its difference in nature from the world. Thus, the prima facie argument stands.

By refuting [the opponent] on the grounds that [his view] contradicts the established doctrine (siddhānta), you yourself have rendered it impossible to establish. For the meaning conveyed by such scriptural passages as "That which was non-existent became existent; it thought, 'May I be many,'" must be accepted exactly as it is expressed in the words. Thus, the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa)—which relies upon the primary sense of agency consisting in the possession of knowledge, will, and so forth—is already effectively refuted by the rejection of the meaning of the word "non-existent" (asat) as referring to antecedent negation (prāgabhāva), given its inherent lack of natural fitness for that sense; it does not deserve to rise again.

Furthermore, since it is possible that this sūtra is merely intended to refute the contradiction with such reasoning as—namely, "disputed entities are non-existent at the time of dissolution because they possess the nature of being entities, like that which is agreed upon"—by establishing the non-existence of all entities whatsoever at dissolution, thereby refuting the status of God as the cause, you should describe the agency of the universe attributed by the opponent to a non-entity (alīka) or a prior absence (prāgabhāva) as being based on nothing but stubbornness; for that [interpretation] is improper.

Nor is it appropriate to refute arguments that are subordinate to scripture for the sake of establishing this particular topic (*adhikaraṇa*) as I intend it; for since agreement with scripture must necessarily be asserted, the agency of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), though irrelevant to the present context, was accepted because it was the position of the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*). As stated in the *Candrikā*: "In this [section], the contradiction with the reasoning that establishes the agency of antecedent non-existence—which is subordinate to scripture—is refuted; however, the doctrine of non-existent causality (*asatkāraṇatva*) obtained through mere convention is not."

It cannot be established by scriptural authority alone, because that is refuted in the second [section]. Nor can it be established by scriptural authority subordinated to reasoning, because that is connected with the third [section] alone. Nor can it be established by both scriptural authority and reasoning of equal weight, because that is also connected with the third [section]. Nor can it be established by reasoning alone; for it must not be argued that what was rejected in the previous section due to conflict with firm reasoning would here arise as a prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) based on mere reasoning, since such a prima facie view does not arise here through mere reasoning.

The reasoning that establishes the non-existence of all entities during the dissolution (*pralaya*) cannot be proven to be rooted in scripture (*śruti*). Nor is it reasonable to claim that the very scriptural passage teaching the agency of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) implies the non-existence of all entities during dissolution for the sake of establishing its own meaning; for even if other entities exist during dissolution, the agency of prior non-existence remains logically possible, and thus the aforementioned implication is unnecessary for that purpose.

Furthermore, because it has been stated that the term "non-existent" (*asat*) does not refer to prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), owing to the absence of its own inherent meaning [in that sense] and because such an interpretation would contradict scriptural passages such as *yat īva* and others; moreover, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) that prior non-existence possesses agency is contrary to the *Tattvaprakāśikā*.

For regarding that [position], one might indeed object: "Even if this were so—that there is an attainment of the non-existent—why could it not be the case that the doctrine (samaya) in this regard is being refuted? To address such a doubt, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) introduces the statement, "It is precisely what is established by scripture," because the doctrine of the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) will be refuted in the subsequent section (*pāda*). The sense is that one must accept that here only the doctrine of non-existence as established by scripture is being negated; otherwise, there would be the fault of redundancy. This is the intended meaning of the commentary. Furthermore, the proponent of emptiness does not assert that antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) functions as a cause.

Since this would result in redundancy with the statement regarding the contradiction of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) acting as a cause, the description of the meaning of the phrase "because of the appearance of redundancy" found in the *Candrikā*—namely, that there is redundancy because there is no time that brings about prior non-existence here, and because it will be refuted later even in the refutation of the Void (*śūnya*)—is simply unacceptable, as it contradicts [the author's] own statements and contradicts the statements in the *Sudhā*.

For instance, in the *Candrikā*, regarding the objection that the section on Smṛti (Smṛtyadhikaraṇa) should not be placed in the quarter (pāda) consisting of the removal of contradictions with reasoning, it is stated: "Since the Smṛtis such as the Pāśupata possess four aspects—namely, being of the nature of traditional precepts (samaya), providing corroboration for its own stated meaning, and presenting scriptural authority and reasoning—their non-contradiction [with the Vedas] is established through these four forms. Consequently, even though they are not included in any specific quarter that establishes non-contradiction with only one of these [four], when they must be accommodated within the chapter on non-contradiction (Avirodhādhyāya), they should be placed first, rather than skipping over the initial [quarter]."

Because there is an absence of a logical reason (*hetu*), because it possesses a fourfold nature, and because it must be refuted first due to its strength, its placement is at the very beginning. In that context, by the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "of the *Smṛtis* such as the Pāśupata," the *Smṛtis* of the Buddhists, the Jains (*Ārhata*), and others are included, since the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣas*) according to their respective systems have already been shown in the *Smṛtyadhikaraṇa*. As for what was stated—that Viṣṇu, the Supreme Brahman, is the cause of the birth and so forth of the entire world—that is incorrect.

This is because [the opponent's position] contradicts the Smṛtis of the Pāśupatas, Buddhists, Sāṃkhyas, Ārhats, and others; for this is stated in the *Sudhā* commentary on the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the "Section on Smṛti" (*Smṛtyadhikaraṇa*). And in the *Sudhā*, regarding this section (pāda) characterized by the removal of contradictions with reasoning (*yukti*), it is stated: "The removal of contradictions with Smṛti should not be undertaken here, because it would be irrelevant."

Or, in response to the doubt as to why "duty" (*kartavyatā*) has primacy, one should introduce the phrase "of that" (*tasyāḥ*) as a restatement of the opponent's view; for this is what is being said: the *Smṛtis* such as the Pāśupata and others, although they take the form of a convention (*samaya*) because they are the words of those whom [the author] himself regards as authoritative, nevertheless corroborate their own intended meaning with reasoning and scripture, and thus consist of the fourfold [means] beginning with reasoning and convention. Consequently, the resolution of contradictions with those [other authorities] regarding the matter stated [in the previous chapter] is indeed included within this very chapter.

However, although this [topic] is connected with all four quarters (pādas), it does not fit exclusively within one quarter alone; therefore, it ought to be stated either at the beginning of the chapter or at its end. Furthermore, it has been stated that in the first section (adhikaraṇa) it is established that there is no reason for bypassing the initial [quarter].

Thus, introducing the root text with the statement that another fourfold division is also taught—namely, that "each [quarter] consists of four aspects"—it is explained as follows: "All four quarters should be understood to possess four aspects each, being endowed with the meaning of the fourfold set of quarters. For example: even this quarter, characterized by the removal of contradictions with reasoning (*yukti*), also consists of the removal of contradictions regarding the three [other] quarters beginning with the *samaya*."

Similarly, the second [section], which consists of the avoidance of contradictions regarding the *samaya* (traditional tenets), also becomes one that avoids contradictions regarding the three means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and so forth. When it is stated simply as "the first section" (*ādyapāda*), it might be understood as referring only to those [topics] contained within this specific chapter due to their proximity; for that reason, the word "all" (*sarva*) is used. The meaning is: "even those connected with all the chapters. It should be noted that whichever section belongs to a particular chapter possesses the meaning of all four sections belonging to that chapter. Not only the sections themselves, but also their constituent parts [are included].

Those which have such quarters (pādas) as their parts are "tadaṃśāḥ," meaning chapters (adhyāyas). The first chapter is a presentation not only of *samanvaya* (harmonization), but also of the triad beginning with *avirodha* (non-contradiction). Since the chapters consist of four quarters each, it follows that the sections (*adhikaraṇas*) likewise consist of four. Nor should it be argued that this results in an untenable distinction between chapters and so forth, or the fault of redundancy; for there is consistency through a difference in intended meaning (*vivakṣābheda*). When the first [chapter] intends to convey the meaning of *samanvaya*, it does not intend the other meanings of the subsequent ones, and so forth.

And likewise, in the case of an unreal locus (*asad-adhikaraṇa*), since the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of that which is to be negated lacks the status of being established by time, it would be impossible for its locus—consisting of a collection of loci including that [non-existence]—or for the "feet" [of the syllogism], to possess four aspects and so forth; for even that which is established by scripture must necessarily be established by time.

Thus, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the agency of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is contrary to your own commentary (*bhāṣya*). For there, it is stated: "In this case, only that view which is established by scripture (*śruti*) is refuted; because the prohibition [of the view] occurs subsequently. If, however, there were an absence of a rule (*samaya*) establishing prior non-existence, then the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "only that which is established by scripture" would be redundant. But in the position that refutes the Void (*śūnya*), since that [view] is established by both scripture and rule, the prohibition here is made specifically as being established by scripture in order to exclude it from being established by rule.

But it is not [negated] by virtue of its being obtained through *samaya* (convention). The purpose of the particle *eva* is precisely to indicate that such a negation does not occur above [the level of *samaya*]. For this very reason, instead of saying "because of the negation of the void (*śūnya*) above," it is said "because of the negation of *samaya* above"; thus, even though the property (*dharma*) is the same, the resolution is stated solely on the basis of the difference in the substratum (*dharmibheda*). Likewise, regarding the scriptural term "non-existent" (*asat*) in the passage "In the beginning, this was non-existent," if one were to establish that it refers to prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and thereby justify its being established by scripture, there would be a contradiction with the *Tattvaprakāśikā* on the section beginning with "By this, all [objections] are explained."

For in that [section], the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) raises an objection against the reconciliation (samanvaya) by asserting that words such as "non-existent" (asat) and so forth do not denote Viṣṇu: "Viṣṇu is not denoted by words such as 'non-existent,' because those words denote an entity known through negation, and because that is incompatible with the Supreme Self, which is a positive existence (bhāva). Nor can it be argued that even if the Supreme Self is not itself known through negation, the non-existent (asat)—which possesses that [negation]—is dependent on the Supreme Self, and therefore He is denoted by words such as 'non-existent.'"

It has been stated that for that which is devoid of its own nature (svarūpa), there can be no dependence on another because it lacks the status of being something to be regulated. However, if the word *asat* signifies prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), then that [prior non-existence] does not lack its own nature. Furthermore, in the *Sudhā* commentary, under the section on *asat*, regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that prior non-existence is the agent, it is stated that since prior non-existence possesses the existence of its own nature and so forth, it is logically consistent for it to be the object of such scriptural applications as "Being alone" (*sadeva*).

Otherwise, the statement "because that which is devoid of its own nature lacks the status of being regulated, it is impossible for it to be dependent on another" would result in an inconsistency; for in the section beginning with "By this, all [other views] are explained," the authors of the *Candrikā* themselves cited passages from the scriptures such as "In the beginning, this was non-existent (*asat*)" as examples in their *Tattvaprakāśikā*, stating that words like "non-existent" primarily denote the void (*śūnya*). Therefore, they could not have argued that the status of being an agent belongs to prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) based on those [scriptural passages].

For thus it is stated in the *Candrikā* on the section concerning the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*): "Regarding the definitions of Vedic words—those well-known elsewhere, those well-known both ways, those well-known elsewhere [than Brahman], and those well-known there [in Brahman]—it is established by means of powerful direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth, that they refer to others alone. Indeed, the strength of direct statement and the other criteria in the definition of those well-known to others lies in the fact that the basis for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*) consists in being the object of that [other entity] and so forth.

Even though Brahman is the primary sense [of the word], the fact that this [word] or its associated sentence cannot be established otherwise than by having another as its primary referent—without resorting to a secondary (aparamukhya) mode of signification—is what is meant; it does not mean that [the word] is, from the outset, incapable of applying to Brahman. Having stated this, it was said: "And thus, by this, all [such cases] are explained. In this context, one should cite words such as "non-existent" (*asat*) and so forth, which reside in sentences intended for another meaning through a secondary mode of signification. This is because of the context and because no specific sentences were cited in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*).

In the *Ṭīkā*, the citation of the passage "In the beginning, this was non-existent" (*asad vā idam agre āsīt*)—which, even in its secondary (gauṇa) sense, is devoid of any other referent—is intended to demonstrate that if the word "non-existent" (*asat*) were taken in its primary sense as referring to the void (*śūnya*) and only in a secondary sense to Brahman, then in the case of "In the beginning, this was non-existent," the void alone must be accepted in order to maintain the primary meaning. Thus—it is not correct [to argue] what was stated previously, namely, that because it is a mere negation, even the non-existent has no causality, just like a hare's horn.

For there is no subverting argument against accepting that even something non-existent can be a cause on the strength of scripture, even if it contradicts reason. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even things like a hare's horn would likewise [be causes], because just as there is a distinction among existent things, a distinction among non-existent things is also logically possible. This avoids contradiction with the *Tattvaprakāśikā*’s introduction to the second sūtra of this section; for there is no disagreement that some prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is a cause while another is not.

If it is argued that this distinction must be accepted so that its causality may be established—that is, the acceptance of a distinction such that among non-existent things like the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of a rabbit's horn, some (the horn itself) is not a cause while others (the prior non-existence, etc. are causes—then we reply: since this is already established, the attempt to prove it is futile. Furthermore, to say "even though it contradicts reason" is a statement that contradicts the very text [of the opponent].

For in that case, since causality—being necessarily connected with time—belongs only to that which is itself connected with time, it would follow (as a logical absurdity) that even though such causality contradicts reason, one might nonetheless accept the causality of some non-existent thing by the force of scripture (*śruti*). Consequently, if causality were possible even for things unconnected with time, then even things like a hare’s horn would possess causality. Thus, even for those who claim that among things connected with time, only some are causes while others are not, [the same problem applies] regarding some non-existent thing unconnected with time, solely by the force of scripture.

The fact that [the Self] possesses causality has been established by the phrase "because of logical consistency. Furthermore, it is quite clear that this [causality] is appropriate in the case of the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyapakṣa*), but not in the case of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāvapakṣa*). This is because, since prior non-existence is connected with time, its status as a cause is not contrary to reason. If it is argued: "By the phrase 'even if causality were contrary to reason,' what is intended is causality in the form of agency (*kartṛtva*); and that is indeed contrary to reason in the case of prior non-existence," [we reply:]...

This being the case, since [the property] is impossible in mere insentience, it would follow that mere insentience would possess that property; and if that were so, it would follow that even things like a rabbit's horn would likewise possess it—this being because it would result in a lack of consistency with the text. If you argue that by the phrase "even though it contradicts reason" (yukty-viruddhasya), what is intended is that which contradicts the reasoning of the Sūtra in the form of a mere negation, and that such a property does not apply to mere insentience, but rather that the consequence of its application is directed only at things like a rabbit's horn; [we reply:]...

Even so, in the case of [the phrase] "of the hare’s horn and so forth," the flaw of violating the natural sense of the word "and so forth" (ādi) as referring to things that are absolutely non-existent would be unavoidable. Furthermore, one understands the intention of the Sūtra-author to be this: having set aside the refutation of agency for all that is insentient by means of the argument from insentience, he performs that refutation as a mere negation; thus, when there is a negation of causality, the negation of its specific form—agency—is also implied by a general negation.

Furthermore, regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is the agent [of creation], if one accepts that the world arises from what is non-existent (*asat*), then at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), only non-existence would remain, because of the rule that when an effect is destroyed, its cause must persist. This would contradict the *Tattvaprakāśikā* commentary on the sūtra "apītau tadvatprasaṅgāt" (At the time of reabsorption, there is the same contingency). For the persistence of that prior non-existence is caused by the future effect; therefore, its persistence is not caused by the destruction of the effect.

For it is not appropriate for the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) to assert that antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva) possesses the status of a material cause (upādānatva), such that—upon the destruction of an effect—it could be argued that only that [non-existence] remains. This is because the status of being a material cause, characterized either as an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) or as a cause non-different from its effect, is impossible in the case of antecedent non-existence; furthermore, it would contradict the very definition of antecedent non-existence for it to exist by overstepping the boundaries of that [non-existence].

Furthermore, this contradicts the statement in the *Candrikā* regarding the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), which holds that since prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is not otherwise established, it is simpler—and thus preferable—to postulate the agency of the well-established prior non-existence rather than postulating both a Lord and His agency.

However, mere agency and the remaining state of being merely an agent are not observed to be invariably concomitant with the destruction of the effect, because [the agent] is the object of a cognition of negation by its very nature, without having the character of non-existence; thus, there is a contradiction with the explanation of the true meaning of the reason (*hetu*) in the Sūtra, namely "because it is a mere negation. Furthermore, in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the agency of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), since antecedent non-existence is defined by its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), it necessarily appears only by way of presenting that counter-positive.

This is because, in its own nature, it lacks the status of being an object for a cognition of negation. Otherwise, since there is a rule that knowledge—being determined by its object—must necessarily manifest itself by presenting its object, there would arise a contradiction with your own statements in the *Nyāyāmṛta* and other works, which hold that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the nature of a cognition devoid of an object. Therefore, by the word "non-existent" (*asat*), the position of absolute emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) alone is intended. And for that [emptiness], which is unrelated to time, the implication of a causality restricted to a relation with time is indeed logical.

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the *Candrikā*, which states that the word "non-existent" (*asat*) here does not refer to the void (*śūnya*). Furthermore, under this view, there would be a contradiction in describing as a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) that which is intended by the proponents of the void (*śūnyavādins*)—namely, that which is indestructible and unconditioned by time and so forth. And it has been stated in the *Tattvaprakāśikā* regarding the indestructibility of the void in the section [sūtra] beginning with "Not from the non-existent, because it is never seen": "Indeed, the one void alone, devoid of the three ends, exists in the ultimate sense; from that alone this entire world arises."

If one accepts the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is the agent, there is a contradiction with the *Tattvaprakāśikā*; if one accepts the prima facie view that the void (*śūnya*) is the cause, there is a contradiction with the *Candrikā*. Thus, it is like a rope caught on both sides. Likewise, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) stated by way of refuting the agency of prior non-existence is also untenable for the followers of Ānandatīrtha; for since they maintain that an entity possesses the nature of the properties of non-existence, it is possible for them to assert that even non-existence possesses the nature of the properties of an entity.

Furthermore, since logicians and others accept that antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) functions as a cause, the reason "being a non-entity" (*abhāvatva*) is unproving (*aprayojaka*) with respect to the absence of causality. Now, it may be argued that because agency is never observed in a non-entity, its absence is made the probans. As it is stated in the *Candrikā* when establishing the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
"Agency is not intended here as the state of being connected with the third case (the instrumental);
rather, it is the state of being connected with knowledge and so forth, and that is not applicable to a non-entity."

The agency mentioned in such sūtras as "janmatā" (arising) is not a technical term (*pāribhāṣika*) intended by the Grammarians in the sense of being a prompter (*prayojaka*) through the use of the instrumental case and so forth; rather, it consists in possessing knowledge, desire to act, and the like. And that [agency] is not possible in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*). If it is argued that this is not incorrect, we say no.

For it would be improper to state merely a reason (*hetu*) accepted by the opponent—which is subject to deviation from the desired conclusion—without first stating a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the opponent who suspects a violation of established rules of observation, such as: "That which is an agent is an existent (*bhāva*); that which is prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is not an agent; that which is time possesses existence," and so forth.

As for the claim that—“if the production of the world from non-existence (*asat*) were accepted, it would follow that at the time of dissolution only non-existence remains, because of the rule that upon the destruction of an effect only its cause remains; therefore, the doctrine of non-existence is inconsistent”—this is the description of the meaning of the Sūtra: *apītau tadvatprasaṅgādasamañjasam*. That too is incorrect, because it is impossible to urge against the opponent the total non-existence of all things at dissolution, which is precisely what the proponent has already accepted.

As for the objection that "the non-existence of all things at the time of dissolution is not tenable; rather, since there is a dispute regarding the existence of entities at that time, their production must proceed from what already exists, because it is a production, like the production of a jar; and the destruction under dispute must leave a residue, because it is a destruction, like an acknowledged destruction"—this can indeed be established by the force of such examples. However, this does not refute our position, because we ourselves also desire that only non-existence remains at the time of dissolution; thus, this is merely a removal of a [hypothetical] doubt and not a refutation based on the absence of examples.

The commentary on this Sūtra by the followers of Ānanda Tīrtha is also untenable. This is because the opponent (the Pūrvapakṣin) has already presented an inference of the following form: "The objects under dispute are non-existent at the time of dissolution, because they are entities, like those [entities] currently admitted [to exist]. If it is argued that even so, the fault of *satpratipakṣatā* (counter-balanced opposition) remains unavoidable, then in that case, just as the Pūrvapakṣa would fail to establish its position, the Siddhānta would likewise fail to establish its own. Consequently, in such a situation, one ought to present a logical argument (*tarka*) that supports the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for one's own position, rather than merely citing the existence of an example; thus, the futility of the Sūtra remains unavoidable.

As for the statement: "The non-existence of everything at your [proposed] dissolution is neither established by perception nor established by scripture, because the latter does not exist; nor is there any inference that proves the non-existence of everything at dissolution, because it is defective due to the absence of an example"—this is the description of the meaning of the Sūtra according to Ānandatīrtha. That too is not correct.

Since it would be improper to employ a general term for the purpose of indicating multiple defects—rather than stating "and because of the absence of an example" (dṛṣṭantābhāvāt) alone—when only the single defect consisting of the absence of an example ought to be stated; and since the interpretation of the sūtra *tarkāpratiṣṭhānāt* favored by Ānandatīrtha is not tenable, this has already been explained previously on the occasion of describing the meaning of this sūtra according to our own method. This is the direction [of the argument]. 11.
This ocean of the refutations of others has been successfully crossed by the youth Raghunātha, who adorns the lotus feet of the illustrious Śaṅkara.
The cause for this commentary, which consists of the discrimination of non-duality, is solely the grace of the Guru,
Rāghavārya, who is like a lion among those skilled in Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya.
Thus ends the section concerning the difference in characteristics.
Now begins the section concerning the learned (śiṣṭa):
"By this, those [theories] not accepted by the learned are also explained. (Sūtra 12)

Having thus established that there is no contradiction with the logic opposed to the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) as favored by [the Sāṃkhyas], the logic opposed to that [theory]—which is favored by the proponents of creation (*ārambhavādins*)—is refuted in this section.

This is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Lest the status of Brahman as the material cause of the world be sublated by the reasoning of the Sāṃkhya and Yoga elders, whose intellects are unskilled in logic; rather, since the Vaiśeṣikas and others are renowned for their skill in logical reasoning, and since their system is unsublated, it is by their logic that Brahman's status as the material cause of the world is sublated."

Thus, it is said that the Vaiśeṣika, who maintains the doctrine of origination (ārambhavādī), thinks as follows: since we observe that the largeness of a cause initiates a largeness in its effect that possesses a degree of excellence exceeding itself, if the material cause of the universe were the largest [entity], then effects such as the earth and the wind would have to be larger than that. For there is the pervasion (vyāpti) that whatever substance is an effect is originated by substances of smaller dimension, just as a cloth is originated by threads. Yet no such possibility is seen here; indeed, there is no room for such a logical conclusion.

Regarding the phrase "there is room for logical argument": as for what was stated there—that this world cannot have Brahman as its material cause because it is of a different nature—that is not an absolute rule. For it is observed in the world that things arise from sources well-known to be of a different nature; for instance, hair, nails, and so forth arise from persons and the like who are well known to be sentient, yet they are of a different nature [being insentient]. Furthermore, it has been stated that scorpions and the like arise from cow-dung and the like which are well known to be insentient, yet they are of a different nature [being sentient].

The sense is this: by this same reasoning, one should not suspect that the world could arise from Brahman, even though He is of the greatest magnitude, as something possessing a smaller dimension. Nor is the argument unestablished (*aprayojakatā*), because there exists a subverting consideration (*bādhaka*) against the contrary position: namely, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of destroying the well-established causal relationship between the magnitude of the substratum and its own superior magnitude. Nor should it be argued that this objection does not apply to the Vivarta-vāda (the theory of illusory manifestation), since such a defect has no place therein. For we do not observe the illusion of a small-sized snake upon a large rope; thus, the superimposition (*āropa*) of a fly or a mosquito upon the all-pervading (*vibhu*) Brahman would be impossible.

Now, it should not be argued that if Brahman is not accepted as the cause, then since all things such as potsherds are effects, and because no eternally established cause would be available, there would be no further creation after the dissolution—since all effect-substances are destroyed at that time and the root-cause would be absent. This is because atoms can serve as the root-cause. Nor is there a lack of evidence for this, as it is established by inference: "A dyad is composed of a substance possessing a dimension smaller than its own, because it is an effect-substance, like a jar."

Nor should it be argued that even for those [atoms], by virtue of their being earth (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth, one could infer they possess parts, and from that, infer they are effects; and that even beyond that, there would be something of smaller dimension, leading thus to an infinite regress. For if one were to postulate that an atom has parts, and if this possession of parts were not restricted, then because Mount Meru and a mustard seed would both have an infinite number of parts without distinction, they would become equal in size due to the lack of difference in their infinitude, which would contradict empirical observation. Therefore, it is impossible to infer that an atom possesses parts on the grounds of its being earth and so forth.

And thus, they hold that atoms alone are the fundamental cause, not Brahman. Furthermore, the Buddha, an incarnation of the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, remembered the non-existence [of the world] as its cause; he maintained a reasoning consistent with that view, namely: "The disputed world, though positive in nature, is preceded by non-existence because it is positive in nature, just as the manifest universe is preceded by deep sleep. Likewise, even the proponents of the theory of aggregation (saṃghātavādins) think thus: "The causality of a permanent entity is possible."

"Because if [Brahman] were capable [of producing all effects], there would follow the consequence of all effects occurring simultaneously. Thus, in response to the further objection—that even for the proponent of *svabhāva* (inherent nature), since the restriction of time for impermanent effects arises from *svabhāva* itself just as the restriction of space for eternal entities does, nothing whatsoever can be the cause of anything, so how can one hope for Brahman to be the cause of the world?—the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated by the sūtra: "By this, those [theories] not accepted by the learned are also explained," which extends the previously stated reasoning to the unmentioned positions. By this...

By means of the present refutation of the doctrine of Pradhāna as the primary cause, those doctrines of atoms and other causes—which have not been accepted in any respect by the learned authorities such as Manu, Vyāsa, and others—should also be understood as explained and rejected as being prohibited. Since the doctrine of Pradhāna as the cause is closely related to the Vedānta scripture through certain aspects such as the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryatva*), its non-attachment (*asamṅgatva*), and self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), and because it is accepted by the learned in those specific respects such as the pre-existence of the effect, it is treated here with emphasis due to its relative strength.

It should be understood that the doctrines of atoms (*aṇu*) and so forth are extended [to this case] because they are weak due to being rootless. This is the intended meaning of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) here: first of all, there is no initial defect in the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*). For we observe that one who has ascended to the peak of a very high mountain may superimpose the identity of minute blades of *dūrvā* grass and the like onto a banyan tree situated on the ground below.

If one were to postulate meanings contrary to the Vedas based merely on the observation of jars and the like, how could one prevent the postulation that even atoms possess parts by virtue of their being earth (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth? Nor is it correct to say that such a view leads to the fault of making Mount Meru and a mustard seed equal in dimension; for although both are alike in having infinite parts, a distinction is established within that very infinity. Thus, because the infinity of parts in Mount Meru and the mustard seed is of a different character, there is no resulting equality of dimension.

For one must necessarily resort to some distinction in the face of infinity; otherwise, because the past moments and the future ones are infinite, there would be a parity between them, and thus a distinction must be postulated within that infinity. Furthermore, in such a case, due to the lack of a resting point for the process of having parts (sāvayavatva), the ultimate cause (*mūlakāraṇa*) itself would be difficult to find according to the views of others. Even if [the cause] were subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), there is no logical inconsistency.

Furthermore, since you yourself must admit that the largeness of the substratum is the cause [of the largeness of the effect] only in cases of heterogeneous largeness and so forth, it is possible for you not to accept a distinctness (*vaijātya*) in the delimitors of effectness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) regarding the largeness residing directly in the effects of Brahman and the like; and it is also possible for you to accept as the delimitor of the initiation of largeness a property that is excluded from the largeness residing in Brahman and such. Moreover, the maxim "when there is a subverting factor, [the rule] 'that which applies to two particulars... does not apply here.

Just as a ball or similar object, though composed of exceedingly long threads, does not possess excessive length, and just as a long wick composed of a mass of cotton possesses minuteness, so too it is logically possible for something composed of the "Great" (mahat) to lack excessive magnitude. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Nyāyapañcādhyāyī* that the body and such things, though devoid of supreme magnitude, are composed of the five elements (*pañcabhautika*). Moreover, even the Sāṃkhya and other schools accept the production of the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) from the "Great" ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), which is itself of greater magnitude.

As for the Buddhists' inference that [dreams] are preceded by non-existence (*abhāva*), even there the example is devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*). Since deep sleep is a particular state, one must admit the existence of the self (*ātman*) as the possessor of that state, which is of the nature of being (*sat-rūpa*); thus, dreams are preceded by existence (*bhāva*). In this way, the stability of the cause and the necessity of the causal relationship have been explained at great length by Brahmānanda and others, and should be understood accordingly.

When the Sāṃkhya Smṛti, which propounds *prakṛti*, *puruṣa*, and so forth, was cited here and there by the crest-jewels of Vedic scholars—the authors of the Purāṇas—only to be rejected as weak regarding the question of the cause of the world, then the weakness of the Kaṇāda doctrines, which were disregarded by all the learned (*śiṣṭa*), must be declared. Indeed, in no Purāṇa whatsoever, such as the Brāhma or the Padma, is the process beginning with the binary atom (*dvyaṇuka*) cited even in passing; on the contrary, in the Manusmṛti it is said: "One should not honor the followers of the Lokāyata (Haitukas) and those who live like herons, even with a mere word."

In the *Mokṣadharma*: "One who is devoted to the useless science of logic (*tarkavidyā*) pertaining to empirical perception—for such a person, the resulting fruit is, in my view, the state of a jackal in the forest."
"Having studied the Mautamī lore, one goes to the womb of a jackal"—thus a censure is found. Likewise, in the Viṣṇupurāṇa as well:
"The earth becomes a jar; from the jar, shards; from the shards, powdered dust; and from that, an atom."

"It is perceived by people whose self-awareness is paralyzed by their own karma; tell me, what is the truth in this matter?"—thus was that procedure censured. As for that which was stated by Yājñavalkya: "The Vedas, together with the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Dharmaśāstra, and the Aṅgas, are the fourteen seats of knowledge and of dharma."

Thus, it has been stated that the *Nyāyamata-prakriyā* (the system of the Nyāya school) serves as a means for attaining knowledge; there is no contradiction, because this refers specifically to the reasoning that purifies the categories of meaning in a manner consistent with the Śruti.

As for what is stated in the *Candrikā*: "By this [argument], the theories of atoms and so forth—which have not been accepted in any part by the learned authorities such as Manu and Vyāsa, and which are not proximate to the Vedic view—are rejected, following the refutation of the Sāṅkhya doctrine (Pradhāna-vāda), which was accepted in some respects by those same authorities and is proximate to the Vedic view."

By this [statement], having restated the meaning of the sūtra "etena," you have committed a tautology, because the very same point has already been stated by you in the passage "etena sarve vyākhyātāḥ. Furthermore, even when compared to the atheistic Sāṃkhya doctrine, the doctrines of the theistic Vaiśeṣikas and others are more worthy of acceptance by learned people (*śiṣṭa*) who profess belief in God, as they maintain that God is the cause [of the world] and are thus closer to the Vedic path. As it is said in the *Anuvyākhyāna*: "Nor is it a fault to say 'the atheistic [Sāṃkhyas] are not accepted by the learned,' for they do not profess belief in God. That is incorrect.

By this, all [theories] have been explained; here, it was stated that there is no scriptural authority for theories such as the atom being the cause. Furthermore, it is stated here that the arguments—which, though accepted by them, contradict Brahman’s being the material cause of the world—are flawed. Thus, since this is clear, raising the charge of redundancy is merely a scattering of dust rooted in hostility toward the Advaita doctrine.

Since it has been stated that the atheistic Sāṅkhya doctrine is not accepted by the learned because its partial adherence to the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) brings it close to the Vedas, whereas the theistic Vaiśeṣika doctrine lacks a foundation due to its theory of atoms as the cause and thus is not proximate to the Vedas, the objection raised in the *Anuvyākhyāna* is not valid. For now, since only the aspect of the material cause (*upādāna-aṃśa*) has been discussed, there is no contradiction regarding the acceptance [of the doctrine] by the learned.

In this regard, although the non-difference of cause and effect was refuted in this very section during the stage of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in this treatise, it should be understood that the reasoning establishing that non-difference was not intended here; rather, it was refuted in the prima facie argument merely for the sake of strengthening that argument.

In this manner, since the possibility of this being a separate topic (*adhikaraṇāntaratva*) exists, by conceiving this sūtra as a supplement to the preceding topic (*pūrvādhikaraṇa-śeṣatva*), [it is argued]: "Because of the absence of examples for the non-existence of the cause and so forth—whereas there are examples for the existence of the cause and so forth—the systems not accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭāparigrahāḥ*) cannot be the cause of the world; even if the non-existent were not the cause, nevertheless, Viṣṇu’s causality of the world is not possible."

The [propositions] that the world is produced without a cause, by an unconscious cause, or by the individual soul (jīva), because it is an effect—like the falling of a riverbank or the coagulation of curds—are contradicted by reason (*yukti*). Nor is a reasoning devoid of a foundation incapable of proving its point, for it is rooted in such scriptural texts as "without a motive" (*akasmāt*). Thus, the doctrines of non-agency, agency by an unconscious being, and agency by the individual soul have been explained. Furthermore, the explanation of the Ānandatīrthīyas—that even in cases such as the falling of a riverbank, the absence of a cause and so forth is not accepted—is incorrect; more has been said on this matter previously. (12)
May this extensive work by Raghunātha, titled *Paradūṣaṇa*, which serves as an ornament for the lotus feet of the illustrious Śaṅkara, bring joy to the section concerning the *śiṣṭa* (the learned).
Thus ends the section concerning the learned (śiṣṭa).

If it be argued that there is no distinction [between the individual soul and Brahman] because of the soul's becoming the enjoyer [of the fruits of action], [we reply: it may be so, as in the case of the world. || 13 ||

In this context, the connection with the beginning of the chapter and so forth arises from the removal of the objection against one's own position—namely, the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the established distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed, proven by perception and other means, would be lost—within the aforementioned samanvaya. In the preceding section, it was stated that ordinary perception, when not supported by scripture, is unstable; therefore, the reasoning (tarka) consisting in the production of an even greater effect from a great cause is not firmly established.

Furthermore, since the distinction between the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) and the enjoyed (*bhogya*) is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the reasoning (*tarka*) rooted therein is not "unfounded" (*apratiṣṭhita*). Thus, because of this counter-objection, there is an immediate connection [to the present discussion]. Here, regarding the non-duality (*advaita*) understood from the aforementioned harmony (*samanvaya*) and propounded by such sentences as "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*) and "All this is indeed Brahman" (*sarvaṃ khalvidaṃ brahma*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—arising from the doubt as to whether it is sublated by the reasoning consisting in the contingency of the loss of the distinction between enjoyer and enjoyed established by perception—is that there must indeed be sublation.

If one accepts the literal meaning of such statements as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) and "All this is indeed Brahman" (*sarvaṃ khalvidaṃ brahma*), then because it would be impossible to avoid the consequence of the loss of the aforementioned distinction—namely, that there would be a mutual non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the world (*jagat*), both being non-different from Brahman—it is necessary to understand these sentences as having a different intended meaning; therefore, this determination of Brahman's causality is untenable.

If it be asked: "Granted that, according to the reasoning already stated, the assertion of non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the world (*jagat*) is untenable, how can the determination of Brahman as the material cause (*upādāna*) also be untenable?"—[the answer is: because the *jīva* and the world are heard in scripture to have Brahman as their material cause, and because the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*), while rejecting the inherence (*samavāya*) between a material cause and its effect, must by process of elimination accept their very non-difference; thus, for the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) who maintains the conceit that "if non-difference is impossible, the relation of material cause and effect is also impossible," such a statement is possible.

In reality, it is now considered whether the previously stated status of the world as the material cause (*upādāna*) is untenable due to contradiction with the aforementioned reasoning, or indeed tenable. On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is untenable. For one who asserts that there is no inherence (*samavāya*) between the material cause and its effect, it must necessarily be admitted by way of elimination that the two are non-different; for if the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) and the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), which are non-different from Brahman, were to attain mutual identity, the consequence would be the absence of any distinction between them.

As for what is stated in the *Candrikā*: "It has been argued by opponents that if Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna*), then the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) who possesses a body would become the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*), and the non-enjoyable objects such as sound would attain the status of enjoyer; thus, there would be no distinction between the two, because both are non-different from the supreme cause, Brahman. [The author] refutes this: "This is not so; for just as in the case of water, waves, and so forth, which are effects of a single ocean, a distinction is possible"—this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Having thus restated the position, he states regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "In the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta-siddhānta*), the aforementioned suspicion of confusion (*saṅkara*) is impossible."

The objection was stated that [Brahman’s] status as the locus—characterized by being the object of ignorance, which is the cause of the world’s nature—is independent of the two types of relations characterized as inherence (*samavāya*) and identity (*tādātmya*). That is incorrect. Merely having the aforementioned status as a locus does not constitute being the material cause (*upādānatā*); rather, it must be either the state of being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the effect, or the state of being a cause non-different from the effect. Otherwise, it would result in a mere technicality (*pāribhāṣikatā*), and furthermore, it would be impossible to establish the knowledge of all things through the knowledge of one. Neither of these two conditions, moreover, is applicable to Brahman.

Because the admission of inherence (*samavāya*) is not accepted; for since the first [alternative] is impossible, the second must necessarily be admitted, and thus the objection that there would be no distinction remains entirely valid.

Furthermore, as stated in the *Candrikā*: "Regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), is it being urged by the opponent that there can be no distinction between effects based on their nature as sentient or insentient, or [no distinction] in any form whatsoever? It is not the first case; for since the sentient is beginningless, the absence of such a distinction between effects is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). [Objection: Even if the sentient is beginningless, because of its non-difference from Brahman, and since it is an effect of Brahman, it would follow that it must possess the nature of that which is insentient, as that which is non-different from Brahman is insentient. [Reply: This is not so."

However, by the very sūtra "But it is seen [to be so]," since it has been stated that Brahman does not lose its consciousness even when having inert matter as its material cause (*upādāna*), the soul (*jīva*) does not incur inertness through its non-difference from Brahman. Nor is the latter [alternative] correct; for, just as we observe a difference among the various effects of a single lump of gold—such as bracelets, crowns, and the like—it is possible for a difference to exist even among the effects of Brahman, such as ether, air, and so forth. If it is argued that the lump of gold possesses parts while Brahman is partless, [we reply:]...

Even in your own view, the objection that "the entire [Brahman] would be involved" (kṛtsnaprasakti) must be raised as a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), just as in the Sūtra, on the grounds that it is not logical for partless Brahman to be the material cause of multiple substances simultaneously; however, it is not the case that the distinction between effects is illogical. Therefore, the criticism stating that "there is no emergence of a prima facie argument" is like a dance performed out of season. Since difference and non-difference are contradictory, if one accepts only difference, then because inherence (samavāya) is not admitted, the status of being a material cause is untenable.

If one accepts only non-difference, the distinction between the enjoyer and so forth would be untenable; thus, our intended prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is stated, because the aforementioned alternatives do not apply. In the sūtra "But it is seen," it is stated that even between two dissimilar things, the relationship of material cause and effect is observed; this addresses the Sāṅkhya proponent who maintains that being a material cause is defined by the cause being non-different from its effect.

But here, regarding the opponent—the logician (tārkika)—who argues that because the relation of cause and effect is restricted by temporal priority and posteriority, it is untenable if one accepts the non-difference of cause and effect, and therefore their difference must be admitted; [we reply] that since there is no room for such an objection, it is easy to state that even though the conscious principle (cetanā) is beginningless, because it is non-different from Brahman, that which is insentient (jaḍa) which is non-different from Brahman by virtue of being its effect would necessarily attain the nature of being identical with Brahman. For this very reason, the example of "a single large mass of gold" and so forth is also not valid.

Since the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) does not admit the non-difference of cause and effect anywhere, it is possible to raise the objection that because effects are non-different from their causes, no distinction between them could exist in any form whatsoever. To this prima facie view, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is: "It may be so, as in the world. Here is the summary of the intended meaning of this conclusion: Just as, according to the logicians (tārkikas), the substance to be produced, such as a jar, is indeed distinct from its material cause, such as the potsherds; [so too may the case be here].

Furthermore, it is said that the relation between these two is simply their inherence (*samavāya*); however, according to our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), two distinct substances are not admitted in a case involving the relationship of material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*). Rather, a single substance—such as clay or water—discards its specific state (e.g., the form of a lump) and, due to particular causal factors, assumes a new configuration such as a necked-pitcher or a wave-foam. Thus, there is even the usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), such as "the very lump of clay has become a jar" or "the very water has become foam and waves.
Likewise, this applies to the statement: "All this, indeed, is Brahman."
Existence, luminosity, and loveliness, along with form and name—this is the pentad of the non-Śiva (the phenomenal).
Of these, the first three are the nature of Brahman, while the latter two constitute the nature of the world.

Thus, according to the statement of the venerable Yāmuna, non-difference is established by taking into account Brahman as the substrate which has entered the world as its material cause in the form of *sattā* (Being) and so forth. However, regarding the aspect of name and form (*nāmarūpa*), since they do not possess the status of being the material cause along with Brahman, there is only identity (*tādātmya*) with Brahman. And this [identity] is a specific relation that accounts for the cognition expressed by words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*); it is not an absolute non-difference consisting in the oneness of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*). Furthermore, since this does not contradict difference, there is no confusion (*sāṅkarya*) between Brahman and the world.

If it is objected: "Surely, even if confusion is avoided regarding the aspect of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) by not admitting identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-aikya*), since the identity of the essential nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is admitted, their confusion remains unavoidable," we reply: No. For even though there is identity of essential nature, confusion finds no occasion because a difference based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*) is also admitted for the two.
