The followers of Ānandatīrtha, however, maintain the following: First, since the scripture stating "In the supreme, imperishable [Brahman], all become one" teaches the non-difference of the individual soul from the Lord in the state of liberation, they establish that there is non-difference even during the state of transmigratory existence; thus, the causality of Brahman with respect to all things becomes impossible—this is the first prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). Secondly, for the sake of the natural force of the suffix *cvipratyaya* (in the phrase *ekībhavanti*), there is indeed difference during the state of transmigratory existence, and only in liberation is there supreme non-difference. Consequently, the definition of the cause of the world's birth and so forth would over-extend (*ativyāpti*) to the liberated soul—this is the second argument.

In the state of *saṃsāra*, there is both difference and non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman; however, upon liberation, there is only non-difference. Thus, the third [definition] suffers from over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to both the liberated and the transmigrating soul. As it is said in the *Candrikā*: "They become one"—thus, non-difference with Brahman is indeed heard in scripture regarding liberation. Yet, by that much alone, the status of Brahman as the creator of all (*sarvakartṛtva*) is not established.

Since there is no contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge regarding the liberated one’s possession of universal agency—just as there is none for the transmigrating soul—and since it is possible for the liberated soul to acquire universal agency through knowledge even though it was previously non-existent (just as liberation itself is acquired), it is possible for Brahman, which is non-different from the liberated soul, to be in some sense the cause of all. Therefore, it is not reasonable to argue that Brahman lacks such [universal agency] because it is non-different from the transmigrating soul whose lack of universal agency is established by perception; rather, on the basis of their non-difference, the non-difference [of Brahman] must be established even during the state of transmigration.

Regarding the statement "they become one," there is one view that the suffix *cvipratyaya* (denoting the transformation of something into what it was not) is used here because it is contradictory to the logic stated in the *Bhāṣya*—namely, that "the state of being another cannot be applied to what is already another"—and thus the suffix intends the cessation of the delusion of difference (*bhedabhrama*), implying a transformation from a prior state into a new one. The second view, however, holds that based on the natural force (*svārasya*) of the *cvipratyaya*, there was previously difference, but now there is non-difference. The logical argument—that "the state of being another cannot be applied to what is already another"—is set aside by the direct scriptural authority (*śruti*) of the *cvipratyaya* suffix itself.

The third [position], however, is as follows: previously there was both difference and non-difference, but in liberation there is only non-difference. In this way, the suffix *cvī* is appropriately applied, because prior to that there was an absence of absolute non-difference. Nor is there any contradiction with the reasoning beginning with "for it does not belong to another," since non-difference existed even previously. Within each of these three positions, three further sub-positions are possible.

Since the resolution of the contradiction is possible through the indication (lakṣaṇā) of a single word alone—and since the teaching of identity would be useless because the difference between pure consciousness (cinmātra) and pure consciousness is never even a possibility—there must be an indication of a single word. This occurs either by abandoning the qualified form in one instance, such that Brahman is established as identical with the individual soul (jīva) through its perceptible characteristics of being a non-agent and so forth; or else, that the soul is established as identical with Brahman, the agent of all, through the characteristics established by scripture; or, according to the view of the proponents of illusion (mithyāvādin), by abandoning the qualified forms in both instances through the indication of both words, resulting in the identity of pure consciousness.

In that regard, in the first case, there is the impossibility of the definition; in the second, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*). If one holds the position that there is always non-difference between the two, then [the definition] over-extends to the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī*); if one holds the position that non-difference exists only in liberation, then it over-extends to the liberated soul; and even in the third position—that there is both difference and non-difference prior to liberation—it over-extends to the transmigrating soul by taking into account the non-difference present in the liberated state. As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): because non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is impossible, there is no such thing as the impossibility of [the Lord’s] being the cause of the world and so forth. If it is argued that this [non-difference] is established because of the designation of unity in liberation, as in the statement "they become one," [we reply: no.

Because there is a deviation [from the rule] even in the worldly usage of "becoming one" at the edge of water, since internal distinctions are still perceived; because the designation of "oneness" can have a figurative meaning based on the identity of location and so forth, as in the case of water becoming one; and because it has been taught in that very way by the Śruti and its corroborating texts (tadubṛṃhaṇa). Thus says the Śruti: "Just as pure water poured into pure water becomes exactly like it, so does the self of the wise sage become, O Gautama. And in the Skanda Purāṇa:

(Regarding the third [position]: in the present-day *Candrikā* manuscript, however, it is observed that in the first case there is an impossibility (*asambhava*) of the definition; in the second, there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*). This is because even if one holds the view that "there is always non-difference from the Pure [Self]," or the view that "non-difference exists only for the liberated among transmigrators," or even the view that "before liberation there are both difference and non-difference"—in all these cases, by taking the aspect of non-difference in the liberated state, there remains an over-extension to the transmigrator. As for the third [position], it is understood that while agency (*kartṛtva*) being real is impossible, its unreality (*asattva*) is over-extended to the *pradhāna* and so forth, and is moreover undesirable to the proponent of the final doctrine (*siddhāntin*).
Just as water poured into water becomes entirely mixed;
And this is not all, since an increase is clearly observed.
In this very way, although the individual soul has attained identity with the Supreme Self,
it does not become [the Supreme], because of its specific attributes such as independence.

Thus they state the application of the *adhikaraṇa* (section). That is incorrect; for there exist numerous Vedāntic texts such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) which always convey the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman—texts accepted by the opponent—and because stating that the non-difference of the transmigrating soul from the Supreme, which has been established through the non-difference of the liberated soul from the Supreme as stated in such Śrutis as "In the highest imperishable," serves as the reason for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), is like touching one's nose while performing a ritual on the head.

Furthermore, since the liberated soul (*muktajīva*) is non-different from the Supreme (*para*), it is pervaded by the delimiting condition (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) [of being a soul]; thus, to assert that the definition exists therein would be an improper statement of over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Moreover, the Siddhāntin’s claim that in the passage "In the supreme, imperishable, all become one," identity of location (*sthānaikya*) and so forth is intended, is also untenable; for since the identity of location between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme is eternally established, the awkwardness (*asvārasya*) of the *cvipratyaya* suffix cannot be avoided.

As for what was also said—that "just as pure water poured into pure water becomes exactly like it"—by this scriptural statement with its restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*), only the equality of the two waters is established, not their identity.

In this regard, the following must be considered: in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it is intended that there be a mere similarity by way of purity. If that were the case, then since the similarity of even unmixed water with pure water would not be lost due to their shared purity and so forth, the portion of the Vedic text concerning the unmixed water would be rendered meaningless; therefore, the similarity must be stated as consisting in being the object of a non-apprehension of difference. This being so, because the mixing of two waters is opposed to the apprehension of difference, it serves as the basis for the aforementioned similarity, thereby establishing the meaningfulness of that portion of the text.

And thus, by one who asserts that such water serves as an illustration, it must be stated that the similarity between the liberated soul and Brahman—consisting precisely in the non-apprehension of their difference and so forth—is here established as culminating in their non-difference. Although the scriptural statement cited is possible even through the non-apprehension of a difference that actually exists, nevertheless [the scriptures declare]: "There is no other seer than this; there is no other hearer than this; for there is no establishment of duality, since the Self alone is established"; "Indeed, there is no division whatsoever here"; and "He who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself."
As long as there is delusion, so long will there be a distinction between the individual soul and the Supreme;

beyond that, however, no distinction exists, due to the absence of any cause for distinction. When the knowledge that produces differentiation has reached absolute destruction, [the distinction ceases].

By reflecting upon the Śruti and Smṛti, one should rightly conclude that because there is no difference [between them], there is no such apprehension [of duality], according to the principle: "Who could create a non-existent difference between the Self and Brahman? Just as the natural purport of such scriptural texts as "There is no other seer but He" is the negation of the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)—as was explained at length previously in the Ānandamaya-Adhikaraṇa—it is likewise logical to maintain that the non-apprehension [of difference] at the time of liberation results from the very non-existence of difference. Otherwise, one would have to assume a defect as the cause for that non-apprehension, which would render liberation itself impossible.

Since liberation is heard to belong only to one whose every defect has been cast away, and since the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad is devoted to the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, it is not appropriate to assume that its meaning is sublated by the statement contained within it, "In the supreme, imperishable, all become one," which lacks any intent toward duality.

Now, how could the passage from the *Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad*, "In the supreme imperishable, all become one,"—which is endowed with the six marks that determine its purport—not have the non-difference as its primary meaning? For instance, in the *Atharvaṇa* [Upaniṣad], there is the introduction: "Two birds... (dvā suparṇā); the conclusion: "He attains the highest equality" (paraṃ sāmyam upaiti); the repetition (*abhyāsa*): "One of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating; when he sees the other, the Lord, as the beloved and His glory, he becomes free from sorrow" (juṣṭaṃ yadā paśyaty anyam īśam asya mahimānam iti vītaśokaḥ).

If it is argued that: (1) *apūrvatā* (novelty) consists in the fact that a difference—unsublated throughout the three periods of time—which has as its counter-correlative the Lord known solely through scripture, cannot be established without scripture; (2) the *phala* (result) is "having shaken off merit and demerit"; (3) the *arthavāda* (eulogy) is "his greatness"; and (4) the *upapatti* (logical justification) is "even while eating, he does not eat. [Response: This is not so. For the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord is already established by perception and other means of knowledge. Furthermore, since it is impossible for the Lord—who is omnipresent, omniscient, and the cause of all—to be the counter-correlative of a difference residing in the individual soul, the notion of such a difference is untenable. Moreover, the shaking off of merit and demerit is possible even through the practice of yoga, and thus lacks the quality of novelty. Finally, the statement "his greatness" is merely a restatement of what is already well-known, and the claim that one does not eat while eating is a contradiction. Therefore, this [interpretation] is not correct. Rather, the meaning is as follows: the term "Brahman" refers to the Supreme Self, who is the cause of the world; the term "Atman" refers to the individual soul, who is the enjoyer of the fruits of karma; and the term "between these two" refers to the space within the heart. The meaning of the passage is that the individual soul, which is distinct from the Supreme Self, attains identity with Him upon the cessation of ignorance. Thus, the *apūrvatā* consists in the fact that the identity between the individual soul and the Supreme Self, which is established by scripture alone, is not known through any other means of knowledge. The *phala* is the attainment of the state of Brahman. The *arthavāda* is the statement regarding the greatness of that state. And the *upapatti* is the scriptural description of the path to be traversed. This is the correct interpretation. Furthermore, the word "difference" (*bheda*) here denotes distinction (*viśeṣa*), not ontological separation (*nānātva*). Therefore, there is no contradiction with the non-dual nature of Brahman. Consequently, the meaning of the passage is that the individual soul, being distinct from the Supreme Self, attains identity with Him through the removal of the veil of ignorance. Thus, the identity of the individual soul and the Supreme Self is established by scripture alone. This is the conclusion.

Regarding this, they say: In the first *muṇḍaka* of the *Ātharvaṇa*, following the question of Śaunaka—"O Blessed One, when what is known does all this become known?"—the two types of knowledge (*vidyā*) to be known are introduced. Having spoken of the lower knowledge characterized by the *Ṛgveda* and so forth, it continues: "Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that Imperishable (*akṣara*) is attained."

Since the syllable that is the object of higher knowledge (*paravidyā*)—described by the passage beginning "that which is unseen, ungraspable, without lineage, without caste," and so forth—is introduced precisely as non-dual, for otherwise its subsequent treatment would be untenable; and since in the second *muṇḍaka*—in the middle of the passage "this whole world is indeed the Person" and "this whole world is Brahman"—there is a reference to that very same [non-duality]; and because at the end of the third *muṇḍaka* it says, "In the highest, imperishable [Brahman], all become one," and "He who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself"; therefore, [the text establishes] non-duality alone.

Thus, because the conclusion is made through the fruit characterized by unity, this Upaniṣad—which consists of three sections (muṇḍakas)—has unity as its primary purport; consequently, even the passage situated in its midst, beginning with "Two birds," must be interpreted as being favorable to that unity, according to the maxim "That which is not connected [to a specific ritual] is subordinate to the context" (*asaṃyuktaṃ prakaraṇāt*) and the requirement for a procedure (*itikartavyatārthitva*), as well as the maxim regarding the act of stepping forward (*abhikramaṇanyāya*). Therefore, it lacks the character of having duality as its introductory theme.

The principle regarding [the term] "unconnected" (*asaṃyukta*) and so forth is as follows: With reference to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "He offers the *samidh* oblations," and so on. Regarding the doubt as to whether this [injunction] possesses the capacity to convey that the *samidh* and others are subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) of the *darśa* and so forth, or not—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) being that it lacks such capacity because the expectancy for the end to be achieved (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*) is satisfied by the connection with heaven and the sacrifice respectively—[the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is: even though those two are satisfied, by virtue of the expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), the statement "He offers the *samidh* oblations" and so forth [is connected] with the *darśapūrṇamāsābhyām svargakāmaḥ*.

In such cases as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), it is necessary for the sentence to convey the aforementioned meaning through the construction of words such as "thus" (*iti*) and so forth, by way of their connection with the *samit* and other subsidiaries. Furthermore, the status of being a procedure (*itikartavyatātva*) consists in the specific form of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) which is known in a general sense from the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Thus, some maintain that when there arises a desire to know the specific activity that serves as the means for the sacrifice, that desire is satisfied by the understanding—derived from the stated sentence—that the *samit* and other rites are means by way of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), while acts such as threshing are means by way of the refinement of materials, deities, and so forth.

The nature of *itikartavyatā* (the procedural requirement) is the capacity to bring about the *apūrva*, which resides in the causal factors such as the sacrifice (*yāga*). The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that whatever is capable of producing something is its generator. Thus, whether one considers the cause itself or the capacity delimited by causality, in either case, according to the Mīmāṃsā school, the understanding of the meaning of the sentence "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa" arises through the expectancy for a generator, directed toward those [sacrifices] possessing the capacity produced by the *samit* and other [subsidiary acts].

Others hold that because power (*śakti*) is non-eternal, even though it consists of the nature of an indivisible cause, that which is qualified by it alone brings about the result; thus, there is necessarily a requirement for its producer. Consequently, even though the *samidh* and other such elements are not connected by a directly applicatory scriptural statement (*viniyojaka-śruti*) and so forth, they are subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*) and others through the context (*prakaraṇa*), which consists of mutual expectancy (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*). This is because, due to the need for a procedure (*itikartavyatā*), they are required by that [sacrifice] as the aforementioned procedure. Such is the meaning of the sūtra: "not connected" (*asaṃyukta*).

Likewise, with reference to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in proximity to the *prayāja* offerings: "He offers while stepping forward" (*abhikrāmaṃ juhoti*). Since the term *abhikrāmam* ends in a *ṇamul* suffix, it has the sense of "having stepped forward. Because this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *srava-homa* (libations) belonging to the context by means of the verb *juhoti*, stepping forward is enjoined with respect to those [libations]. This is because, although the *prayāja*s are in close proximity, the general context (*prakaraṇa*) is stronger than mere proximity (*saṃnidhi*).

Otherwise, [the act of pouring] would become an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the *uttamaprayāja* (the final fore-offering) because of its extreme proximity. This being the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), [the author replies]: Having prescribed the three *prayājas* with the words, "Having performed three *prayājas*, pour together from the *upabhṛt*," thereby enjoining the pouring together (*samānayana*) such that half of the clarified butter (*ājya*) residing in the *upabhṛt* is to be placed in the *juhū*, and having stated, "He offers while stepping forward," and then, with the passage beginning, "He who knows the pairing of the *prayājas*—he offers the *samidhs* as if many, the *tanūnapāt* as if one," and ending with, "Having performed the *prayājas*, he sprinkles the oblations (*havīṃṣi*")... [the conclusion follows].**

Because the context is determined to be that of the *prayāja* offerings due to the reference to those offerings, and because it is certain that whatever is enjoined within that [context] is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *prayāja*, this is precisely the principle of "enclosure" (*saṃdaṃśanyāya*). Thus, just as the fact that the meaning of the sentences concerning the *samit* and other [offerings] is determined to be subservient to the *darśa* and other sacrifices, by that same principle—since they serve to assist the cognition of the unity between the meanings of the preceding and following sentences—it must be determined that the meaning of the verse "dvā suparṇā" situated in their midst is likewise subservient to that [unity].

If it is argued that—just as in the case of the "stepping forward" (abhikramaṇa) and other rites—the first section establishes [Brahman] as the source of all beings (*yad bhūtayoni*), the second establishes [the distinction between] the two birds (*dvā suparṇā*) and so forth, and the third also establishes the qualified [Brahman]—therefore, the intermediate section beginning with "Puruṣa indeed is this" (*puruṣa eva idam*) is likewise favorable to that [qualified Brahman]—we say: No.

Since the opening statement in the first Muṇḍaka—beginning with "By the knowledge of one, all is known"—and the concluding statement—"In the supreme Imperishable, all become one; he who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself"—as well as the intermediate reference beginning with "This [universe] is indeed the Person," are all firmly rooted in non-duality (advaita), non-duality alone constitutes the primary subject matter of the entire section. Consequently, it is impossible to claim that passages such as those concerning the "source of beings" (bhūtayoni) intend to establish a qualified (sakhaṇḍa) Brahman, which would contradict this non-dual context. This is analogous to how the act of stepping forward (abhikramaṇa) and so forth [are subordinate to the main sacrifice].

However, the fact that [the individual soul] serves as an auxiliary to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth does not contradict the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*). Furthermore, because the third *muṇḍaka* concludes with the fruit characterized by unity—namely, "All become one in the supreme Imperishable" and "He who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself"—even the intermediate statement, "He attains supreme equality," must, according to the principle of the "sandwich" (*saṃdaṃśanyāya*), refer to similarity in the form of non-difference, and not to a conclusion regarding difference.

For this very reason, the word "supreme" (*param*) is a qualification of the similarity. Since the similarity—consisting in the absence of suffering and so forth—which distinguishes [the Self] from those in transmigratory existence, has already been obtained through the preceding sentence, "He is stainless" (*nirañjanaḥ*), it would be useless to establish that similarity again. Furthermore, a similarity qualified by supremacy is of the nature of non-difference itself.

Nor is it the case that in the sentence, "He who indeed knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself," the second occurrence of the word *brahman* refers only to the individual soul (*jīva*). This is because the word *brahman* is well-known in the *Nirukta* (Kośa) as having multiple meanings, such as genus (*jāti*), individual soul (*jīva*), and the lotus-seed vessel (*kamala-saṇādi*). Thus, the meaning is: he who knows the supreme Brahman becomes the individual soul (*jīva*) itself, and not the supreme Brahman. For this very reason, the first word *brahman* is qualified by the term "supreme" (*parama*).

Thus, in the case of "in the evening the cows become one in the pen," "all the kings, having become one, rained down arrows upon the Pāṇḍava," and "the insect became one with the bee"—since we observe the designation "becoming one" (*ekībhāva*) based on identity of location, identity of mind, or similarity, as seen in the examples of the cow and the bull, or the insect and the bee—it is possible here too to apply the designation "becoming one" figuratively (*gauṇa*) through one of those same causes. Therefore, this [verse] refers precisely to difference (*bheda*). For this very reason, the locative case in "in the supreme imperishable" (*pare 'vyaye*) is justified.

Otherwise, one would have to resort to the assumption of an unheard-of instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*). While it might be possible to apply the word "Brahman" to the individual soul (*jīva*), in the present context, it is more appropriate to take it as referring to Brahman. Otherwise, since the state of being a soul and the state of not being Brahman are already established prior [to realization], the state of being Brahman could not be something to be accomplished through the knowledge of Brahman. Consequently, the scriptural statement, "He who knows the supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself," which describes that state as the fruit of knowing Brahman, would result in logical inconsistency.

This being the case, the second mention of "the abode of Brahman" (*brahmabhavana*) is also, by implication, qualified by "supremacy. Thus, since the beginning and the conclusion have as their single subject the state of unity, it is logical—according to the reasoning stated previously—that the intermediate passage, "In the supreme imperishable, all become one," should likewise, in accordance with that context, establish the unity of the liberated one consisting in the fact that he is no longer an object of the perception of difference from Brahman. This being so, the locative case in "in the supreme imperishable" (*pare 'vyaye*) is also appropriate, because it denotes the objective domain associated with the perception of difference.

Regarding the statement, "In the evening, the cows become one in the cow-pen," since there is a perception of difference [among the cows], it is impossible to establish the aforementioned unity; therefore, it is correct that such conventional usage is established by their being situated in a single location and so forth. Nor should it be argued that there is no decisive factor (vinigamaka) because such usage is possible in both ways; for in our proposed method, the concordance between the beginning and the conclusion serves as the decisive factor.

Since it is impossible for actions (*karma*) to go to Vaikuṇṭha, and because [otherwise] there would arise the inconsistency of [the statement] "actions and that which consists of knowledge" (*vijñānamayaśca*) etc., such usage can be justified in the present context by [interpreting it as referring to their] abiding in a single location and so forth. Therefore, the attempt to justify such usage on the grounds of identity with the mind (*mati-aikya*) is also refuted; for since it is impossible for actions to be identical with the mind, the phrase "actions" (*karmāṇi*) would result in an inconsistency.

The suspicion that the conventional usage of "becoming one" here is based on similarity—just as in the case of the statement "the insect has become one with the bee"—is refuted by the fact that the locative case would otherwise be untenable if the intent were merely similarity. In my view, however, there is no inconsistency; for when karma is dissolved into Brahman, due to the absence of any perception of difference from it, there is the possibility of the very meaning of the stated sentence being "oneness" in the form of being an object of non-perception of difference residing in that [Brahman], through the relinquishing of its own form, just as in the expression "salt has become one with water. Thus, there is no lack of coherence.

In this regard, the analogy of rivers and the ocean is appropriate. As it is said: "Rivers flowing toward the ocean, upon reaching the ocean, go to their setting"; by this statement regarding the loss of their prior forms, it is expressed that their distinctions are no longer perceived. However, there is this distinction: because mutual identity is impossible due to the difference between their respective parts, in that case (the ocean) there is merely a non-perception of a pre-existing distinction; whereas here (in the case of Brahman), it is because of the total absence of distinction itself. Thus, the analogy is accepted only in respect to the aspect of the non-perception of distinction.

For there is no requirement for complete similarity in an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). By this, the position of the author of the *Candrikā*, which will be discussed later regarding the proof of the distinction between combined waters, is refuted; for in our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), their identity is not admitted. For this very reason, in the *Nibandhana* on the sūtra "On account of the persistence, [the individual soul is] the Kaśakṛtsna" (BS 1.4.22), it is stated that even upon the merging of a river and the ocean, there is no identity of their essential nature, beginning with the words: "But what, according to you, is the intended river? and so forth.

Even though non-duality (*advaita*) has not yet been established, the objection that the citation of the analogy of rivers merging into the ocean—found in the verse "Just as rivers [enter the ocean]" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 3.2.8)—is inappropriate, is addressed by stating that the analogy is valid because its purpose is merely to illustrate the dissolution of clearly perceived difference. Likewise, the sentence from the *Aṇḍūkyopaniṣad* which aims at unity—"He attains the supreme, divine Person" (*Aitareya Upaniṣad* 1.3.12)—does not mean that one reaches a Brahman located in another place. This is because that attainment is the fruit of meditation on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇopāsanā*), and therefore it cannot be the fruit of the knowledge of the [non-qualified] Brahman.

The statement of Skanda also intends the intermediate liberation (*avāntaramukti*), provided it is not in contradiction with the *Nirukta*, the *Śruti*, and the *Smṛti*. For this very reason, it is said that for one who has gone to the world of Brahmā, "at the end of the other [Brahmā], those who have perfected their selves enter the supreme state," thus describing the attainment of the supreme state as being of the nature of identity with Him. Having introduced the statement from the *Tattvaprakāśikā*: "By this, he states the final conclusion of this section's established doctrine through the insertion of the negative particle (*nañ*) and so forth," the following is the intended meaning:

"And because of contradiction with other passages, because of internal inconsistency between earlier and later parts, and because of contradiction with logical reasoning, these three views are not at all tenable."

It has been stated that all three positions, including the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), depend upon non-difference (*abheda*) in liberation; however, that very [non-difference] is unestablished. This is because the commentary on the scripture "they become one" points out its contradiction with the other scriptural passage "like water [into water]. Furthermore, in the *Nyāyavivaraṇa*, the contradiction with the preceding statement "the stainless one attains supreme equality" and the contradiction with the subsequent statement "he goes to the divine Person who is higher than the high" have been stated. Moreover, if the intent were non-difference, the third case ending would be used as in "by the supreme, the immutable" (*pareṇāvyayena*), rather than the seventh case ending.

If it is argued that [the passage] means "in the evening the cows become one in the cow-pen," like the calf [joining the herd], that is not so; for in that case, only the unity of location (*sthānaikya*) would be understood. Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the word *karman* (action) in the preceding sentence, which states, "the actions and the self consisting of consciousness. This is because the identity of actions with Brahman is impossible, as such objections have been stated in other texts. Moreover, even in the view of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*), since non-difference already exists previously, the sudden emergence of non-difference at the beginning and end is untenable. Finally, in the middle and final views, there is a contradiction with the reasoning stated in the *Anuvyākhyāna*: "There is no difference between what is different and what is not different," as those views intend something else entirely. Furthermore—
This very Śruti, by employing the analogy of rivers merging into the ocean,
clearly declares that it does not intend its own meaning in a figurative sense.

For indeed, immediately following the statement "they become one," there is the illustration of distinct rivers and the ocean: "Just as rivers flowing toward the ocean, upon reaching the ocean, disappear. And likewise:
"The water of the street has attained oneness with the water of the Ganges;
cows that have wandered here and there have attained oneness at evening."
"That army, having become one, advanced against the Pāṇḍavas"—
from such [examples], there would be Vedic statements such as "becoming one" (*ekībhavantī*).

Nor is there unity in the merging of one water with another; for this is contradicted by the emphatic scriptural statement cited in the Bhāṣya, "It remains just as it was," and by the Smṛti text, "From which increase is observed. Furthermore:
"Even upon mixing, there is no identity between two waters due to differences in measurement and due to prior differences in touch and taste, just as in the case of milk and water."

It is not merely a difference in dimension as stated in the Smṛti—"from which there is increase"—but rather, even in the case of cold and heat, or touch and taste, a difference in touch and so forth is observed when waters belonging to different rivers are mixed. Otherwise, there would be no distinction even between milk and water being separated by a swan. Furthermore, if there were non-distinction due to the mixing of molten gold and copper, there would be no difference in price and other qualities between the resulting coin and a coin made of pure gold alone. Moreover, wine poured into milk would itself become milk.

Furthermore, it is well known that there is a distinction between the waters of the seven rivers, such as the Kṛṣṇā, and the waters of the thousands of rivers, such as the Gaṅgā; even though they are each divided for the purpose of joining the ocean, they possess distinct differences in terms of their form, taste, and other qualities. Moreover, regarding the Sūtra, "On account of the abiding [of the soul], [it is] Kāśakṛtsna," the *Bhāmatī* itself asks: "But what is intended by 'the river' according to your venerable self? Is it the water-atoms, or the particular configuration of those atoms, or rather the composite whole (*avayavin*) produced from them?"

In that regard, since the whole (avayavin) characterized by a distinct shape is destroyed upon entering the ocean, how could there be identity with the ocean? As for the atoms of the river water, they possess only difference from the previously existing atoms of the ocean water, not non-difference. Likewise, they possess only difference even from the ocean; in this manner, the non-difference between the river and the ocean is refuted. And thus: "Just as with a heap of beans and the like, or as Brāhmaṇas and others in an assembly, so too there is a mere contact of one body of water with another, but no identity."

As for the statement in the *Candrikā* that "there is no perception of difference when there is mutual mixing due to having two substances," almost all of it has already been refuted; this is the general direction [of the argument]. || 13 ||
This work by Raghunātha, titled *Vyākhyādvayāviveka*, is an ornament for the lotus feet of the illustrious Śaṅkara and a refutation of the views of others, intended for the virtuous.
Born from the grace of Rāghavārya, who has mastered the principles of Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya, may this [work] bring great joy and victory in debate for those who hold the position of the enjoyer (bhoktṛ).
Thus ends the section concerning the identity of the enjoyer (bhoktrāpatti).
Now begins the section concerning the origin (Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa):
"The non-difference of that [effect] from that [cause], on account of such terms as 'origin' and others. (2.1.14)

In response to the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) concerning the contingency of the previously mentioned distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed, a resolution was stated by resorting to the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) in the form: "It may be so, as in the world" (*syāllokavat*). This present Sūtra, however, is intended to provide the primary resolution through the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*) regarding that very point. Accordingly, the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) at the beginning of its exposition of this Sūtra states: "Having provisionally accepted this empirical distinction characterized by the enjoyer and the enjoyed, the refutation was stated as 'it may be so, as in the world. But this distinction does not exist from the standpoint of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), and so forth."

At the conclusion of this commentary on the Sūtra as well, the venerable author of the Bhāṣya will state: "The author of the Sūtras also says 'non-difference from that' with the intention of referring to the ultimate truth (paramārtha). But with the intention of conventional usage (vyavahāra), he says 'it may be as in the world,' thereby describing Brahman as being like the great ocean. Without denying the phenomenal world of effects, he resorts to the method of transformation (pariṇāma) because it will be useful for the meditations on the qualified (saguṇa-upāsana). In this context, the meaning of the phrase "having accepted" (abhyupagamya) is "without establishing [it] as false."

The passage beginning with "pariṇāma" (transformation) cites the process of transformation as an illustrative example; the resulting meaning is that he states a unique illustrative example for the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*). Furthermore, the extensive discussion in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) within this section regarding the proof of the falsity of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca-mithyātva*) implies that the non-difference of Brahman from the inner self (*pratyag-abhinnatva*) is not possible, because it is impossible for two contradictory attributes, such as agency and non-agency, to coexist in a single locus.

The claim that "this fault does not apply because the falsity [of contradictory properties] is established through their perceptibility and so forth" is not correct; for this is stated to dispel the doubt that falsity cannot be established by a weak inferential mark (*liṅga*) when it is countered by a powerful perception (*pratyakṣa*).

However, some say that since it was stated in the previous sūtra "as in the world" (*lokavat*), there might be the misconception that the refutation was shown while merely accepting the reality of the modification (*vikāra*), because in common worldly experience the unreality of modifications is not established; and likewise, there might be the misconception that even if the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the reality of those adjuncts would be ultimate. To dispel these [misconceptions], they maintain that this sūtra establishes the falsity (*mithyātva*) of modifications.

If it is asked: "Even though the context is the establishment of falsity (*mithyātva*), what is the purpose of mentioning the non-establishment of falsity in this sūtra through the commentary (*bhāṣya*) which says, 'And having granted this'?"

To this we reply: There might be a doubt that, since the conclusion established by the previous sūtra would not arise without proving falsity, this present section—being a proof of such falsity—would necessarily be a mere supplement (*śeṣa*) to it rather than a separate section; therefore, in order to demonstrate the necessity of this section and to show that the conclusion of the preceding section is possible even without proving falsity, it is appropriate to mention that [conclusion] here. Alternatively, it may be argued that the stated view—that Brahman is the material cause of the world—is not tenable.

In response to the objection that this would entail the collapse of the changelessness (nirvikāratva) maintained by the Siddhāntin, the falsity of modification (vikāra-mithyātva) is established here; furthermore, there is no lack of coherence because the purpose of this section (pāda) is the refutation of direct objections against one's own position. Thus, the statement in the Bhāṣya is intended to demonstrate the connection with the aforementioned objection. It should be understood that if that [falsity] were explained in the previous section itself, such a connection would not be possible; therefore, the mention of the non-establishment of falsity is indeed appropriate through the phrase "having accepted [it as necessary]."

And here, according to the method already stated, since the sublation of the opponent’s position—namely, the sublation of the reality of opposing attributes such as [the Self's] being distinct—is removed, there is a connection with the chapter and so forth. As for the immediate sequence of the connection: although the counter-argument based on the impossibility of the distinction between the knower and the known (due to identity not being opposed to difference) might be unstable, the counter-argument based on the impossibility of the Lord's being devoid of activity—which is supported by Scripture—is indeed stable; thus, the connection follows from this rebuttal.

Regarding this, the doubt arises as to whether Brahman’s status as the material cause of the world is contradicted by reasoning (tarka) due to the consequence of destroying its changelessness, or not; in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), it is indeed contradicted by reasoning. Since even the proponent of the final conclusion (siddhāntin) accepts Brahman’s changelessness, there is no room for the objection that this is merely an "unwelcome consequence" (iṣṭāpatti), and because there is no weakness in the root [of the argument], there is no contradiction with the aforementioned reasoning. Thus, in the prima facie view—it is not contradicted by the stated reasoning.

There is no contradiction with the non-modification (*nirvikāratva*)—as intended by the opponent—which consists in being devoid of modifications that possess the same ontological status (*samānasattāka*) as the substratum (*dharmin*), because Brahman is not the material cause (*upādāna*). This is because modification is illusory (*mithyātva*) while Brahman is real (*satyatva*). Even if material causality were accepted, there would be no loss of its nature as non-modified. And this illusoriness is "indefinable" (*anirvācya*). The non-difference of the effect—the entire collection of modifications—from that [cause] means non-difference from the cause; that is to say, it means illusoriness. Why? From the word "originating" (*ārambhaṇa*) and so forth.

First, regarding the term "originating from speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*): it is stated in view of the illustration that through the knowledge of one thing, there is the knowledge of all—namely, "As, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, everything made of clay would be known; the modification is a mere name originating from speech; 'clay' alone is the truth"—of such a form.

From the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one should include the collection of scriptural passages such as "All this has that as its self; that is the Truth, that is the Self; thou art That," "All this is what this Self is," "Brahman alone is all this," "The Self alone is all this," and "There is no diversity whatsoever here," as well as the inference—"The universe is false because it is visible and because it is limited"—as presented in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) and other works. Furthermore, in this context, the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "on account of the words 'originated,' etc. (*ārambhaṇa-śabdādibhyaḥ*) takes the scriptural passage "an origination in speech" (*vācārambhaṇam*) and so forth as the reason for the argument.

And since its natural inclination lies precisely in stating the falsity of phenomenal proliferation (prapañca), it should be understood that by means of the term "non-difference" (ananya), it is falsity itself that is intended as the probandum.

Now, one might ask: "How is falsity (*mithyātva*) understood through the term 'non-difference from that' (*tadananyatva*)? For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to grasp its denotative power (*śakti*) and so forth in that sense; and if one were to accept a modern figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*), it would result in a lack of naturalness regarding the words of the Sūtra, as well as the abandonment of the arrangement 'falsity [is established] from the word 'originating' (*ārambhaṇa*) and others, leading to a state of being groundless. To this, it is replied: In the Sūtra "non-difference from that" (*tadananyatvam*), the word "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*) is supplied as an ellipsis (*adhyāhriyate*). Furthermore, the word "non-difference" (*ananyatva*) is to be repeated.

And thus, that phrase "non-difference from that" (*tadananyatva*) refers to non-difference in reality and aims at identity (*tādātmya*). This is because, in the expression "non-difference from that," the word "other" (*anya*) signifies absolute difference; therefore, identity can be understood from it as well. For those who maintain that earth and its qualities possess both difference and non-difference, identity cannot be the mere absolute absence of difference in that which possesses difference. Rather, identity is something entirely distinct from that [mere absence].

And whether that [effect] is of the nature of a specific property inherent in it or something distinct is another matter. In reality, its non-difference from that [cause] is intended for the purpose of permitting the remainder; thus, the unreality—also synonymous with falsity—of the world-form as something other than Brahman is obtained, and so the aforementioned fault does not apply. Nor should it be suspected that, since the refutation of the stated prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is possible simply by proving its reality and its non-difference from that [cause], the proof of identity (*tādātmya*) is redundant.

It should not be suspected that the proof of identity is redundant for the purpose of dispelling the objection that if the world's falsity is accepted on the basis of its being devoid of a real nature distinct from Brahman—a property common even to the non-existent (*tuccha*)—then Brahman’s status as its material cause would be untenable due to the world’s resulting non-existence; for identity must also be asserted therein in order to dispel that very objection.

Furthermore, according to the theory of *asatkhyāti* (the apprehension of the non-existent), even though things such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell lack a real nature distinct from the jar, they are nonetheless recognized by the cognition of the jar as possessing a cognized real nature. Consequently, it would be impossible to establish the "knowledge of all through the knowledge of one" (*ekavijñānena sarvavijñāna*)—which will be discussed later—as consisting in the fact that ether and other elements possess a cognized real nature through the cognition of Brahman. Moreover, since the identity (*tādātmya*) between those two must necessarily be asserted in order to demonstrate that Brahman possesses the real nature of ether and the rest, [the theory of *asatkhyāti* is untenable].

In the *Bhāṣya* as well, both forms of the definition—namely, "non-difference" (*ananyatva*) and "absence through exclusion" (*vyatirekeṇābhāvaḥ*)—are intended. Indeed, in the *Bhāmatī* it is stated: "We do not say that 'non-difference' means identity; rather, we exclude difference. Thus, the intended meaning is that non-difference is not identity, nor is it the possession of a real nature other than that [of Brahman], nor is it the possession of a difference from it that does not share the same locus as its identity; therefore, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. By this, [the objection]—"Non-difference from Brahman is not their non-otherness"—is refuted.

Because there can be no identity with the entire unreal [world] due to the impossibility of non-difference from Brahman, and because such a thing is not admitted. If it is argued that there is non-difference with the material cause as qualified by ignorance (*ajñāna*), we reply: for the sake of the knowledge of everything through the knowledge of the pure Brahman—which is to be known by one seeking liberation—non-difference must be stated precisely with the pure [Brahman]. Otherwise, even ignorance would fall within the category of the knowable mentioned in the scriptural passage, "By which the unheard becomes heard. Nor do we say that non-difference means "not otherness" (*ananyatva*).

However, according to the method stated in the *Bhāmatī*—"we deny difference"—"non-difference from that" (*tadananyatvam*) means merely the absence of difference. This is because, in the absence of difference, non-existence would necessarily follow; and because, if difference were absent, the distinction between the real and the unreal would be untenable. Furthermore, if the distinction were maintained through the absence of non-difference, then by that very same knowledge, there would also be the state of knowing everything through the knowledge of one.

If, on the grounds that the occurrence of all cognitions within a single cognition is untenable, you postulate the absence of difference (*bheda*), and on the grounds that the distinction between the real and the unreal is untenable, you postulate the absence of non-difference (*abheda*), then—since both are untenable—why not, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), postulate both difference and non-difference? This would accord with the natural sense of such scriptural texts on grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as "All this is what this Self is" and "Not this, not this," as well as with the scriptural texts on difference and the illustrative examples of the lump of clay and so forth.

Furthermore, the scriptural statement regarding the single flavor (*ekarasa*) of Brahman may be explained—even in the absence of a distinction from the manifold world of diverse flavors—merely by the absence of non-difference, despite the existence of difference. Just as it is not logical for the real to be non-different from the unreal, so too [it is illogical] in the absence of difference from it. Nor can its non-existence apart from Brahman constitute its non-difference from it; for the negation of a specific thing implies the admission of everything else, which would result in the individual soul’s consciousness being identical with Brahman, just like bliss and other attributes.

Furthermore, being superimposed upon Brahman is not the meaning of the term "non-difference" (*tadananyatva*). For the word "non-different" is never applied to silver that is merely superimposed by a power of illusion (*śakti*). Moreover, if there were no difference between the apparent (*prātibhāsika*) and the empirical (*vyāvahārika* [levels]) on the one hand and the empirical and the ultimate (*pāramārthika*) on the other, the indeterminability (*anirvācyatva*) of the former two would be unestablished. Additionally, it would be impossible for the knowledge of all things to follow from the knowledge of one, and the analogies of the lump of clay and so forth would be untenable. Thus, the statement in the *Candrikā*—"How indeed could everything become known through the knowledge of Brahman?"—is a manifestation of a failure to understand the intended meaning of the previously cited Bhāṣya, and is therefore to be disregarded.

Because of the portion of the sūtra beginning with "from the words such as 'origin' and so forth" (*ārambhaṇa-śabdādibhyaḥ*), which cites scriptural passages such as "the origin is a mere verbal handle" (*vācārambhaṇam*); and because that [scripture], by its very natural sense, speaks only of the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—and because, according to the method stated, the intended meaning of the sūtra "non-difference from that" (*tadananyatvam*) is understood as falsity consisting in identity; and because the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) cognition, "that which appeared as silver was mother-of-pearl," is universally accepted even in the case of a superimposed object.

Since there is no contradiction in employing the term "non-different" (*ananya*) with respect to the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*), and since the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatā*) of both the apparent (*prātibhāsika*) and the empirical (*vyāvahārika*) levels is established beyond dispute—given that even these two are not ultimately different from the empirical and the absolute respectively—the aforementioned objection raised by the author of the *Candrikā* finds no footing. Now, one might ask: since it is possible to explain the meaning of such scriptural passages as "beginning with speech" (*vācārambhaṇam*) even while accepting the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-satyatā*), how can it be said that the natural intention (*svarasa*) of that scripture lies solely in declaring the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the world?

For some describe it as follows: although the non-difference between cause and effect is indicated by the statement "by the knowledge of one, all is known," there arises the doubt—upon seeing a lump of clay—how the scope of objects such as a jar, the difference in their functional efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and the difference in name and so forth can be accounted for. To this, the remainder of the sentence is: "it is a matter of speech" (*vācārambhaṇam*). "Speech" refers to words such as "fetch water with the jar," and the practical activity (*vyavahāra*) preceded by such words is the meaning of the term "speech."

For that purpose, the third case ending is used because the result is intended to be expressed as a cause, as in the expression "he dwells for the sake of study" (*adhyayanena vasati*). A "modification" (*vikāra*) is a jar or the like, and its "name" (*nāmadheya*) refers to the clay; the meaning is that it is to be touched (*ālambha*)—that is, it is to be connected. This is because of the rule stating that the root *ā-labh* signifies both touching and killing. In this context, the root *ā-labh*, which has the sense of touching, culminates in the sense of connection. The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).

In the passage beginning with "mṛttike" (O clay), it is established that for the purpose of linguistic usage—such as the expression "fetch that"—and for the purpose of practical activity based thereon, such as bringing it, the clay becomes connected with its specific configuration (saṃsthāna) like a conch-necked vessel and its designation (nāmadheya) such as "pot. Thus, it is stated that although the lump and the pot are one and the same substance, all instances of doubt and so forth are logically possible due to the difference in their states (avasthā).

One might object: "Granted that the identity of substance is accepted, why is the doubt regarding [the identity of] the pot and so forth resolved on the basis of a difference in states? Why is a difference between the causal substance and the effect-substance not accepted, as is done by the logicians (tārkika) and others? Anticipating this objection, it is said: "In this case, 'clay alone is real' (*mṛttikevetyeva satyam*). Supplying the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*), the meaning is: "The pot is clay alone. "Real" (*satyam*) means "established by valid means of knowledge" (*prāmāṇika*). The non-difference [of the pot from the clay] is understood through the world-renowned recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "the pot is clay."

Therefore, one must establish linguistic usage and so forth by taking the identity of substance alone. This is not natural, because such an interpretation involves an excessively strained method: accepting that the instrumental case in "vācā" (by speech) has the sense of the dative; supplying the word "mṛttikā" (clay); transforming it into an instrumental form as "mṛttikayā"; and supplying the word "ghaṭaḥ" (pot) in the phrase "mṛttikaiveti."

As for the statement: "The modification (*vikāra*), such as a jar or a bowl, is not different from the clay"—the sense is that it is a "matter of verbal expression" (*vācārambhaṇam*), meaning it is dealt with by words alone and does not exist in reality. The name "jar" and so forth is real only insofar as the substance "jar" and so forth is actually clay. [The word *satyam*] is correct (*sādhu*) because it refers to an established (*prāmāṇika*) fact. In this context, the suffix *-yat* is used in the sense of "that which is correct" (*tatra sādhuḥ*).

The explanation that the distinction between names such as "pot" and "clay-lump" must be made solely according to the difference in states (*avasthābheda*), and that one should not, on that basis, postulate a real difference in substance (*dravyabheda*) between cause and effect—this is the ultimate sense [of the passage]. However, even that [explanation] is not natural, because it involves the forced assumption of a restriction by supplying the word "different" (*bhinnaḥ*) in the phrase "other than clay" (*mṛdo bhinnaḥ*), thereby accepting that the term "name" (*nāmadheya*) refers specifically to the pot and so forth, and because it further supplies the words "the substance [is] the pot and so forth" (*ghaṭādidravyam*) in the phrase "it is clay" (*mṛttiketi*).

Furthermore—that which has its origin in speech alone, that is, the organ of speech, is a mere name, a modification (*vikāra*), because it undergoes transformation into the forms of Sanskrit and Apabhraṃśa. That which is produced by the organ of speech depending upon grammar is "clay alone," which is real (*satya*) and eternal; the meaning is that it is imperishable in the form of a continuous flow. It is not slain by the slaying of this [body]. This is the city of Brahman (*brahmapura*). In this context, the word *satya* is used in the sense of the eternal.

Furthermore, because the word *sadā* (always), being a form ending in a *kṛt* suffix (*tyap*), functions as a synonym for the word *satya* (real/true), it carries the sense of "eternal. Indeed, the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one occurs either by way of similarity or by way of predominance. In that regard, when there is knowledge of the one Brahman—by virtue of its existence and so forth—there is knowledge of that which is similar to it; for this, the examples of the lump of clay and the earthenware vessels are given. When there is knowledge of everything subordinate to it through the knowledge of that which is predominant, the example of the refined [metal] and the broken [ornament] is given.

For the fruit that arises from the knowledge of Apabhraṃśa is indeed surpassed by the knowledge of Saṃskṛta, which yields universal linguistic usage and other benefits; thus, Saṃskṛta is primary. Furthermore, in order to establish such an analogy between the subordinate and the primary, the Ānandatīrthīya commentary maintains that even in passages such as "beginning with 'vācārambhaṇam,'" the phrase "just as, my dear, [the clay alone... (*yathā saumyaikena*) and so forth must be supplied. However, this too is unsatisfactory. For instance, by the word *vāc* (speech), only the organ of speech (*vāgindriya*) is intended to be indicated.

Otherwise, since it could not be produced by grammar, it would follow that it is an apabhraṃśa (corrupt form). In my view, however, the figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word *vāc* meaning "mere speech" and in the word *nāmadheya* meaning "mere name" is based on the impossibility of the literal co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) being established, and this is well-known in the world; this will be explained later. Furthermore, because the word *satya* is conventionally fixed (*ruḍha*) in the sense of "non-sublatable," its meaning of "eternity" also occurs only through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Furthermore, since even *saṃskṛta* lacks primary permanence (*mukhya-nityatva*), it is impossible for it to be connected with the word "always" (*sadā*); thus, there would be the fault of resorting to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to mean a secondary permanence consisting in not being produced by grammar. Moreover, the fact that the word *sadā* ends in a *kṛt* suffix (the suffix *kvip*) is itself unestablished by grammar. If the word "modification" (*vikāra*) were taken in its primary sense of a derivative transformation, your desired meaning would not be established; therefore, it must refer to that which is uttered due to an inability to utter *saṃskṛta*, and this can only be through metaphorical indication. Likewise, the word "name" (*nāma*) also refers to "word" (*śabda*) only through metaphorical indication.

Because Apabhraṃśa lacks the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) established by convention, such that it could possess a meaning; furthermore, the claim that [the phrase] "O gentle one, with one... and so forth must be supplied (*anuṣañjanīya*) is also not correct. For *anuṣaṅga* (supplying) consists in the recognition (*pratisaṃdhāna*) of a portion that has entered into a preceding sentence as being a constituent of a subsequent sentence, and that is not possible in the present case.

For in the present context, the passage beginning with "Only clay is real" must be understood as intended to provide the illustrative example later in the text—namely, "Just as, my dear, by one clod of clay all its modifications are known"—and this [example] was not already contained within the preceding sentence.

Furthermore, just as the subordinate and primary status [of the effect and cause] is indicated by the Śruti through the passage beginning with "for the modification is a mere verbal handle" (vācārambhaṇam), so too, since it is impossible to know the modifications such as the jar through their specific forms like "jar-ness" when the lump of clay is known, one realizes upon reflection that the knowledge of the jar and so forth occurs only in the form of "clay" based on the knowledge of the lump of clay; thus, it is stated that the knowledge of the similar [effect] is dependent upon the knowledge of that [cause]. If, however, it is argued that because the knowledge of an Apabhraṃśa word is impossible from the knowledge of a Saṃskṛta word, the phrase "it is clay" (mṛttiketi) intends to show that the Saṃskṛta word performs the function of the Prakṛta word...

If it were possible for the statement "all this modification is known" to be expressed by the scripture itself [as the primary subject], then why would it be stated through the passage beginning with "a mere modification of speech," which indicates the relationship between the subordinate and the principal? Thus, there would be a loss of the natural sense (*svārasya*) of the scripture.

Moreover, following the examples such as "iron" (*kārṣṇāyasa*) and "antimony" (*anta*), where it is said that "modification is a mere verbal handle, a name," it would be more appropriate to state generally that "the conditioned is real" (*saṃskṛtaṃ satyam*), rather than specifying at the end of each individual example like "clod of clay" that "each one is clay. Furthermore, since other refined Sanskrit words could also be employed, the restrictive formulation "only clay" (*mṛttiketyeva*) and so forth would be inconsistent.

The doubt—namely, that since "it is indeed iron" (*āyasam eva satyam*) is sufficient to establish its fullness, why was "made of black iron" (*kārṣṇāyasam*) stated?—is likewise without answer in your view. In my view, however, there is no fault even if another lighter synonym for "black iron" exists; for just as when one intends to express the meaning of a "jar," synonyms such as "kalaśa" and so on are also employed alongside words like "ghaṭa. Furthermore, the claim that by the knowledge of one thing everything similar to it and dependent upon it is known is also inconsistent, because there is no such rule.

For there is no fixed cognition of a gavaya and so forth within the cognition of a cow, nor a fixed cognition of a prajādi (offspring, etc. within the cognition of a king; and since cognition is not fixed, there is simply no answer to the question of why only things such as similarity are employed [as grounds for comparison]. This is the general direction of the argument.

Thus, since other systems accept the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-satyatā*), their interpretation of the meaning of the scriptural passage concerning "the beginning of speech" (*vācārambhaṇa-śruti*) lacks natural consistency; therefore, our own commentary demonstrates that the explanation which regards the passage as being intent upon the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*) is the one that accords with its natural sense. For the commentary states: "By knowing a single lump of clay—which is in reality of the nature of clay—one comes to know everything made of clay, such as jars, bowls, and water-pots, because there is no difference in their being of the nature of clay. For the modification is merely a name, beginning with speech."

It is by speech alone that one begins to say, "The modification exists"—namely, the pot, the bowl, and the water-jar. In reality, however, no such thing as a modification exists at all. For this is a mere name, which is untrue; "clay alone is the truth."

If it is asked: "How can the explanation of the word *nāmadheya*—which, by including the meaning of the word *mātra*, results in the conclusion that [the world] is unreal—be considered natural (*svarasa*) here? To this it is replied: For in this context, what is naturally understood is the injunction that [the world] is a name, following upon the restatement of what was declared in the sentence, "The modification is a mere beginning in speech" (*vācārambhaṇam*).

In that context, having taken up the meaning as heard, since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is impossible [otherwise], one might resort to the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of being denotable by the name within the word for the name to establish coreferentiality; however, this would result in redundancy. Furthermore, because of the natural force of the supplementary statement "Only clay is real," it is more consistent to accept a restriction of the object (*arthaparisaṃkhyā*) and explain its meaning as culminating in falsity (*mithyātva*), with the word "only" (*mātra*) included therein.

Furthermore, it is observed that a name can serve as a mere semblance or indicator—as in the passage: "They sacrifice with name-sacrifices, out of hypocrisy and contrary to the injunctions. In common worldly usage as well, there is the designation "son" for one who is merely a semblance of a son; yet in this case, true sonship does not exist. As for the statement, "Only 'earth' is real," its natural intent is to establish the unreality of modifications by first restating the reality of the clay, according to the maxim of the "sweetness on the tongue" (guḍajihvikā-nyāya). He demonstrates this same principle in the case at hand: "In this way, my dear, that instruction is given."

By the word "thus" (evam), it is established that modification is a mere verbal handle (*vācārambhaṇam*), and that only the instruction (*ādeśa*) is real. Furthermore, by the etymological derivation "that which is pointed out is the instruction" (*ādiśyata ity ādeśaḥ*), it is shown that this refers precisely to Brahman—the subject introduced in the passage, "Did you ask for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard?"—which is accessible solely through such instruction.

And in this very context, at the occasion of describing the tripartite evolution (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) of fiery substances, it is clearly established: "That which is the red color of fire is the color of fire; that which is white is the color of water; that which is black is the color of food (earth). The 'fire-ness' of fire has departed; modification is a mere beginning in speech, a name; the three colors alone are real. Here, by the statement "the fire-ness of fire has departed," the unreality of the modification is explicitly demonstrated.

Therefore, it is determined that the scriptural passage concerning "originating from speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*) has as its primary purport the unreality of modifications. Alternatively, in passages such as "Only clay is real," the phrase "originating from speech, a modification, a mere name" serves as the reason; "originating" (*ārambhaṇa*) means production, or rather, being merely speech—that is, incapable of withstanding inquiry. Thus, the sense is that since it is impossible to determine whether the origin is from the existent or the non-existent, the general category of "that which has originated" is incapable of withstanding inquiry.

Since even that much fails to provide a reason because it is common to beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), he says: "The modification is a mere name" (*vikāro nāmadheyam*). This means that what is joined with modifications such as destruction is a mere name, incapable of withstanding inquiry. Because a non-difference of name from the object is impossible, the sense of "incapability of withstanding inquiry" is obtained by including the meaning of the suffix *-mātra* (mere), as in the case of expressions such as *abbhakṣaḥ* ("one who eats water"). The meaning of the phrase "Liberation alone is the truth" (*muktiketyeva satyam*) will be explained on the occasion of refuting the objections stated in the *Candrikā*.

Thus, even the Śruti passage, "All this has that as its self; that is the Truth; that is the Self; That art thou, O Śvetaketu," possesses its natural force precisely in the demonstration that modifications are unreal.

For instance: because of the other scriptural passage, "All this is indeed this Self," and because of the introductory statement, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," one forms the *bahuvrīhi* compound *ātmāsya* ("this has the Self as its [nature]"), and then applies an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). Since an abstract suffix refers to the meaning of the base word (*prakṛti*) which has become the qualifier (*prakāra*), it refers back to the Self that serves as the qualifier in the sense of the *bahuvrīhi*; thus, it establishes that "This Self is all this."

While it would have been sufficient simply to say "this Self is all this" (eṣa ātmā idaṃ sarvam) using grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the employment of both the *bahuvrīhi* compound and the possessive suffix (*bhāva-pratyaya*) is for the purpose of dispelling the suspicion that such coreferentiality might be merely figurative (*aupacārika*), based on the relationship between the self and what belongs to the self (*ātmāmīyabhāva*). This is because, were that the case, once the relationship of self and property had already been established by the *bahuvrīhi* itself through its primary function, the further exertion of employing the possessive suffix would be redundant; thus, by this reasoning, that suspicion is refuted.

Furthermore, that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) occurs in two possible ways: either with the intention of transformation (*pariṇāma*), as in "the clay is the jar," or with the intention of sublation of a superimposed [identity], as in "that which appeared as silver was mother-of-pearl. Therefore, in order to determine between these two, there is the statement "That is Truth" (*tatsatyam*). For in that context, the word "that" (*tat*) refers back to the Self (*ātman*) under discussion; because, within this section of the text, that alone is primary as the intended object of the teaching; because in the statement "That is the Self" (*sa ātmā*), it is that very same [Self] which is referred back; and because of the requirement for consistency with that single referent.

Consequently, by making known the unreality [of the world] through that word ["tat"], it establishes that the previously demonstrated grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) exists only in the sense of sublation (*bādhā*). Therefore, even the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) is exactly as it is heard, in accordance with its own internal consistency and in accordance with the consistency of its opening context.

But [the phrase] "tasmai tvaṃ tattvam" is not used in the sense that "you are to be surrendered to Him," according to the Śruti: "One should unite the self with the Self, saying 'Om'—to Brahman, to Thee, the Immortal"; nor in the sense that "you have arisen from Him," according to the Śruti: "From which indeed these beings are born"—[expressed as] "tasmāt tvaṃ tattvam"; nor in the sense that "He is your master," according to the Śruti: "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of causes"—[expressed as] "tasya tvaṃ tattvam"; [but rather] because of the Śruti: "O gentle one, these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode."

Regarding the phrase "sat-pratiṣṭhitāḥ" from the Śruti, if one were to interpret it as "you are established in that," the suffix *ṭa* would have to be applied; or else, one would have to laboriously explain it as "you are that reality" (*tattvam asi*) by means of the elision of case-endings according to the rule *sup-āṃ suluk...* and so forth. Since multiple meanings are possible for this [word] as shown, such an interpretation leads to confusion because no specific meaning can be determined. Likewise, even the description of the meaning of the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*)—by accepting that words denoting the body extend to the embodied self and intending a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) based on the relationship between the body and the embodied—is not natural.

For here, it is not accepted that the word *tvam*—which denotes the individual soul (*jīva*) who constitutes the body of the Lord—has its application in the Lord. This is because the meaning of the word *tvam* cannot function as a qualifier for the meaning of the word *tat*. Rather, it is the word *tat* itself, which refers back to the subject under discussion, that provides the qualification for the individual soul (the meaning of *tvam*) through the relation of non-difference (*abheda*). Otherwise, the use of the second person (*madhyama-puruṣa*) in the form "asi" would be untenable. Furthermore, if the meaning of the word *tvam* were a qualifier of something else, there would be no syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), and thus coordination with the verb (*ākhyāta-sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be impossible.

Because the rule "when *yuṣmad* is an upapada, when it is in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), even if it remains uninflected, the second person is used" prescribes the second person only when the word *yuṣmad* is in apposition with a verb; therefore, the meaning of the word *tvam* must be accepted as the substantive (*viśeṣya*). And in that case, the application of the word *tat*, which refers to the Supreme Self, is not possible—even if one accepts that words denoting a body extend to the embodied soul—because the Lord does not stand in the relation of being a body to the individual soul (*jīva*).

Therefore, for the sake of establishing the second person, one must accept a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) that has the individual soul (*jīva*) as its primary qualificand. Indeed, a reversal of the second and first persons is observed when there is a reversal of the relationship between qualifier and qualified in the referents of the words "you" (*tvam*) and "I" (*aham*): "O venerable deity, you indeed am I," and "I indeed am you."

Thus, the inherent tendency of the *Sadvidyā* to establish the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*) has been made clear by the venerable author of the Sūtras, Vyāsa, through the corroborative narrative (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of the story of Śvetaketu and Suvarcalā found in the *Mokṣadharma*. For it is related there as follows: the celestial maiden Suvarcalā, desiring a husband who possessed the innate experience of the reality of Brahman attained in a previous birth, heard that Śvetaketu had acquired the awakening to the nature of the Self from his father, and she chose him as her husband.

His father also informed him that he had remained established in the householder’s life, devoted to the performance of Vedic rites, under those two parents who were fixed in Brahman. There, between them, a conversation consisting of discourse on Brahman was underway;
then, at one time, Suvarcalā asked her husband Śvetaketu: "Tell me, O best of the twice-born, who are you here?"
The eloquent Blessed One said to her: "Without a doubt, you have recognized me;
I am the foremost among the gods, devoted to truth and vows."
She said to that Great-Souled One, "I ask him who dwells within my heart.
Having heard that, the omniscient bull among sages replied to her.
If you consider yourself to be joined with the mind alone, that is false; for as long as the lineage [of existence] persists, one remains bound to the body.
Even for me, the thought "I am this" and "I am all" continues to arise;
that which you ask me about is not the ultimate reality in this regard.

In this context, within the *Ṣaḍvidyā*, Śvetaketu had been instructed repeatedly by his father with the words "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). Desiring to know how he understood the Self, Suvarcalā asked the question, "Who are you, O best of the twice-born?
