Thereupon, although Śvetaketu understood the intent of the question, he thought that she should be led to realize the truth gradually; thus, he gave the reply: "Since you addressed me as 'best of the twice-born,' it is already understood that I am a Brāhmaṇa; what is there to be asked in this regard?"

Then, Suvarcalā said: "I do not ask about the Brahminhood that is perceived as superimposed upon the Self by means of the body as its limiting adjunct; rather, I ask about that Self which you point to in your heart with the word 'I' as 'I am the best of the twice-born,' and which is distinct from the body. To this, the following answer was given: "The word 'I' refers to the nature of the Self as colored by the mind (*manas*). And the nature of the Self as colored by the mind is false, just like the Brahminhood [superimposed] upon the Self whose limiting adjunct is the body born in a Brahmin family."

Therefore, those desiring to know the reality of the Self should not inquire about the referent of the word "I" (*ahaṃ-śabda-artha*), but rather about the ego-sense (*ahaṃ-bhāva*), which is common to all and established through direct perception. Consequently, if one desires to know the ultimate reality, the ego-sense itself is not fit to be the object of inquiry. Subsequently, when asked, "If you understand the ego-sense—endowed with agency, enjoyership, and so forth—to be unreal, then how do you perform Vedic rites preceded by such agency?", it was stated that the performance of Vedic actions is for the sake of maintaining social order (*loka-saṃgraha*).

Immediately thereafter, keeping in mind how the word "I" (ahaṃśabda), which is employed by everyone with reference to themselves, could not possibly have anything other than that [the Self] as its referent, he addressed the question regarding the relationship between a word and its meaning. He stated that the relationship between a word and its meaning is not one of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or the like, but rather the relationship of the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*). Following that, this sequence of questions and answers took place between the husband and wife:
Suvarcalā:
This word "I-conceit" (*ahaṃkāra*) always resides in the manifest Self (*vyaktātman*).
It would be false to say that words do not operate there.
Śvetaketu said: "O lady of auspicious luster, the word 'I' indeed refers to the ego-sense (ahaṃbhāva) and not to the nature of the Self;
nor do words characterized by qualities apply to the supreme, inconceivable [Reality]."
Suvarcalā said:
"O bull among sages, what indeed is this 'I-ness' (ahaṃbhāva), and likewise, what is the nature of the self (ātmabhāva)? Tell me that according to the proper method."
Śvetaketu said:

"For just as the appearance of a jar is essentially made of clay, so too is the state of 'I-ness' (ahaṃbhāva) here accepted as being of that same nature. Indeed, within the supreme, inconceivable [Self], the great and supreme state of the Self (ātmabhāva) exists."
It is not at all contradictory that words do not function there [in the Self].

Here, when the question is raised, "If the relationship between word and meaning in the form of the signified and the signifier exists here, how could the word 'I' not be a denoter of the Self?", the answer given is that the word 'I' does not function toward the Self through its primary (mukhya) mode of operation, but rather toward the object of the 'I' (ahamartha).

Then, when asked, "Who indeed is the Self other than the object denoted by 'I'?", [the teacher] demonstrates the distinction between the object of "I" and the Self by showing that even the sense of "I" (ahambhāva) within the Self is a mere appearance, like the appearance of a jar in clay. A word functioning through the mediation of a superimposed form does not extend as far as the pure substrate, just as the word "silver" used for mother-of-pearl functions through the mediation of silver.

Thus, it was concluded that the word "I" (ahaṃ), being caused by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the intellect (kalipata), does not function in its primary sense with respect to the pure Self; therefore, there is no contradiction. Having then taken for granted—as an established fact—that the Self alone, distinct from the ego (ahaṃkāra), is Brahman, the substratum of the phenomenal world (prapañca), [the text proceeds]. Just as space, despite being the locus of the phenomenal world, remains unattached to it, so too is the unattached nature of Brahman demonstrated by Śvetaketu; and then follow these further questions and answers: "O Suvarcalās, for [Brahman] is changeless, formless, partless, and all-pervading."
And the sky is seen to be non-eternal, yet the Self is not seen to be like that.
Śvetaketu said:
"One indeed touches with the skin the wind situated in space again and again;
likewise, one smells the fragrance residing therein and sees light with the eye."
The mass of darkness, the multitude of rays, the network of clouds,
and even the showering host of stars— once again, the sky is no longer visible.
Furthermore, it is certain that even the space of space is of the nature of existence;
everything imagined within the object of existence is that Truth, and that is indeed Viṣṇu.
Those names which are indeed figurative and applied metaphorically to the Supreme Self cannot be perceived by the eye, nor by the mind, nor by any other [sense] before [the realization of that Self].

"It is contemplated by a subtle intellect; it cannot be expressed by speech. This entire manifold universe (prapañca) is established in that very [Brahman] alone. Regarding this, to the question "Why is Brahman, the substratum of the manifold universe which is like space, not perceived?", the answer is that there is only the perception of air and so forth situated within space, but space itself is not discerned separately. When such is the case even for the empirical space, what need is there to speak of the Supreme Self, which is subtler than that? Therefore, everything is imagined upon the Reality (Sat). And that Reality, being the substratum of all, is all-pervasive.

Regarding this, the answer was stated that words functioning by depending upon limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) do not apply directly to the pure [Self]. In this sequence of questions and answers, the meaning of the Śruti passage concerning "the origin of speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*) is conveyed by the illustrative statement, "For the appearance of the jar is indeed composed of clay. The meaning of the sentence "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) is conveyed by the statement that the subject under discussion—the individual soul (*jīva*)—is of the nature of Being (*sad-rūpa*), expressed by the word "Self" (*ātman*). And the meaning of "All this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*) is conveyed by the statement, "All this is indeed Viṣṇu, imagined within the reality of Being."

Furthermore, the meaning of the scriptural passage, "That is the Truth, that is the Self," has been shown to be conducive to the realization of Brahman as non-different from the inner self (pratyagātman) which is devoid of phenomenal expansion (niṣprapañca). Thus, when it is established by the aforementioned corroboration that the Sadvidyā primarily concerns Brahman as non-different from the inner self devoid of phenomenal expansion, it is clear to the learned that—since this [realization] would otherwise be untenable without the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca)—the scriptural passages such as "beginning with speech" (vācārambhaṇam) have their primary purport in establishing the falsity of the phenomenal world.

In this way, even the sentence beginning with "there is not even the slightest diversity here" (*evam neha nānāsti kiṃcana*) has its natural force (*svārasya*) precisely in establishing the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*). For here, by the method of superimposition (*adhyāropa*), through the word "here" (*iha*), which purifies the meanings of the words within the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), there is the presentation of Brahman as qualified by the world. And therein, when diversity is being negated, the meaning conveyed is that "not even the slightest thing"—that is, nothing whatsoever—exists in any manner; thus, it provides the predicate consisting in the absolute absence of all duality.

For, in cases where there is no sublation (*bādhaka*), the appearance of being delimited by the time and other factors that delimit the scope of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) in relation to the connection between the subject and the predicate (*uddeśya-vidheyabhāva*) is established by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). Furthermore, since the cognition of the absence of duality at another time is already established through such scriptural texts as "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow," "The wise one is freed from name and form," and "Having known God, one is released from all bonds," as well as through other means of knowledge such as inference—based on the mark (*liṅga*) of "being an object of sight" (*dṛśyatva*) which implies destruction by knowledge—the statement "neither here nor... (*neha nānā*) serves to communicate that [absence].

Otherwise, the statement would result in being purposeless (*vaiyarthyāpatti*). For, when something is commonly accepted (*saṃpratipanna*) in a certain locus by a certain relation and in a certain form, it is the very nature (*svarasa*) of that statement to convey the falsity (*mithyātva*)—defined as being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of an absence residing in that [locus], delimited by that relation and delimited by that form—at the time of that [acceptance]. However, the meaning established in the opponent's view—that "here in Brahman there is no plurality," meaning "there is no difference (*bheda*) whose counter-positive is not Brahman"—is not its natural sense.

Furthermore, because difference (*bheda*) exists in Brahman with respect to its correlates—the individual soul (*jīva*), the jar (*ghaṭa*), and so forth—it is impossible to negate it; thus, since a negation of difference in general is untenable, the term "diversity" (*nānātva*), which naturally implies difference in general, would have to be interpreted as referring to a specific difference that does not have Brahman as its correlate, resulting in a strained meaning. Moreover, even with that interpretation, the phrase "not anything at all" (*na kiñcana*) remains awkward and redundant. This is the direction of the argument. As for what was stated in the *Candrikā* after refuting those objections: "Because the knowledge of everything through the knowledge of one is impossible, and because the illustration of the lump of clay is inapplicable."
For it is said that through the knowledge of Brahman, everything becomes known;
indeed, from the knowledge of the true nature of mother-of-pearl, there is no cognition of silver.
On the contrary—
just as the cognition of silver arises from the non-recognition of the power [of the substrate],
so too is omniscience appropriate [in this case] due to the non-recognition of the true nature of Brahman.

Thus the objection has been stated; yet that too is weak. In the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*), it is universally accepted that through the knowledge of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), that which is superimposed is known in its true nature (*tattvataḥ*). And that [knowledge in its true nature] consists in [the superimposed object] having as its own real essence the very nature of the substrate. For it is said in the *Bhāmatī*: "When the rope is known, the reality of the snake becomes known; for that [rope] is its true nature."

And thus, immediately after the direct perception of the mother-of-pearl, because of the cognition "this is mother-of-pearl" which arises from the appearance of silver, the fact that the silver is known in its true reality as having the nature of mother-of-pearl—specifically, the fact that it possesses a real essence consisting of being known as mother-of-pearl—is entirely intact through that knowledge of the mother-of-pearl. Furthermore, the statement "by the knowledge of one, all is known" intends precisely the knowledge of all in their true reality.

And thus, when Brahman—the substratum—is known, the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in such statements as "All this is this Self" and "All this is indeed Brahman" is understood through sublation (*bādhā*). Since the world superimposed upon Brahman possesses the same real nature (*tāttvika-svarūpatva*) as the Brahman already known, there is no inconsistency in the knowledge of all things arising from the knowledge of one, just as the knowledge of jars and the like arises from the knowledge of clay. It was stated previously that this [knowledge of the world] is merely by way of the "sugar-on-the-tongue" analogy (*guḍajihvikā-nyāya*);
therefore, there is no lack of consistency with the aforementioned example.

As for what is stated in the *Candrikā*, which quotes the *Bhāmatī*: "When the rope is known, the reality of the snake is known, for that [rope] is its reality; and thus, through the knowledge of Brahman, everything becomes known in its true nature. This is not correct, for in this way the meaning would be that through the knowledge of Brahman, Brahman alone is known. And that is improper, because it is impossible for something to be its own cause.

This is because it would be impossible for the words "the unheard becomes heard," "the unthought becomes thought," and "the unknown becomes known" to apply to that which has already been heard and so forth. Furthermore, a reality (*tattva*) is defined as either an uncommon essential nature (*svarūpa*) or a unique property (*dharma*); it cannot, however, be the locus of an error. If it were so, then bliss (*ānanda*) would not be the reality of Brahman, nor would "rope-ness" be the reality of a rope. Moreover, a rope is neither the essential nature nor a property of the snake, which is sublated by the knowledge of the rope.

Nor can there be a single underlying substrate that is common to multiple superimpositions that are not mutually distinct; for such a substrate would not be the unique, non-common locus of each individual thing that is superimposed. Furthermore, it does not follow from the mere fact that something is superimposed that it possesses the reality of what it is superimposed upon. You yourself have accepted this: even though the snake lacks existence apart from the rope and thus lacks identity as something other than the rope, the rope nonetheless possesses existence apart from the snake and is therefore other than it. Moreover, the cognition "this is a snake" with respect to a rope would be a valid cognition (*pramā*), just as the cognition of Brahman is in the case of bliss, or as the cognition of a snake is in the case of an actual snake.

Because that [sublation] occurs through the knowledge of that reality; for, just as the error of a snake is removed by the knowledge of the rope, the knowledge of the reality of the locus is opposed to the error caused by ignorance of it. Nor should it be argued that the example of clay and so forth is appropriate because a jar and the like are superimposed upon clay, for even when the reality of the clay is known, the jar and so forth are not thereby sublated.

Although, as in the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), there is no separate substance such as a jar produced from clay, nevertheless, even in your own system, there exists the referent of words like "jar"—which consists of a particular state (*avasthāviśeṣa*) similar to the clay, capable of performing functions such as carrying water, and established through the operation of causal factors (*kāraka*). In reality, however, even the clay does not exist. Furthermore: if the jar and so forth were known through the knowledge of mere clay, then after determining that it is clay, there would be no further doubt regarding the jar and the like.

By this, that which was stated in the *Bhāmatī*—namely, that by the knowledge of clay, pots and the like are known in their true nature (*tattvataḥ*), for clay alone is the true nature of pots and so forth—is refuted. For even when the "clay-ness" is known, because the specific configuration (*saṃsthānaviśeṣa*) known as "pot-ness" is not known, there is the common usage that "the pot is not known in its true nature. Furthermore, the objection was raised that the superimposition (*āropa*) of being a bowl (*śarāva*) and so forth upon the pot would not cease; but that too is weak.

Regarding the statement that "by the knowledge of Brahman, everything becomes known in its true nature," the instrumental case in *brahmavijñānena* denotes non-difference (*abheda*). Furthermore, this non-difference is construed with the act of knowing expressed by *vijñātam*. Thus, the final meaning is: "Everything is Brahman, which has as its object a cognition that is non-different from the cognition of one's own true nature, [that cognition] being itself non-different from the cognition of the true nature [of Brahman]. In this established sense, there is no room for the objection that a thing cannot be its own cause (*svasya svahetutvāpatti*).

Even in passages such as "By which the unheard becomes heard," the term *aśruta* (the unheard) refers to the ether and so forth; and the meaning is that these become heard in reality—that is, they come to possess their own true nature, which is non-different from the nature of the Śruti (Veda). Thus, through a grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) resulting in a sublation (*bādhā*) of the literal sense, there is no inconsistency with the application of words such as "heard" and the like.

As for the objection raised in the *Candrikā* that the examples of the lump of clay and its products are untenable under the theory of illusory transformation (*vivartavāda*), that too is based on a failure to understand the heart of the venerable author of the *Bhāṣya*. To explain: the intention of the *Bhāṣya* in its commentary on the phrase "an emanation of speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*) is as follows: in the passage "by which the unheard becomes heard," there is grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the sense of sublation (*bādha*).

The meaning is that everything "unheard"—beginning with space (*viyat*)—is in reality devoid of its own ultimate nature as something distinct from the Brahman heard [in scripture] and non-different from it. Thus, the proposition is established: Brahman alone is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of everything. In this regard, the analogy—that just as an effect does not exist in reality apart from a lump of clay—is set forth by the passage beginning, "Just as, my dear, by one [clay]," and so on. Furthermore, because of its association with the word *eka* (one) in its primary sense, the term *mṛtpiṇḍa* (lump of clay) refers to the earth (*bhūmi*) itself in the form of a lump.

The term *piṇḍapada* (lump-word) indicates a specific gross form for the purpose of establishing its fitness as being composed solely of clay. The term *mṛnmayapada* (clay-made word), moreover, signifies merely a modification (*vikāra*) of earth. Thus, the meaning is that every form whatsoever, such as a jar, does not exist in reality apart from earth. Furthermore, since the state of being a modification of earth exists directly in things like trees and so forth, there is no deficiency even if the various modifications do not take a distinct lump of earth as their material cause.

Although earth is not the substratum [of its modifications], nevertheless, just as there is the conventional usage that "in reality silver and so forth do not exist apart from the conch-shell and other things which serve as the delimiters of their substratum," so too, at the time of investigating the true nature of the modifications of earth and the like, there is the conventional usage that "in reality those modifications do not exist apart from the earth and so forth which serve as the delimiters of their substratum. It is for this reason that the Śruti has spoken in such a manner. And thus, in the statement "All that consists of clay is one with the lump of clay," the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is used in the sense of sublation (*bādhā*), because the true nature of the object itself has been realized.

In this context, the reason is given as: "Only 'clay' is real. This is because it has been stated that the nature of Brahman is established as being cognizable through all means of knowledge (*pratyaya*). For "clay" (*mṛttikā*) is earth; that which is not perceived as such is Brahman, whose nature is Being (*sad-rūpa*) as delimited by that [earth]. That alone is real, because the nature of clay lacks reality. Since the nature of clay is not real, when the example is presented in the state of cognition, clay is known as "earth" because it is not distinguished from [Brahman] due to ignorance. Therefore, for the sake of attaining its true nature as Being, it is said in the phrase "only clay is [real]" that "only [clay is real]. Thus, the word "iti" (thus/only) is used here.

Otherwise, that [word] would result in being purposeless. By this same reasoning, in the context of grammar and similar fields, one must abandon the word-referentiality established by the context; for just as the word *na* in the sūtra *na veti vibhāṣā* refers to its own meaning because the referentiality to the object is obtained from the context of the object itself, so too here, since word-referentiality alone must be asserted, and that is useless in the present case, the word *iti* in the phrase *mṛttiketyeva* would be utterly purposeless according to your view.

The criticism raised by the opponent is entirely without foundation. Alternatively, the word *iti* in the present context signifies "beginning with" (*ādi*). This is supported by the *Amara-kośa*, which states: "*iti* is used for reasons, types, kinds, and so forth, as well as for completion. Accordingly, when the nature of the transformation is investigated, that [transformation] is likewise unreal, just as the earth is unreal when its own nature is investigated. Only the unevolved (*apañcīkṛta*) elements, which serve as the cause of those [transformations], are real. When even their own nature is investigated, they too are unreal; only their cause, the primordial matter (*mūla-prakṛti*), is real. Such is the meaning obtained.

The same principle should be applied to the subsequent examples as well. Regarding the statement, "Only 'clay' is real," the reason is provided by the passage beginning with, "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name," and so forth; this has already been explained previously. In this very sense it is said:
"Who are you?"—this designation is indeed a useless verbal handle;
[for what is seen] is merely a collection of wooden parts of a palanquin arranged in the form of words and bones.
O best of kings, let that separation of the palanquin be sought by you;
likewise, let the distinctness of the ribs of the umbrella be reflected upon.
The maxim "Where has the umbrella gone? applies equally to you and to me;
for that which in the world is called "king" and that which consists of the king's soldiers—[all are but names].
Likewise, O King, that which is other than this is not composed of real volitions;
thus alone is this entire universe (Brahman), and the whole world is without duality.
The true nature of the Supreme Self, who is designated by the name Vāsudeva.

The scriptural passage from the *Sadvidyā*—beginning with "That which is its red color is the color of fire, that which is white is the color of water, and that which is black is the color of food; the 'fire-ness' of fire has departed; the modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; the truth is simply these three colors"—is the authoritative proof, as its purport is determined by thousands of corroborative statements from the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa* and other sources, such as "The world-appearance (*prapañca*), which is synonymous with the 'ineffable' (*anirvacanīya*), is false."

For in that [passage], by taking as the reason—from "the state of being fire" at the end up to "unsubstantiality"—the fact that the threefold form consisting of fire and so forth cannot withstand analysis apart from its non-trivṛtkṛta nature as light, water, and food, it is established through the words "a mere beginning in speech" and so on that the merely trivṛtkṛta is false. As for the meaning stated by the opponent, there is no evidence whatsoever, and its lack of internal consistency has already been mentioned; enough of this elaboration.

Furthermore, objections such as whether reality (*tattva*) is the unique essential nature (*svarūpa*) or a property (*dharma*) are weak; for since reality is defined as that which is non-superimposed (*anāropita*), those aforementioned objections find no footing. For this very reason, Udayanācārya stated in his commentary on the *Bhāṣya* that "reality is the non-superimposed essential nature," according to which the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results from the knowledge of reality.

Thus, in the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), due to the delusion that [the silver] is not superimposed upon the shell and so forth, and because it is characterized by identity with the silver, there is the worldly usage that "the shell is the true nature (*svarūpa-tattva*) of the silver," and likewise the usage that "shell-ness and so forth are the true nature of the attributes (*dharma-tattva*) of the shell. However, in the state of discrimination (*viveka*), Brahman alone is known as being non-superimposed; therefore, in accordance with the actual state of things (*vastu-gati*), that alone is the true nature of all things. It was precisely with this intention that Amara Siṃha stated: "Brahman is *tattva*, austerity, and the Veda."

According to Hemacandra, *tattva* (reality) refers to the Supreme Self, a specific category of discourse, or essential nature (*svarūpa*). For you, who maintain that the world is real (*prapañcatattvavādin*), being a proponent of reality does not mean being a proponent of a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*), but rather simply being a proponent of a non-superimposed world. Since even in your own view it is accepted that only an un-superimposed essential nature constitutes reality, your statement that reality is either an essential nature or a unique property is based solely on a failure to remember your own doctrine.

Furthermore, from the word *tattva*—derived through the etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*) that "the state of that [thing] is its *tattva*"—neither a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) nor another uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharmāntara*) is understood. This is because, from words such as *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness), there is no cognition of another property co-extensive with the universal (*jāti*) that constitutes the mode of the cognition produced by the word *ghaṭa*. Moreover, conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is universally accepted only for an ultimate reality (*pāramārthikavastu*), and thus uncommonness (*asādhāraṇya*) need not be included therein. Consequently, what is intended is that the very nature of a thing, when it is not superimposed upon it, is its *svarūpa-tattva* (essential reality).

And it was stated previously that "belonging to that" (tadīyatva) consists in being the counter-correlative of identity residing in that [entity]. Since identity is possible because there exists a conceptual difference between Brahman and bliss, it is established that bliss has the nature of the reality of Brahman. Furthermore, the rope-ness (*rajjutva*) of a rope is not its essential nature (*svarūpatattva*), but rather its property-nature (*dharmatattva*); thus, there is no room for the objection that "in that case, bliss would not be the reality of Brahman, nor would rope-ness be the reality of the rope."

Even in the case of one who has been bitten by a snake, its status as having that [snake] as its own essential nature (*svarūpatattva*) is established by resorting to the conceptual non-difference (*kālpānikābheda*) according to the method already stated. Furthermore, the cognition "this is a snake" regarding a rope is not valid knowledge (*pramā*), because it lacks the property of having an uncontradicted object as its content. Nor does it possess even the status of empirical validity (*vyāvahārikapramātva*), because its object is subject to sublation at the time of worldly transaction. You cannot maintain that the definition of its validity consists in being a cognition whose qualificandum is that [rope] and whose qualifier is that [snake].

If that were the case, then in your view, cognitions such as "substantiality in the pot"—which have the pot as their qualifier and the relation of being-located (*ādheyatā*) as their mode—would result in lacking the status of valid knowledge (*pramātva*) regarding the aspect of the pot and so forth. This is because you have stated that the specific nature (*asādhāraṇasvarūpa*) of those [entities] alone constitutes their respective reality (*tattvarūpatā*), whereas substantiality and the like do not possess the specific nature of the pot and so forth. Furthermore, it is only the cognition of that reality which serves as the substratum that can remove error; thus, even when "clay-ness" (*mṛttva*) is known, the non-cessation of the [erroneous notion of] the pot and so forth is logically consistent.

Furthermore, even the non-cessation of doubt—such as "Is this a jar or not?"—is established once the knowledge of clay and so forth has arisen, because only a certainty (*niścaya*) regarding the same object is the direct opposite of doubt. It was demonstrated previously that the state of jars and other things having their own true nature known through the cognition of clay and so forth is justified by the maxim of the "sugar on the tongue" (*guḍajihvikā-nyāya*) and similar principles. Thus, the statement that "by the cognition of clay, jars and the like become known in their true nature, for clay alone is the true nature of jars and so forth" is indeed correct, as stated in the *Bhāmatī*.
By this, the objection raised in the passage beginning with "by this [it is refuted]" is also set aside.

As for the objection raised in the *Candrikā*—namely, that according to the Advaita view, this [section] is redundant because of the two sections on *prakṛti* (the material cause) and *adṛśyatva* (the invisible), since in both cases the status of Brahman as a vivarta (illusory manifestation) is stated—that criticism is extremely weak. For the very purpose of the *prakṛti* section is to establish that Brahman possesses the nature of the material cause (*upādānatā*) while simultaneously being the efficient cause (*nimittatva*).

In response to the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that accepting such a state of being the material cause (*upādānatā*) would result in the loss of the distinction between the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) and the enjoyed (*bhogya*), [the author] first offers a rebuttal of that objection against his own position by appealing to the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) through the analogy "as in the world. Then, in order to provide the final resolution—that from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*) such a distinction does not exist at all—he employs the doctrine of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*). However, even with this mention of *vivarta*, it is because this [doctrine] is not the subject matter (*prameya*) of this particular section (*adhikaraṇa*). For in the section on "Invisibility" (*adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa*), the subject matter is precisely the establishment of the passage concerning the "Source of Beings" (*bhūtayoni*) as referring to Brahman, after having refuted its interpretation as referring to the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*).
To establish that point, even though the term *vivarta* (illusory manifestation) is used there, it does not constitute the subject matter (*prameya*) of this particular section (*adhikaraṇa*).

Furthermore, as for the objection raised in the *Candrikā*: "Moreover, in your view, there is a contradiction between the statement of difference in the previous sūtra and the statement of non-difference here; nor is it appropriate to resolve the contradiction between two authoritative sūtras by claiming that one has a false subject matter"—this too is irrelevant, because according to the method already explained, the sūtra *tadananyatvam* teaches precisely a falsity (*mithyātva*) consisting of identity (*tādātmya*), and thus it does not state non-difference at all.

Furthermore, it is logical that even between two authoritative aphorisms (*sūtra*), there may be a difference in their respective subject matters, as is the case with two authoritative scriptures—one general and one specific. Since the preceding aphorism stated "as in the world" (*lokavat*), and since in the world there is no established doctrine regarding the unreality of transformations (*vikāra*), the present aphorism is commenced to dispel the misconception that the resolution offered was based on the reality of the distinction between the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) and the enjoyed (*bhogya*). Moreover, this is because the intention of the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*)—expressed by the commentators of our own [tradition]—is that this distinction between enjoyer and enjoyed is accepted as merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*).

As for the objection raised in the *Candrikā*: "Furthermore, the word *ārambhaṇa*, which establishes that a jar and so forth are non-different from clay, is not a direct reason (*hetu*) for your probandum—that the world is non-different from Brahman—whereas it is a reason for me," that too is weak. For even in your own view, the word *ārambhaṇa* alone does not establish the reason; rather, there is an objection [in the scripture]: "What was the support? What was the material cause (*ārambhaṇa*)? And how was it? [Thus, the term by itself is not the intended reason].

By what substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and so forth did the Creator, while producing the earth and the sky, become distinguished as a creator? What was that substratum? What was the "commencement" (*ārambhaṇa*)—that by which something is begun—or what was the instrument (*sādhana*)? And how was it? [The answer is: "Nothing at all, nor in any way. Thus, an objection is raised regarding the instrument and other factors. This is because the objection reaches its conclusion [in this manner]. Since the interrogative pronoun *kiṃ* is common to both questioning and objection, one might ask: why should it not be taken here in the sense of a question? To this he replies: "Because no substratum and so forth have been mentioned. If it were a question, an answer would have to be stated.

Just as in the question, "What indeed is the remedy for cold? the answer is, "Fire is the remedy for cold," so too here, this is not a question because no locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) or other such factors are mentioned for the sake of a reply; rather, it is a censure (*ākṣepa*). This is understood from a careful examination of your own *Tattvaprakāśikā* text, wherein you intend that the entire textual context containing that [sentence] constitutes the reason (*hetu*), since the word *ārambhaṇa* alone cannot establish the probandum (*sādhya*)—which you accept as being of the nature of non-difference from That—as a self-sufficient means of proof. Thus, even in my view...

Regarding the phrase "the non-difference of that" (*tadananyatvam*), the non-difference of those two—the effect and the cause—is their identity (*tādātmyam*). Therefore, the intended probandum (*sādhya*) to be established consists of two aspects: the non-difference of the effect from the cause in reality, and [the unreality of the effect]. This is because the textual passage containing the word *ārambhaṇa* (along with its illustrative examples), as well as the subsequent passage consisting of the illustrative statements such as "Thus, my dear, is that instruction," serve as direct proofs for these [two] reasons.

As for the objection raised in the *Candrikā*—that because the word *vācārambhaṇa* is a compound, the sūtra should have been formulated as *vācārambaṇa-śabdādibhyaḥ* (from words such as *vācārambaṇa*), since it is more appropriate to employ the complete term rather than taking only a portion of a word, which is improper—that too is not correct. For in the Bhāṣya, which states, "Only by speech is it begun [to exist], as 'pot,' 'dish,' and 'water-jar,'" the word *vācā* is indeed employed in its uncompounded form.

Nor should it be argued that since this is the case, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) in *vācā* is untenable due to the application of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) when used in connection with a verbal noun (*kṛt*); for in the word *vācā*, the third case is accepted as expressing the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). Furthermore, in the *Chāndogyabhāṣyavivaraṇa*, it is stated that the third case in *vācā* signifies the meaning of the sixth case, and that there is a separate word [for each]. As for the *Chāndogyabhāṣya* statement, "speech is the starting point" (*vāgārambhaṇam*), meaning "speech is the support" (*vāgālambanam*), that is intended merely to state the resultant meaning.

There is no contradiction even when a portion of a compound is employed for the purpose of manifesting a specific sentence that constitutes a particular context; for it has already been stated that the mere word *ārambhaṇa* lacks the capacity to establish the reason in either of the two systems. Furthermore, the objection raised in the *Candrikā*—namely, that in your view, since the meaning of the words in the Sūtra and such passages as "All this is what this Self is" are themselves verbal in nature, the formulation in the Sūtra ought to have been "from the words *vācārambhaṇa* etc. rather than "from the words *vācārambhaṇa-ādi*"—is also weak.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), it is implied "and by reasonings. Thus, even in your own commentary, as with the examples of reasonings such as "by means of the reasonings regarding the pot, the water-jar, and so forth," [it is shown that] just as the spaces within a pot, a water-jar, and the like are non-different from the great space (mahākāśa), and just as the water of a mirage and the like are non-different from the saline desert (ūṣara) and so forth—because their nature is seen and then lost, and because they cannot be described in terms of an intrinsic nature (svarūpa).

Thus, by our own commentary stating that this manifold world (prapañca) consisting of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and so forth, has no existence apart from Brahman, we have demonstrated that the phrase "and so forth" (ādi-śabda) includes such reasons as "being an object of perception" (dṛśyatva) and "being limited" (paricchinnatva). Consequently, the claim that the word "only" (mātra) alone constitutes the meaning of the term "and so forth" is rooted in error. Furthermore, by the expression "because its nature is seen and then lost," an inference has also been shown to establish the falsity of the world as proven by scripture.

Two inferences are intended here: "The disputed ether and so forth are false, because they are visible and because they are counter-correlatives of non-destruction," as is evident from our own commentary on that [text]. || 14 ||
And because [the self] is perceived when there is existence. || 15 ||

In this context—prior to the word "kāraṇasya" (of the cause) in the sūtra—one must supply "kāryasya" (of the effect) before "upalabdheḥ" (because of perception). The term "bhāva" means "existence alone. By the word "ca" (and), being perceived only when the cause is perceived is conjoined. Thus, the status of being the probans for the probandum—which consists in non-difference from the cause—is obtained for that which exists only when the cause exists, as conjoined with the fact of being perceived only when the cause is perceived.

Precisely for the sake of obtaining these two meanings, instead of stating "because of existence in the locus" (*bhāve ca sattvāt*), it was stated as "and because of perception in the locus" (*bhāve copalabdheḥ*). In that context, the inclusion of the combined qualifiers serves two purposes: first, to prevent deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of the specific form of the perceived jar and so forth—which, while being perceived in the locus (the light), are distinct from the light; and second, to prevent deviation by means of the specific smoke which, though existing only when fire exists (as explicitly stated), is distinct from the fire itself.

The phrase "the existence (bhāva) and presence (sattā) of the cause, as well as its apprehension (upalambha)"—as stated in the *Ṭīkā*—intends these two [existence and apprehension] to fall within the scope of the qualification of the reason (*hetu*); this is the implied meaning (*śeṣa*). This is because the passage of the *Ṭīkā* is intended to state the resultant meaning [of the syllogism]. Furthermore, it would entail numerous faults, such as the non-application of the words *bhāva* and *upalabdhi*, the necessity of changing their case-endings, and the requirement of supplying the two words "of the cause" and "of the effect."

However, regarding my [position], there is no room for the objection stated in the *Candrikā*—namely, that "because of the consequence (*prasaṅga*)" should be understood merely as a reason (*hetu*) following from the word "but" (*tu*)—since it is simpler to supply the phrase "of the cause, which is an independent proof. As for the interpretation of "from perception" (*upalabdheḥ*) as meaning "due to the consequence of perception," this is merely an excessive refinement on the part of the opponent.

Since the non-perception of an independent means of proof (*svatantra-sādhana*) by means of valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*) is established by its very nature, the statement of it would be purposeless; therefore, the phrase "because of perception" (*upalabdheḥ*) must necessarily mean "because of the consequence of [its] being perceived. For instance, the explanation of others is as follows: "If there were an independent means of proof distinct from that [Veda] in the creation of the Blessed One, then it would be perceived by means of valid cognitions such as the Veda. Yet it is not perceived. Therefore, the meaning is that it does not exist."

As for the claim that "only when the cause exists does the reason, which consists in being existent, contradict the probandum, which consists in being unreal (anṛtatva)," that is not so. For the "existence" included as a qualification of the reason is of the nature of actual presence (*vidyamānatā*), and thus it contradicts unreality in the sense of being indefinable (*anirvācyatva*). Furthermore, in this Sūtra, it is precisely non-difference in the form of identity (*tādātmya*) that is intended to be the probandum. And it has been stated by the venerable Advaitānanda: "By this Sūtra, a specific essential relation called identity is established as the regulator of the relationship between material cause and its effect."

As for the objection that there is no perception at all of that which is pure, consisting of consciousness alone and accessible through scripture alone, or of that which is qualified by attributes such as omniscience—arguing that the reason stated in the Sūtra is unestablished (*asiddha*) because of the perception of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—that too is not correct. For by the phrase "perception of that" (*tadupalabdhi*), what is intended is precisely the perception having as its object either [the pure nature] or one of the forms superimposed upon it. Furthermore, if the reading is *bhāvāccopalabdheḥ*, "existence" (*bhāva*) means identity (*tādātmya*); the ablative case is used in the sense of eliding the verbal root *lī* (to dissolve/merge).

The meaning is: "because there is perception [of the effect] having brought its existence (*bhāva*) within the range of the senses. By the word *ca* ("and"), there is a conjunction with the previously mentioned inference and other means of knowledge. Furthermore, the commentary beginning with "And because there is perceptual apprehension" (*pratyakṣopalabdhibhāvāt*) is intended to state the resultant meaning. For there indeed exists perceptual apprehension when there is non-difference between cause and effect; here, in the subsequent commentary, the locative case in the term *ananyatve* signifies the sense of being the object (*viṣayatva*). And it should be understood that this commentary is of the nature of an explanation for the term *bhāva* and so forth.

Thus, on this view, the objection that the word "bhāva" (existence) is redundant is refuted. As for the argument that, since the non-difference of cause and effect is established on this view, the unreality of the effect cannot be proven—that has already been largely refuted. 15.
And because of the existence of what follows. || 16 ||

In the preceding sūtra, by establishing through perception and inference that cloth and other effects are non-different from their threads and other causes, it was shown by that same example—that the effect is the material cause—that the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), beginning with space (*viyat*), is non-different from Brahman. The meaning is that because the subsequent [effect] exists, it exists in the cause only in the form of the causal self; thus, it possesses identity (*tādātmya*) with the supreme cause, Brahman, in its own subtle form. The essential point is that scripture declares the identity of the subtle form of space and the rest—which exist in the state of being an effect—with pure Being (*sattā*).

Because it is necessary that the state of being an effect—which qualifies the *sat* (Being) as being identical with ether and so forth—must enter into the meaning of the sentence only as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), since it is impossible for that which exists at the initial moment [of creation] to possess the existence of the state of being an effect; and it should not be argued that the statement that the mere state of being an effect is the secondary indicator is incorrect, because it is possible for ether and so forth, precisely when they have reached the state of being an effect, to serve as secondary indicators.

The sense is this: since the focus on a qualified object (*viśiṣṭārtha*) is the general rule (*autsargika*), when there is no [contrary] qualification, the sublation of the exception (*apavādaka-bādha*) is achieved merely by abandoning that [qualification]; therefore, even regarding the substantive portion (*viśeṣyāṃśa*), it is improper to abandon it without a specific cause. To illuminate the utility of the meaning of the cited scripture for the upcoming doctrine of the world’s material causality (*jagad-upādānatā*), he says: "And that which, in its own nature... Thus, the purpose of the inclusion of the word "this" (*idam*) in the scripture is demonstrated.

One might object: "Even so, it remains unproven that the world, when in its state as an effect, possesses identity with Being (*sattādātmya*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Therefore, prior to its production... And thus, the ether and other elements, when in their state as effects, possess identity with Being, because they have subtle forms that possess identity with Being at the same time as themselves. Whatever has a subtle form that possesses identity with Being at the same time as itself, possesses identity with that [Being].

The point is that, just as a jar—consisting of its own subtle form which is non-different from the clay universal coexisting with the jar—is identical with the clay universal, so too, by means of an inference supported by a generality-based pervasion (*sāmānyamukhavyāpti*), the identity of every effect with the ultimate cause is established.

He begins to explain the Sūtra by another method with the words "And just as... The meaning is that existence (*sattva*) does not deviate across the three periods of time; thus, it is not the case that it is not the object of any cognition whose content is the existent (*sat*). The same applies hereafter. And so, ether and the rest possess identity with existence (*sattādātmyavān*), because they are not objects of a cognition that does not have the existent as its object. Whatever is not the object of a cognition that does not have X as its object [is identical with X].

The meaning is that the identity between the world and Brahman is established by the inference: "That [the world] possesses identity with That [Brahman], just like the [well-known] agreed-upon instance. Nor should it be suspected that this point has already been covered by the Sūtra *bhāve copalabdheḥ* (and because of perception when there is existence); for in that [Sūtra], having established the identity of threads, cloth, and so forth, the identity of Brahman with the world was established through that example on the basis of its being the material cause (*upādāna*). Here, however, there is the distinction that it is established directly. Nor is there a defect of the probandum being included in the reason, since the status of being a material cause necessarily involves identity.

This is because, in that context, what is intended as the cause is precisely the status of being a material cause (*upādānatā*), which consists in possessing its prior non-existence (*tatprāgabhāvavattva*). Nor does the same logic apply here such that the point would already be established; for while it is unproven that the world is not the object of a cognition that excludes Brahman—just as cloth and the like are not the objects of a cognition that excludes threads and the like—it must instead be established by resorting to parsimony (*lāghava*) that the single, common reality (*sat*) is the object of the uniform cognitions such as "the pot exists" (*ghaṭaḥ san*) and "the cloth exists" (*paṭaḥ san*).

And such simplicity is not without scriptural authority, because it is supported by such Śruti texts as "Existence alone" (*sadeva*). For it is evident that if Brahman were to have a second of its own kind in terms of ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), the determination of its oneness would be untenable. Furthermore, since it is possible for the term to exclude other similar entities in the form of the delimitor of the subjecthood (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*) co-referential with it, it is improper to resort to the labor of a different interpretation. Moreover, "ultimate reality" is well-known as the delimitor of the meaning of the word "existent" (*sat*).

The term *sattva* means "the state of being" (*sataḥ bhāvaḥ*). Because the compound is formed with a word ending in a *vibhakti* (case-ending) that establishes the unity intended [by the sutra], the fact that the sutra indicates the stated meaning is established. Furthermore, in accordance with the illumination of such reasoning, the example of the aforementioned sentence was given rather than citing the sentence "All this is indeed Brahman" (*khalvidaṃ brahma*). By this, [the objection] that "the existence (*sattva*) of the later-born ether and so forth is contrary to the unreality (*anṛtatva*) you intend to prove; therefore, the argument 'because of the existence of the later' is incoherent" is refuted.

Furthermore, the objection that there is the burden of supplying an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) by [interpreting] "prior to origination" (*utpatteḥ prāk*), and that the second sūtra has as its subject matter threads and cloth while the third has Brahman and ether, etc.—thus having different subjects—rendering the word "and" (*ca*) unseemly; and the objection that because the supplementary statement "It created fire" (*tat tejo ’sṛjata*) shows that the passage beginning with "Being alone" (*sad eva*) refers to the cause, the difference between effect and cause remains unproven even now, and therefore the existence of the effect cannot be established—all this is refuted.

Since existence—characterized by identity with being (*sattādātmya*), relation to time, and so forth—is necessarily distinct from non-existence, it is compatible with indefinability (*anirvacanīyatā*) and therefore cannot be contradictory to it; moreover, absolute non-existence is not what is being established here.

When it is stated that "because the effect is heard to have identity with existence" (*sattādātmya*), a doubt may arise: "Since space (*viyat*) and so forth, when in the state of being effects, cannot be made to understand the aforementioned identity through the cited statements in the manner previously described, how can this [statement] have been made? To dispel this doubt, the *Bhāṣya* proceeds; and although the phrase "prior to origination" (*utpatteḥ prāk*) is mentioned there, because there is no intrusion of an unreal object (*asadartha*) into the meaning of the sentence in question, there is no burden of supplying ellipses (*adhyāhāra*). Furthermore, the passage beginning with "In the second Sūtra," etc., is clearly only superficial (*āpātataḥ*). || 16 ||

"If it be argued that [the soul is not eternal] because of the designation of its non-existence, we say no; for [this is said] with reference to another state, as is clear from the remainder of the passage. (Sūtra 1.3.17)

"Is it not the case that even non-existence [is mentioned] in some places? This is the intended meaning: in the passage "this was indeed non-existent" (*asadevedam*), the word *asat* is not a compound. For if one were to say "it was non-existent" (*asadāsīt*), a contradiction would arise. Rather, there are two words: *asaḥ* and *at*. And thus, it is heard in some places that "that which consists of this [world] did not exist. Alternatively, the meaning is: "In the beginning, this world existed as non-existent. And so, in order to maintain the authority of both scriptural passages, in the sentence "Being alone" (*sadeva*), the word *idamagre* is a compound; or else, *idam* is an adjective qualifying *sat*.

Even in the sentence "Ātmā vā idam" (The Self, indeed, this), it must be stated that this is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "this" (*ayam*) and "that one" (*asau*) and "one" (*eka*). And thus, the identity of the world with Brahman is not established by this sentence. Now, [the opponent may object]: "This is inconsistent; for the supplementary passage, 'That which was non-existent, make it existent; let your mind be so,' shows that the aforementioned sentence refers to the cause, and therefore it does not entail the non-existence of the effect. Nor is it correct to say that there is no suspicion of the non-existence of the effect because of the acceptance of the non-difference between cause and effect; for since the acceptance of non-difference is intended to establish the existence of the effect as well, the suspicion of non-existence does not arise from that acceptance of non-difference. [Reply: No.

For it is the result of a great delusion regarding your own position to assert that an opposing prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) cannot arise due to its contradiction with the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), which is determined by the remainder of the scriptural passage; for such an assertion has as its sole fruit the manifestation of a profound ignorance concerning you. Furthermore, the possibility of proceeding with the prima facie argument remains even by adopting the interpretation that "the mind, which was non-existent at the time prior to the creation of those [elements], made itself the existent Brahman. (17)

Although there appears to be a redundancy here with the sūtra "And because of the existence of what follows" (*sattvāccāvarasya*), since the commentary has already cited other words such as "Being indeed" (*sad eva*) and so forth, nevertheless, in the immediately preceding sūtra, the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) interpreted that [word] otherwise. If that were overlooked, one might fall into the error of thinking that even in such a sentence-meaning there is no contradiction whatsoever. To prevent this, the repetition is made. Thus, when the purport of the sentence beginning with "Being indeed" has been described according to the aforementioned method, the previously stated interpretation of the Śruti is not tenable.

This being the case, since it would follow that the initial words [of the Sūtra] are redundant and one would have to accept definitions such as "meaninglessness" (nirarthaka), the proof of that [non-difference] by the previously cited scripture will result as being beyond refutation. Otherwise, since all preceding and subsequent arguments could be subsumed under the word "reasoning" (yukti), or all arguments could be included by the word "etcetera" (ādi) in the phrase "the word 'originating' etcetera," the purposefulness of this specific Sūtra would remain difficult to justify even then. || 17 ||
And like a cloth. || 19 ||

Regarding this, the first [example] is presented by those learned in the tradition to demonstrate the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the inference: "The effect is different from the cause, because even when resting upon it, it is of a greater dimension, just as a hare is [different] from a gnat. The second is presented to demonstrate the fallacy of deviation in that same [inference] regarding the reason of having a distinct mode of action (*vilakṣaṇakāritva*). Such is the stated purpose of presenting the two examples.

Furthermore, because a complete similarity between the illustration and the illustrated is not required, the two illustrations of the rolled-up cloth and the breath do not conflict with the proponents of *vivarta* (illusory manifestation). Thus, the objection—that since the expansion and so forth of the world are not superimposed upon Brahman in the same way they are upon a cloth, and that contraction and expansion are impossible in partless Brahman as they are in a cloth that is rolled up and then spread out—is without merit.
In the *Pādabhūṣaṇa*, a critique of the views of others, composed by the disciple of Raghavācārya Sūri, who was himself a master of the five systems of Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya, and a follower of Śaṅkara.
May this work spread joy in this discernment of the [nine] sentiments.
Whatever Śārīrakabhāṣya was composed by the venerable Śaṅkararūpa Śaṅkara Mahācāryas— who were honored by the noble and free from defects— after careful deliberation,
whatever faults were alleged against it have been refuted by me without exception.
And those very [arguments] have been refuted at every step by means of ill-conceived and illogical constructions.
This work, which serves as an ornament for the first two quarters of the first and second chapters of the Śārīraka [Bhāṣya], has been completed under its truly meaningful title: *Śaṅkarapādabhūṣaṇa*.
Those whose ancestors were renowned for their valor under the name Śaṅkara obtained, from the very beginning, a most excellent reputation as ministers pleasing to the minds of the world;
they whose dwelling place was the city of Bhoga, situated near the shore of the Nīrā river.
They were intent on the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and had set their hopes upon the prowess of the best of the Raghus.
This book, which has attained completion and been inscribed in stone characters, is renowned because it relies upon various authoritative sources.
May that Prāṅvivāka named Bhiḍe, who is established by my own treatise as the supreme refuge,
and Gopāsaluṇa, who bears the name Viṣṇu and is proficient among the devotees of Śiva, both live long.
Thus ends the section concerning the "Underlying Material" (Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa).
This work, titled Śāṅkarapādabhūṣaṇa, is hereby completed.
